item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Just a few days after the Red Sox’ roller-coaster 2026 season came to an end in the Bronx, manager Chad Tracy, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow, and president/CEO Sam Kennedy addressed the media at Fenway Park.
Despite Boston’s impressive 32-5 surge in the summer and mid-year turnaround, the theme of Monday’s press conference was one of disappointment.
“The way it ended Wednesday night in New York was painful and deeply disappointing to all of us,” Kennedy said.
Here are five takeaways from Monday’s presser:
Breslow met with Willson Contreras for two hours after ‘computers’ comment
Beyond the disappointment of the Red Sox’ season coming to a close with a listless showing against the Yankees last week, Wednesday’s postgame press conferences with Red Sox players in New York were rife with grievances and head scratches from a few veterans.
First baseman Willson Contreras raised a few eyebrows when he seemingly insinuated that the Red Sox organization has been too reliant on data and analytics — which he believes doesn’t always translate to success out on the field, especially in October.
“It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” Contreras said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
Breslow was asked directly about Contreras’ comments and whether or not he’s had discussions with the veteran over the state of Boston’s baseball operations.
“I saw Willson’s comments,” Breslow said. “My interpretation is a little bit different than there are clearly things that he wants fixed and changed.”
Before the players went their separate ways to begin the offseason, Breslow said that he had an extended conversation with both Contreras and Tracy on Sunday.
“We met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things,” Breslow said. “Many of those I will keep private just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things.
“Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he’s looking forward to 2027 and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox.”
Tracy says ‘decisions are mine’ with managing pitching staff, roster
Chad Tracy earned Boston’s full-time managerial title this fall after righting the ship with this roster.
But the Red Sox manager found himself in hot water during Boston’s two-game series against New York when it came to quick hooks with his starting pitching.
A strong rotation was a foundational piece in the Red Sox’ success this season. But Tracy opted to pull both Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4.2 innings of work in Games 1 and 2, respectively, against New York.
At the time, both righties had only given up one run and kept Boston in close contests in the Bronx, only for the Yankees to feast on the Red Sox bullpen.
In both games, Tracy immediately turned to lefty Erik Miller to close out the fifth inning — with the southpaw giving up a solo shot to Ben Rice in Game 1 and surrendering an RBI single to Cody Bellinger in Game 2.
Tracy’s approach to Boston’s pitching staff in the playoffs raised questions over whether or not there was a set plan or “script” in place for the Red Sox to turn to their bullpen immediately — rather than let their starters face New York’s line for a third time through the order.
Tracy pushed back against that sentiment, adding that all of Boston’s decisions on the field last week were his and his alone.
“Not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, ‘Use this number right here to decide in this inning,’” Tracy said. “Those decisions are mine. As far as that specific one, my decision. That obviously didn’t go great, and that falls on me.
“Do we have data and analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me saying, ‘You have to do this, this and this?’ Absolutely not.”
Boston’s bullpen was also a strength all year long, only for it to splinter in the postseason. While Tolle and Gray allowed two earned runs over their 9.1 innings of work, Boston’s relievers coughed up 15 earned runs over 6.2 innings.
“Believe me, I see both sides and I don’t need to get too deep into defending this or that because I certainly could have gone the other way with that and that could have gone well,” Tracy said. “We wouldn’t even be having this conversation. But I do trust Sonny Gray and I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well.
“There is a factor of having a really strong bullpen that was pretty heavily left-handed in our sense. Was there scripts? No, there wasn’t anything scripted out. Just games got to certain points where you felt like it was time to go. We didn’t also want to ignore that we had some pretty good arms in our bullpen if we could get there and use those.”
Clearing the air with Gray
Tracy’s decision to pull Gray after just 4.2 innings of work in Game 2 clearly rankled the 36-year-old veteran once Boston’s season came to an end.
“I would have liked to be trusted in that moment,” Gray declared after Boston’s loss on Wednesday.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time,” Gray added after getting the hook after 70 pitches and one run allowed. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked [for Tracy] to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am.”
Despite Gray’s blunt comments — including the pending free agent not exactly committing to a potential return to Boston — Tracy said on Monday that he’s hashed things out with the Red Sox’ top starter this season.
“Yes, I have had a chance to talk to [Gray]. The relationship there is good. Do I think he was wanting to stay out there? Quite obviously,” Tracy said. “But five months of relationship-building. I think there are some things that get painted sometimes, that that [ending] stained it or ruined it. No.”
“I have a very good working relationship with him and have had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year. I was able to talk to him and it (the relationship) is in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings [about] it.”
Offseason needs
While Boston’s pitching was strong for most of the 2026 campaign, its offense left a lot to be desired.
Boston was outscored, 18-2, and outhit, 26-7, in its two-game series in New York. But the Red Sox dealt with inconsistent offense and a dearth of power throughout the 2026 campaign.
The Red Sox closed out the 2026 season ranking 23rd in baseball in runs scored (689) and 26th in home runs (163).
Much like last offseason, Breslow said that Boston needs to prioritize adding more pop to the lineup in the coming months.
“Our offense was inconsistent. We got on base at a decent clip, but we didn’t really slug, didn’t hit a ton of home runs, and I’m not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that we play in,” Breslow said. “So naturally, we’re going to spend some time thinking about how we can improve our offense, particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park.”
“There are a lot of reasons to believe the existing offense should be better in 2027,” Breslow added. “But we’re also going to do everything we can to improve beyond that.”
Injury updates
The 2026 campaign was a lost season for Roman Anthony, who missed over 100 games in the regular season due to a nagging wrist/hand injury — only for it to resurface in the playoffs and keep him out of Boston’s eventual season-ending loss last Wednesday.
Speaking on Monday, Breslow said that he doesn’t expect Anthony to need surgery this winter to correct his ailing injury.
“He’s had a bunch of follow-up appointments, including imaging,’’ Breslow said of Anthony. ”We’re still collecting information, still working through what the right course of treatment is, and at this point, it doesn’t seem as there’s any type of surgical intervention [needed], and that rest is likely the best path to recovery.”
While months of rest didn’t exactly help Anthony fully recover in time for the playoffs, Breslow said that a full offseason for Anthony should help him turn the corner — rather than a few months of intensive rehab in the summertime, as was the case from May through August of this year.
“Yes, he was trying to get healthy,” Breslow said, “but he’s also trying to do everything he could to get back on the field. And when he felt comfortable and confident, he pushed to get back on the field. … He was trying to swing and doing tee work and dry swings as soon as he could, and a couple of times, he tried and had to take a step back and would try again.
“Versus now having this window to rest it completely and make sure we don’t progress to step two until it’s completely clear.
Breslow also shared that Garrett Crochet is “fully healthy” going into the offseason — adding that Boston had no regrets over not trying to rush him back on the mound in August or September.
“There maybe could have been an opportunity to get him back on the field in what would have been an accelerated timeline, but it would have required unnecessary risk to do so, and potentially have longer-term implications,” Breslow said. “So we wanted to make sure that we had checked every box as it related to his return to play, and get his shoulder strength back up to where it was, or even better than it was at any point in 2025 when he pitched a full, healthy season.”

item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy has taken responsibility for the decision to pull Sonny Gray early in the Boston Red Sox's season-ending loss to the New York Yankees. Tracy said the move was his call after Boston fell 9-2 in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series.
Gray was removed with two outs in the fifth inning and Boston trailing 1-0. He had thrown 70 pitches and allowed two runs on six hits with five strikeouts before Erik Miller replaced him.
The decision drew attention because Gray had put together one of the best regular seasons of his career. He finished 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA, 149 strikeouts and a 1.15 WHIP across 29 starts.
Chad Tracy says pulling Sonny Gray in Game 2 was his call.
“The biggest thing, for me, coming into this, was dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper, or with a computer.”
(Via: @NESN) pic.twitter.com/BPW9MTR4Av
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 5, 2026
According to Foul Territory on X, Tracy said the decision was his and that he wanted to dispel the idea that decisions were made before games through a predetermined plan or computer. His comments came after Gray openly expressed frustration with the early hook following Boston's elimination.
Gray said he wanted the chance to face Cody Bellinger for a third time through the lineup. He had held opposing hitters to a .180 average the third time through during the regular season, which was the best mark among qualified American League pitchers.
The decision became more difficult to defend when Miller allowed an RBI single to Bellinger after replacing Gray. The Yankees then broke the game open with a six-run sixth inning, turning a one-run game into a 9-2 victory and completing the two-game sweep.
Boston's season ended after a dramatic turnaround that saw the Red Sox recover from a 32-46 start and make the postseason. They finished 87-75, third in the AL East behind the Tampa Bay Rays and Yankees, before being outscored 18-2 in the Wild Card Series.
Tracy's explanation now provides more context for one of the biggest decisions of Boston's short postseason run. With the Red Sox eliminated, the focus shifts to the offseason and whether the club will continue with Tracy while determining Gray's future after a standout 2026 campaign.
This story was originally published by Athlon Sports on Oct 5, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add Athlon Sports as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Met With Red Sox Manager, Exec for 2 Hours After Comments Following Yankees Loss
Willson Contreras didn't mince words after the Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Round, seemingly taking aim at analytics in particular after Sonny Gray was pulled in the fifth inning of Game 2 despite throwing just 70 pitches and giving up just two earned runs.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do. Because this is baseball," Contreras told reporters. "And the data is here to help us. But at the end of the day, you're gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
TOP NEWS
Aaron Boone Calls Out Yankees Catcher 🗣️
Wells on Getting Thrown Out 👀
Rays Hype Drew Rasmussen
On Monday, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he met with Contreras and manager Chad Tracy and had a constructive discussion.
"We met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things," he told reporters. "Many of those I will keep private just to kind of preserve the relationship that we have. But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things. Willson would be the right person to ask directly, but he spoke very, very highly of his time here, how much he's looking forward to 2027 and the way that he and his family appreciated the Red Sox."
Contreras was not alone in his frustrations regarding the Gray decision, especially considering the bullpen went on to give up another seven runs.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that's a fact," Gray told reporters. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Tracy, meanwhile, said the decision to pull Gray was his and wasn't a predetermined move coming from the front office or analytics department.
"The decisions are mine," he told reporters. "We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information. Everybody has that. I've said this before: Since I've been here, do I sit in the office and talk through who's available throughout the entire season, who's available today, what's the best way to deploy them, who's down every single day? You do that. But not one time since I've been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, use this number right here to decide in this inning. Those decisions, they're mine. So as far as that specific one, my decision that obviously didn't go great. That falls on me. Do we have data, analytics? Of course we do. Everybody does. Is somebody standing there pushing me, saying, 'You need to do this, this, and this?' Absolutely not."
The Gray conversation—and pitching struggles overall during Wild Card Round—has somewhat overshadowed the fact that Boston's offense managed just two runs in the two losses against the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
Aroldis Chapman seguirá con los Medias Rojas de Boston en la MLB. El estelar cerrador cubano estará en 2027 con la franquicia de Massachusetts, luego de pasar exitosamente el examen físico que activa automáticamente su opción de una campaña más a cambio de 13 millones de dólares.
El trámite sella su continuidad en el Fenway Park, salvo un movimiento inesperado de cambio antes del arranque de la próxima temporada.
La permanencia de “El Misil” con los Medias Rojas estaba condicionada a dos requisitos. Además de la evaluación física, la extensión, firmada el pasado agosto, dependía de lanzar 40 entradas en 2026.
Chapman cumplió el primer requisito al sumar su aparición número 40 de la temporada el pasado 15 de agosto, lo que dejó la puerta abierta para completar el trámite.
Su salario base final aún no está definido. Dependerá de su posición en la votación del Relevista del Año 2026, con incentivos que van desde 100 mil hasta un millón de dólares. Si gana el premio de la BBWAA o el Mariano Rivera de Relevista del Año, recibirá un millón adicional.
El pacto original se firmó el 31 de agosto de 2025. Craig Breslow, jefe de operaciones de béisbol del equipo, recordó que esa mañana Chapman ya estaba en el gimnasio, una muestra de la disciplina que ha caracterizado su etapa en Boston.
Aroldis Chapman is now officially under contract to the #RedSox for the 2027 season:
https://t.co/py5A4ZeEVh https://t.co/wIo1jPRNqB
— MLB Trade Rumors (@mlbtraderumors) October 5, 2026
Temporada sólida
A sus 38 años, Chapman completó otra campaña de élite. Terminó la temporada regular con 35 salvamentos en 37 oportunidades, efectividad de 1.92, WHIP de 1.12 y 71 ponches contra 23 boletos en 51.2 entradas, de acuerdo con las estadísticas oficiales.
El holguinero lanzó en 53 juegos y formó con Garrett Whitlock un dúo que sostuvo al mejor bullpen de las Mayores, con 2.99 de efectividad colectiva.
El hito más destacado llegó el pasado 6 de septiembre. En la victoria 3-1 que completó la barrida de cuatro juegos sobre los Orioles de Baltimore, Chapman se convirtió en el noveno lanzador en la historia con 400 salvamentos.
El cubano cerró el juego con un ponche a Christian Encarnacion-Strand con una recta de 101 millas por hora. Después sumó dos más y llegó a 402 para cerrar el casillero de la temporada.
Además, disfrutó de su novena selección al Juego de Estrellas, pero la temporada terminó con una nota amarga. Boston quedó eliminado en la ronda de comodines por segundo año consecutivo, esta vez ante los Yankees de Nueva York en el Yankee Stadium, al caer en dos partidos consecutivos frente a sus eternos rivales de división.
Renacer en Boston
Su llegada a los Medias Rojas en diciembre de 2024 fue una apuesta de bajo riesgo. Firmó por un año y 10.75 millones de dólares y su rendimiento superó las expectativas.
El holguinero se ganó el puesto de cerrador en los entrenamientos primaverales y en 2025 fue elegido Relevista del Año de la Liga Americana.
Hasta mediados de agosto de 2026, en su paso por Boston sumaba 1.50 de efectividad, 0.902 de WHIP, 34.3 % de ponches y 59 salvamentos en 102 entradas.
Chapman debutó con los Rojos de Cincinnati en 2010 y su brazo pronto lo convirtió en una atracción, principalmente por una velocidad más allá de lo común.
Entre las marcas más llamativas en su poder está el lanzamiento más rápido de la historia de las Mayores, de 105.8 millas por hora (170.3 km/h). También domina el liderazgo histórico entre los relevistas al acumular más de 1400 ponches, con más de 14 por cada nueve entradas.
Además, en sus vitrinas exhibe dos anillos de la Serie Mundial (Cachorros de Chicago en 2016 y con los Rangers de Texas en 2023), después de haber defendido las camisetas de los Rojos (2010-15), Yankees (2016-22), Cachorros (2016), Reales (2023), Vigilantes (2023), Piratas (2024) y Medias Rojas (2025 en adelante).
El futuro
Para la gerencia de los Medias Rojas, la continuidad del cubano ofrece estabilidad.
Con Chapman en su róster de la temporada venidera, Boston evitará ahora una carrera por contratar a un cerrador en la próxima agencia libre. No obstante, el club sigue siendo escrupuloso a la hora de firmar a jugadores de avanzada edad, lo que deja en la incertidumbre una extensión para 2028.
Entre sus objetivos personales, Chapman tenía los 400 rescates. Una vez conseguido, le resta solo seguir ensanchando los números que, de acuerdo con la mayoría de expertos, le deben conducir al Salón de la Fama de Cooperstown.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox: Roman Anthony's recovery path is rest, not surgery
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam
item.description: BOSTON — Roman Anthony, who missed more than four months of the season with a finger/hand/wrist injury then was removed from the active playoff roster with a recurrence of symptoms, does not appear to need surgery, the Red Sox reiterated Monday. item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — Roman Anthony, who missed more than four months of the season with a finger/hand/wrist injury then was removed from the active playoff roster with a recurrence of symptoms, does not appear to need surgery, the Red Sox reiterated Monday.
"He's had a bunch of follow-up appointments (in Boston), including imaging," said chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. "We're still collecting information, still working through what the right course of treatment is and at this point, it doesn't seem as there's any type of surgical intervention (necessary), and that rest of likely the best path to recovery."
Anthony was placed on the IL in early May. At the time, it appeared as though he'd be sidelined for a relatively short period of time. However, Anthony experienced several setbacks and it was months before he could successfully grip a bat. Following an extended rehab time spent in Fort Myers, he had about a 10-day rehab assignment split between Portland and Worcester, then returned to the lineup in late August.
But it was later revealed that Anthony was never pain-free upon his return, and the discomfort he experienced intensified in the final few days of the season.
After feeling pain with check swings in his initial at-bat in Game 1, he felt the same sensation in his second at-bat and was removed from the game. The Red Sox took him off the active roster the following morning.
During his recovery from the initial injury, Anthony more than once said doctors told him the problem couldn't be surgically repaired and that rest was the only option.
"I'm going to avoid speaking in absolutes, particularly as one who is not a medical expert," said Breslow. "My understanding is that there's no surgical intervention that is planned or that merits consideration because what (Anthony) said is exactly what we've been told, that we don't even know surgery we would do.
Breslow went on to say that resting the hand in the winter is far different from what it is while a player is rehabbing and attempting to return to play.
"Yes, he was trying to get healthy," Breslow said, "but he's also trying to do everything he could to get back on the field. And when he felt comfortable and confident, he pushed to get back on the field. In the offseason, you can truly think about getting healthy. He was trying to swing and doing tee work and dry swings as soon as he could and a couple of times, he tried and had to take a step back and would try again.
"Versus now having this window to rest it completely and make sure we don't progress to step two until it's completely clear (he's ready)."

According to Jon Heyman of the New York Post, Ramírez is seeking a job as a hitting coach, either at the MLB or minor league level: TOP NEWS Players Who Were Worse Than You Think in 2026 ⚾ Sox Brass Met With Contreras Latest Free Agent Rumors 👂 It is not the first time Ramírez's ag
item.content:encoded:
Manny Ramirez Eyes MLB Coaching Role, Red Sox Legend Hit 555 Career HR
Manny Ramírez was one of MLB's best hitters during his playing career. Now, he's hoping to parlay that accumulated knowledge into a coaching role.
According to Jon Heyman of the New York Post, Ramírez is seeking a job as a hitting coach, either at the MLB or minor league level:
TOP NEWS
Players Who Were Worse Than You Think in 2026 ⚾
Sox Brass Met With Contreras
Latest Free Agent Rumors 👂
It is not the first time Ramírez's agent has let this be publicly known. In fact, it was almost exactly one year ago that Heyman posted the following:
"I'm available to work as a hitting coach for any of the 30 MLB teams," Ramírez said back in May 2025. "I'm confident I can help any team significantly improve their offense."
Ramírez, 54, hit .312 with 2,574 hits, 555 home runs, 1,831 RBI and a .996 OPS during his 19-year MLB career. The two-time World Series champion, 12-time All-Star and nine-time Silver Slugger would assuredly be a Hall of Famer were it not for the three separate positive tests for performance-enhancing drugs during his career.
But there's little doubt the man knew how to swing a bat at the highest level. Whether that would translate to teaching others and helping big leaguers make the necessary adjustments throughout a season is another question entirely.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Should Boston Red Sox Hire Manny Ramirez as a Hitting Instructor?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the Red Sox bringing in franchise legend Manny Ramirez as a hitting instructor. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
For 19 years, Manny Ramirez terrorized pitchers as one of the greatest right-handed hitters of all-time. Now, he's reportedly looking for a job as a hitting coach in Major League Baseball.
"Manny Ramirez is seeking a hitting coach job in MLB, agent Hector Zepeda said," tweeted Jon Heyman of the New York Post on Monday afternoon. "He's so determined to get back in the game he's willing to go to the minors," he continued.
Ramirez spent 19 seasons in the big leagues, hitting .312/.411/.585/.996 with 555 career home runs. He spent eight years with the Boston Red Sox, where he hit .312/.411/.588/.999 with 274 home runs. He won World Series titles with the team in 2004 and 2007 and was named World Series MVP in '04.
If Ramirez, now 54, lands a job as a hitting coach, it would be his first foray into coaching in the big leagues. He spent the 2014 season with the Chicago Cubs Triple-A affiliate, the Iowa Cubs, as a player-coach, where he worked with Red Sox All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras. After the 2014 season, he joined the Cubs front office as a hitting consultant through 2016.
Ramirez was also set to serve as a player-coach for the Sydney Blue Sox of the Australian Baseball League in 2020-21, but uncertainty around the COVID-19 pandemic meant he never appeared in a game.
Should the Red Sox hire him?
The Red Sox did little to answer any questions about the state of their coaching staff, many of whom were working under interim tags, in Monday's end-of-season press conference. However, given his reputation as a clubhouse annoyance and his repeated suspensions for PED use, it seems unlikely any team would take a chance on bringing Ramirez in. It feels especially unlikely that Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, who did not play with Ramirez, would bring in the should-be Hall of Famer as the team increasingly shifts its hitting philosophy to a more analytically based approach.
That said, after third baseman Caleb Durbin turned his season around with an outside hitting instructor and with key pieces like Contreras openly questioning the team's reliance on analytics, what's the risk?
Throughout the season, plenty of questions arose about Breslow and the coaching staff's ability to communicate and connect with the players. At the bare minimum, Ramirez represents a guy who knows what it takes to succeed at the highest level. At best, he's a voice INSIDE the organization to help players who don't feel like they're getting the most out of the analytical approach, like Durbin.
That's not to say they should hand him the keys to the hitting department, but bringing him in as a hitting consultant seems like one of the lowest-risk moves you can make. If it doesn't work out, you simply move on.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox bosses say they’ve met with frustrated veterans since season ended
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: In the immediate aftermath of the Red Sox’s season-ending loss to the Yankees in Game 2 of last week’s Wild Card Series, both Willson Contreras and Sonny Gray — two of the club’s most respected veteran leaders — expressed frustration with the way decisions were being made by the organization. item.content:encoded:
In the immediate aftermath of the Red Sox’s season-ending loss to the Yankees in Game 2 of last week’s Wild Card Series, both Willson Contreras and Sonny Gray — two of the club’s most respected veteran leaders — expressed frustration with the way decisions were being made by the organization.
During Monday’s hour-long year-end press conference, Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy said they’d met with both players to help clear the air.
Breslow said he and Tracy both spoke to Contreras for two hours on Sunday, covering a wide range of topics. Breslow wouldn’t delve into specifics but described the conversations as productive while pushing back on the notion that Contreras wants things fixed and changed.
“We had a great conversation, Trace and I, with Willson yesterday, we met for over two hours and we talked about a host of things, many of those I will keep private to preserve the relationship that we have,” Breslow said. “But it was incredibly constructive and covered a wide scope of things, and Willson would be the right person to ask directly but he spoke very very highly of his time here and how much he’s looking forward to 2027 and the way he and his family appreciated the Red Sox.”
Tracy said he spoke to Gray as well and, while the veteran understandably disagreed with his decision to pull him in the fifth inning of Wednesday’s loss, their relationship is in a good place.
“I didn’t suspect most starters, especially in that case, guys are going to be happy about being pulled. I thought he answered the questions that were asked of him in a very professional manner and yes, I have had a chance to talk to him. The relationship there is good,” Tracy said. “Do I think he was wanting to stay out there? Quite obviously. But five months of relationship building with players and I think there’s some things that get painted sometimes that that’s stained it or ruined it and I have a very good working relationship with him and I’ve had numerous conversations with him throughout the course of the year. But yeah I was able to talk to him, it’s in a fine place, while also understanding his feelings on it.”
Both Gray and Contreras expressed unhappiness about Tracy’s decision to pull the starter early, with Gray telling reporters postgame that he would have “liked to have been trusted in that moment” while Contreras simply zipped his lips when asked.
Contreras was willing to speak more directly on his frustration with the club’s heavy reliance on data and analytics, saying that ultimately teams need experience and veteran players to win games.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game,” Contreras said last week. “You have to do a lot of different stuff, and it’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that’s telling you what to do. Because this is baseball. And the data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you’re gonna have to need experience and veteran guys to win games. And yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but not saying.”

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox provide update on Roman Anthony’s injured hand
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Since aggravating his previous sprain while suffering additional injuries during Game 1 last week, Roman Anthony has had several follow-up appointments and undergone a fresh round of imaging on his right hand. Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said based on those visits, the expectation is Anthony won’t need surgery. “At this point it doesn’t seem that there’s any type of surgical intervention and rest is likely the best path for recovery,” Breslow said. Anthony’s health and the handl
item.content:encoded:
Since aggravating his previous sprain while suffering additional injuries during Game 1 last week, Roman Anthony has had several follow-up appointments and undergone a fresh round of imaging on his right hand.
Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said based on those visits, the expectation is Anthony won’t need surgery.
“At this point it doesn’t seem that there’s any type of surgical intervention and rest is likely the best path for recovery,” Breslow said.
Anthony’s health and the handling of his injury was a consistent focus of the hourlong press conference, with the club’s leaders pressed on whether they knew he was playing through pain, if it would have made sense to undergo additional imaging before he was activated to weigh the risk of a recurrence and if the club is concerned the injury could become a chronic problem.
Over the course of the session Breslow defended the club’s process, saying everyone was on the same page throughout the summer.
“I think we had a pretty good understanding of what the diagnosis was and that Roman was very confident he could contribute, and over the course of a game there would be a swing or two that might give him he’d describe it as a bit of a zinger, and a few seconds later that feeling would subside,” Breslow said. “We wanted to balance Roman’s desire to get on the field and compete and his ability to help us win games with making sure we were doing the medically responsible thing and not trying to put him in any greater danger.”
Breslow added later that there is a big difference between rest during the season while trying to get back and perform and rest in the offseason when you can truly shut it down and allow your body to recover.
As far as other Red Sox injuries are concerned, Breslow said third baseman Caleb Durbin’s pinky is still being evaluated and it remains undetermined if he’ll need surgery.
Garrett Crochet, who missed most of the season with a left shoulder injury, came out of his Wednesday outing feeling good and is positioned for a full healthy offseason. Breslow was asked for clarity on the specific nature of his injury, which has never been disclosed beyond “left shoulder inflammation,” but did not offer a formal diagnosis.
“The imaging that we got revealed some irritation and strain to the shoulder,” Breslow said. “But as we started to peel back the layers it made more and more sense to make sure we were getting this right for the long term as opposed to just getting him back on the field as quickly as we could.”
Extra innings
Breslow confirmed that Aroldis Chapman passed his physical, formally triggering his $13 million vesting option for next season. Breslow said the team hasn’t made a decision on Garrett Whitlock’s $8.25 million club option for 2027. … Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said the club hasn’t made a decision on any of the coaches who were brought up midseason and that a decision on their futures will be made in the coming days. … While Tracy stopped short of declaring Curtis Mead the club’s starting second baseman in 2027, he said that is “broadly our plan.”

item.dc:creator: Ronald José Jiménez
item.description: Willson Contreras tuvo la mejor temporada ofensiva de su carrera en 2026, justo el año en que cambia de aires para los Medias Rojas de Boston y ello le valió para estar entre los finalistas al Premio Hank Aaron. El galardón reconoce al jugador ofensivo más destacado de la temporada regular en cada liga y que este año contó con la particularidad de que Atlanta festejara el aniversario 51 del jonrón 715 de Hank Aaron en el Juego de Estrellas celebrado en el Truist Park. Este año, además, se cumple
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras tuvo la mejor temporada ofensiva de su carrera en 2026, justo el año en que cambia de aires para los Medias Rojas de Boston y ello le valió para estar entre los finalistas al Premio Hank Aaron.
El galardón reconoce al jugador ofensivo más destacado de la temporada regular en cada liga y que este año contó con la particularidad de que Atlanta festejara el aniversario 51 del jonrón 715 de Hank Aaron en el Juego de Estrellas celebrado en el Truist Park. Este año, además, se cumple el aniversario 27 de la creación del premio, que solamente ha visto ganar a tres venezolanos, Miguel Cabrera (dos veces, 2012-2013, Americana), José Altuve (2017, Americana) y Ronald Acuña Jr. (2023, Nacional).
Lee también: Jackson Chourio se unió a un club selecto en postemporada
Las Grandes Ligas nominaron a 20 toleteros y el criollo es uno de ellos. La nominación de Willson Contreras tiene mucho sentido, pues encabezó a los Medias Rojas en jonrones (27), impulsadas (81), OBP (.386), SLG (.516) y OPS (.902), terminó segundo en promedio (.275), tercero en anotadas (68) y cuarto en hits (123).
Además, varios de esos números se irguieron como los mejores de su carrera de 11 temporadas en las Grandes Ligas, como el caso de los cuadrangulares y las impulsadas. Por otro lado, estuvo a tres indiscutibles de su mejor registro (2025) y terminó como la tercera mejor campaña en promedio, tras el .282 de 2016 y el .276 de 2017. Sin embargo, se podría decir que es su campaña con mejor promedio, pues en las dos mencionadas anteriormente tomó menos turnos y conectó menos imparables.
Adicionalmente, en esta corta postemporada para Boston (barridos por los Yankees en el comodín) Willson Contreras sacó la cara por su equipo en seis turnos.
Los otros finalistas junto a Willson Contreras
Pete Alonso – Orioles de Baltimore.
CJ Abrams – Nacionales de Washington.
Yordan Álvarez – Astros de Houston.
Jake Bauers – Cerveceros de Milwaukee.
Randy Arozarena – Marineros de Seattle.
Pete Crow-Armstrong – Cachorros de Chicago.
Junior Caminero – Rays de Tampa Bay.
Elly De La Cruz – Rojos de Cincinnati.
Willson Contreras – Medias Rojas de Boston.
Shohei Ohtani – Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
Yandy Díaz – Rays de Tampa Bay.
Matt Olson – Bravos de Atlanta.
Riley Greene – Tigres de Detroit.
Kyle Schwarber – Filis de Filadelfia.
Ben Rice – Yankees de Nueva York.
Sal Stewart – Rojos de Cincinnati.
Miguel Vargas – Medias Blancas de Chicago.
Fernando Tatis Jr. – Padres de San Diego.
Bobby Witt Jr. – Reales de Kansas City.
Jordan Walker – Cardenales de San Luis.
Los ganadores, uno por cada liga, se anunciarán el próximo miércoles 11 de noviembre. Los ganadores son elegidos por un panel de exjugadores que ganaron el premio y especialistas, así como los aficionados, que tendrán la oportunidad de votar por sus favoritos desde este 5 de octubre hasta el próximo lunes 12.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox manager Chad Tracy owns playoff pitching decisions: ‘My call’
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: Six days after managing his first-ever postseason game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sat in the Fenway Park interview room on Monday morning and answered perhaps the biggest question viewers had while watching the team be outscored 18-2 and swept by the hosting New York Yankees in last week’s Wild Card round: Who made the call? Specifically, who thought it best to pull Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in their respective Game 1 and Game 2 starts? Who thought struggling left-han
item.content:encoded:
Six days after managing his first-ever postseason game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sat in the Fenway Park interview room on Monday morning and answered perhaps the biggest question viewers had while watching the team be outscored 18-2 and swept by the hosting New York Yankees in last week’s Wild Card round:
Who made the call?
Specifically, who thought it best to pull Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in their respective Game 1 and Game 2 starts? Who thought struggling left-hander Erik Miller should relieve the starter not one, but both nights?
Was it the rookie manager, whose interim tag had been removed barely one week before the playoffs? Or was it chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and by extension, the front office, drawing up a pre-game road map for Tracy to follow?
“None,” Tracy said Monday. “The decisions are mine.”
Miller, the trade deadline addition from the Marcelo Mayer deal, had allowed earned runs in four consecutive appearances before a scoreless performance in his last regular-season game on Sept. 24. During that stretch, the 28-year-old southpaw openly admitted he was “working through some stuff.”
“Well, his last outing here at Fenway was exceptional, so he obviously fought it for much of September,” Tracy said, adding that Miller also had a “very good” extended side session before the end of the regular season. “Believe me, I see both sides. I don’t need to get too deep into defending this or that, because I certainly could have gone the other way with that, and that could have gone well, and we wouldn’t be having the conversation.”
Tolle’s pitch count was 83 after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball. He struck out four, walked one, and yielded five hits in his first career postseason start. There were moments in which the rookie left-hander was grinding, but it was a 1-0 game and the Boston bullpen had lost several key arms to injuries, including righties Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten.
Tracy went to Miller after Tolle retired Yankees No. 9 hitter Paul Goldschmidt on one pitch. Ben Rice turned Miller’s third pitch into a solo home run. Though Miller only faced the minimum three batters before Tracy went to righty Greg Weissert, Rice’s homer was the dam-burster moment that led to a 9-0 Yankees win in Game 1.
With earned runs allowed in five of his last six appearances between the regular season and playoffs, it was even more stunning to see Tracy turn to Miller in nearly the same situation in Game 2.
Gray was on even better footing than Tolle, with 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball on just 70 pitches when Tracy went to the mound to take the ball. Though Gray allowed singles to Trent Grisham and Rice to put runners on the corners in the fifth, he also dominated the third time through the order all the regular season, holding opposing lineups to a .180 batting average and .515 OPS, and just seven extra-base hits in 162 plate appearances.
“I felt good, I felt crisp, I felt sharp, I felt like I was just out there competing,” a clearly-frustrated Gray said postgame. “I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact.”
“I would have liked to live-or-die with me in that moment,” Gray added. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
Yet again, it was Miller who emerged from the bullpen. And again, Rice immediately scored to double the Yankees lead, this time on an RBI single by Cody Bellinger. The Red Sox ultimately lost 9-2 to end an even shorter playoff run than the year before, when they at least won Game 1 against the Yankees before dropping the remaining two.
With the entire Boston bullpen well-rested for Game 1, and all of the top arms available for Game 2 after not pitching in the series opener, doubling down on Miller seemed baffling that it could only be a decision handed down from the powers-that-be.
But not according to Tracy.
“We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information,” Tracy said. “I’ve said this before, since I’ve been here, do I sit in the office and talk through … who’s available today? What’s the best way to deploy them? Who’s down? Every single day, you do that.
“But not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, ‘Use this number right here to decide in this inning.’ Those decisions, they’re mine. So as far as that specific one (to pull the starter), my decision, that obviously didn’t go great. That falls on me.”
Tracy added: “Do we have data analytics? Of course we do, everybody does. Is somebody standing there, pushing me, saying, ‘You need to do this, this and this? Absolutely not.”
Tracy in the hour-long press conference again refuted that he was forced into those pitching changes by anyone else and said “the biggest thing for me coming into this was, maybe dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper or with a computer.”
“I do trust Sonny Gray, I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well,” Tracy said. “I think the easiest way to say it is like, it was my call. It was my decision. It went south. Here we are.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox' Craig Breslow eyes offensive upgrades for 2nd straight winter
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam
item.description: BOSTON — The Red Sox' 2026 season was strikingly similar to that of the 2025 season. For the second straight season, the team finished third in its division, accumulated a win total in the upper 80s, and got eliminated by the New York Yankees in the wild card round. item.content:encoded:
BOSTON — The Red Sox' 2026 season was strikingly similar to that of the 2025 season. For the second straight season, the team finished third in its division, accumulated a win total in the upper 80s, and got eliminated by the New York Yankees in the wild card round.
So maybe it shouldn't be much of a surprise that the team's chief baseball officer, Craig Breslow, identified the same offseason priority as (almost exactly) a year ago.
"We're in the initial stages of evaluating the season and thinking about our approach to 2027," said Breslow, "but it's not hard to look at the composition of our roster and recognize our starting pitching was consistently very good. I think by a handful of metrics, I think we had the best bullpen in baseball and the best outfield defense in baseball and an infield defense that showed marked improvement relative to the last few years.
"Our offense was inconsistent. We got on base at a decent clip but we didn't really slug (.398, 20th in MLB), didn't hit a ton of home runs (163, 26th) and I'm not sure that we took advantage of the unique venue that we play in. So naturally, we're going to spend some time thinking about how we can improve our offense, particularly how we build a roster that can thrive at Fenway Park."
Indeed, the Red Sox were just 18th in runs scored at home this past season.
Breslow expressed hope that the Sox could see significant jumps in the power department from a number of players just now entering their prime — Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Caleb Durbin included – while anticipating a full season from Curtis Mead, who was sidelined for more than two months after being injured in his second at-bat with the Sox.
"And also we're going to have to look at what may be available that's not currently on the roster," Breslow said, "and figure out if there's an opportunity down that path as well."
Breslow said much of the same thing after last season, while making the observation that home runs were the quickest and most efficient way to score runs, and noting that home runs become even more valuable in the postseason. A year ago, teams out-homering opponents were 30-5 in the postseason, and the same pattern is already evident this fall.
The Sox acquired their one major offensive upgrade last winter by trading for first baseman Willson Contreras, and that move paid off handsomely. Contreras enjoyed the best year of his career, leading the team in homers, RBI and OPS. He also hit one of two homers the team managed in its brief postseason.
But clearly, more is now needed.
"There are a lot of reasons to believe the existing offense should be better in 2027," said Breslow. "But we're also going to do everything we can to improve beyond that."
The problem, in part, is that the free agent market is a relatively thin one when it comes to run producers. Last year, Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso headed the free agent class; this year, the two best offensive players appear to be Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, neither of whom has that kind of power ceiling.
Another issue: should the Sox acquire another bat, where does that fit into the lineup? The team is currently set at catcher (Adley Rutschman), first (Contreras), second (Mead), shortstop (Trevor Story), third base (Durbin) and the outfield is deep with Rafaela, Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran. There could be a DH opening, but it's possible either Anthony or Duran could fill that.
"It can be a bit of a challenge when you kind of go around (the field) and say, 'We think this player is very good, this player is very good and this player is very good,'" said Breslow, "and we think that there's another step forward for them to take. Sometimes that improvement comes from taking a good player and turning them into a great player. That can be internal development or adding players to the organization who are currently out here right now."
This offseason will offer plenty of variables, not the least of which is the looming Dec. 1 lockout and the uncertainty surrounding what a new collective bargaining agreement might bring.
That could mean a busy November as teams rush to get trades or signings done before the sport closes down – or that same flurry might be postponed until a new CBA is agreed upon.
One thing, however, remains clear: the Red Sox, as currently constituted, aren't good enough offensively. And unless they want a third straight winter in which they pursue improvements, that has to be addressed.
More Red Sox coverage
Read the original article on MassLive. Add MassLive as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [Awful Announcing] David Ortiz declares Padres-Brewers NLDS 'over' after Game 2
item.dc:creator: Matt Clapp
item.description: The National League Division Series between the San Diego Padres and the Milwaukee Brewers is televised on FS1, but one MLB on Fox analyst thinks you have no reason to tune in to the rest of the series. Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio hit a walk-off two-run single vs. San Diego star closer Mason Miller to stun the Padres in a 4-3 Game 2 victory at American Family Field on Sunday. The victory gives Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in the best-of-five NLDS. JACKSON CHOURIO AND THE BREWERS WALK OFF MASON MILLER AN
item.content:encoded:
The National League Division Series between the San Diego Padres and the Milwaukee Brewers is televised on FS1, but one MLB on Fox analyst thinks you have no reason to tune in to the rest of the series.
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio hit a walk-off two-run single vs. San Diego star closer Mason Miller to stun the Padres in a 4-3 Game 2 victory at American Family Field on Sunday. The victory gives Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in the best-of-five NLDS.
JACKSON CHOURIO AND THE BREWERS WALK OFF MASON MILLER AND THE PADRES IN GAME 2!
Milwaukee takes a 2-0 lead in the best-of-five NLDS.
Adam Amin with the call for FS1. ⚾️🎙️ #MLB
https://t.co/d4ZLFBPGEp
— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 4, 2026
The Brewers won an MLB-best 103 games this season and entered the series as the favorites. Taking a 2-0 series lead significantly elevates those chances.
And Fox Sports’ David Ortiz gives the Padres no chance to win the series.
After Sunday’s game, Ortiz told FS1 viewers that the series is “over.”
“I got so much love for San Diego and everything,” Ortiz said. “But golly. You were supposed to win this game. Now you are against the rope. It’s over. I’m sorry.”
“That game tonight says so many things,” Ortiz added. “You were supposed to be flying to San Diego, dancing on the airplane tonight, and you let that one get away from you.”
Game 2 followed a series opener that featured a controversial, unfortunate ninth inning for the Padres in a 3-2 loss.
The Padres now have to win three games in a row vs. a great team that can still use ace Jacob Misiorowski for another in the series. It’s a tall task.
But the Padres have been excellent in their home stadium, putting together a 51-30 record in the regular season at Petco Park before adding a two-game sweep over the Chicago Cubs in the NL Wild Card series. So, if they can find a way to win the next two at home, they can get the series back to Milwaukee for a winner-take-all Game 5.
It’s a long shot, and chances are much better that the Brewers just sweep the series in Game 3. But the series isn’t quite over, and much weirder things happen in baseball.
Game 3 will be on Tuesday night in San Diego at 9:30 p.m. ET on FS1.

item.title: [NBC Sports] Breslow: Crochet is 100 percent healthy for offseason
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski; Garrett Crochet
item.description:
Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow insisted that Garrett Crochet (shoulder) is one hundred percent healthy heading into the offseason.
In his press conference, Breslow mentioned that Crochet felt some initial discomfort in his shoulder back in April, but the Red Sox reviewed his medicals and decided it was best to take a long-term approach to his rehab. Specifically, Breslow said the team focused on strengthening Crochet’s shoulder, not simply get
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow insisted that Garrett Crochet (shoulder) is one hundred percent healthy heading into the offseason.

In his press conference, Breslow mentioned that Crochet felt some initial discomfort in his shoulder back in April, but the Red Sox reviewed his medicals and decided it was best to take a long-term approach to his rehab. Specifically, Breslow said the team focused on strengthening Crochet’s shoulder, not simply getting him healthy enough to pitch in 2026, but hoping to withstand any further injury in future seasons. That also meant changes to his posture and mechanics to smooth over any residual issues that had built up from the shoulder discomfort. The team feels that he is fully healthy heading into the offseason, and there’s a chance his shoulder is now healthier than it was in 2025.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Red Sox believe Roman Anthony won’t need surgery to fix right hand injury - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: After playing through pain upon returning from the injured list, Red Sox outfielder Roman Anthony will not need surgery to fix his right hand/wrist, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said Monday. Instead, the Sox plan to simply have him rest — really, truly rest, in a way that he did not when trying to return during this season. “My understanding is that there’s no surgical intervention at this point, that is planned or that merits consideration,” Breslow said at Fenway Park, during the club’
item.content:encoded:
After playing through pain upon returning from the injured list, Red Sox outfielder Roman Anthony will not need surgery to fix his right hand/wrist, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said Monday.
Instead, the Sox plan to simply have him rest — really, truly rest, in a way that he did not when trying to return during this season.
“My understanding is that there’s no surgical intervention at this point, that is planned or that merits consideration,” Breslow said at Fenway Park, during the club’s end-of-season news conference. “What we’ve been told [is] that we don’t even know what surgery we would do.”
Breslow noted that the Red Sox are “still collecting information” on Anthony, who missed most of the season because of a partially torn ligament in his right ring finger, returned in late August, and dealt with a recurrence of that as well as other hand issues in the first of the Sox’ two postseason games.
The difference moving forward versus Anthony’s summer recovery revolves around urgency.
When trying to get better, Anthony’s ostensible rest included “trying to do everything possible to get back on the field,” Breslow said.
“When he felt comfortable and confident that he could help contribute, he pushed to get back on the field,” Breslow said. “And so he was trying to swing and he was doing tee work and dry swings as soon as he could, and a couple of times he tried and had to take a step back and would try again.”
Now, with no games for six months, there is no such pressure. The offseason provides “this window to rest it completely and make sure we don’t progress to step two until we’re complete,” Breslow said.
As for Anthony playing through pain over the month or so after he returned: The Red Sox knew that once or twice per game, he would experience a “zinger” after swinging, Breslow said, but that discomfort subsided within seconds.
When the pain became unbearable last week, Anthony was done.
“From the standpoint of, did we have a pretty good understanding of what we thought was going on, and was there kind of alignment and everyone on board with the plan? The answer is yes,” Breslow said. “Roman deserves a ton of credit for doing everything he possibly could to get back on the field. … Rest is likely the best path to recovery.”
Chapman locked up
Closer Aroldis Chapman passed his end-of-season physical, triggering his vesting option for 2027, Breslow said. He is due to make $13 million next year as part of the extension he signed in August 2025.
Breslow said the Sox have not decided on Garrett Whitlock’s $8.25 million team option for next season. They have until early November to make that official.
Wait and see for Durbin
The Red Sox don’t know yet whether Caleb Durbin will need surgery to pair his injured left pinkie finger.
“He’s had some initial appointments. He’ll have some follow-up appointments,” Breslow said. “He deserves a ton of credit for what he played through.”
Varitek update
In April, during the coaching staff overhaul, the Red Sox said Jason Varitek would be reassigned within the organization.
For now, though, he is not with the Red Sox in any capacity, team president Sam Kennedy said.
“We’ve connected with each other, but we’ve got no update on that,” Kennedy said. “Look forward to continuing dialogue as we go forward.”
Coaching continuity?
Among the unresolved loose ends in the first week of the offseason: The Red Sox are not ready to reveal the fate of the members of the makeshift coaching staff, thrown together in late April after the firing of Alex Cora.
Manager Chad Tracy is here to stay, having received a three-year contract last month. Those on his staff remain in flux.
“We’re going to continue to talk about that in the coming days,” Tracy said.
Breslow did highlight his satisfaction with the hitting staff: lead hitting coach John Soteropulos (elevated from assistant hitting coach after one month in that role), interim hitting coach Collin Hetzler, interim hitting coach Nelson Paulino, and interim hitting assistant Jack Simonetty.
“We’re confident in the job that John and the hitting group did and confident, I think, in their development backgrounds to be able to continue to push these players,” Breslow said.
Checking on Crochet
Garrett Crochet was among the Red Sox still in town as of Monday, Breslow said, and was due for one last “follow-up” with the medical staff. Breslow noted that after missing five months because of a left shoulder injury, Crochet was “feeling pretty good” in the days after pitching in the Sox’ last game Wednesday and will “go into the offseason full healthy.” … The Red Sox have Curtis Mead penciled in as the second baseman heading into 2027. “That would be, I would say, broadly our plan,” Tracy said. “He was acquired for a reason. You see the numbers that kind of project at least toward a 30-home run season. And adding that, we were really excited about that.” After being acquired from the Nationals, Mead got hit by a pitch and fractured his left wrist in his first game with the Sox … Kennedy, summing up the season: “As painful as the first half of the season was, and as sort of magical and historic as the second half of the summer became, the way it ended Wednesday night in New York was painful and deeply disappointing.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox president of baseball operations Craig Breslow said that he, Willson Contreras, and manager Chad Tracy met “for over two hours [on Sunday] to discuss a host of topics.”

We assume the primary topic was Contreras’ locker room comments after the Game 2 loss to the Yankees, where he insinuated, pretty strongly, that the Red Sox were far too reliant on data to make decisions for the team. Tracy has been roundly criticized for his decision to pull both Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in each of the games. As a first-year manager, Tracy could use the experience and the subsequent meeting with Contreras as a learning experience heading into 2027.

item.title: [FanSided] Cam Schlittler’s Cy Young case is closed, but his biggest Yankees test is next
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: No one ever said pitching for the New York Yankees was fair. If that sounds like recency bias, it really isn't: Schlittler's 215 ERA+ in 2026 — basically, ERA adjusted for ballpark and era, where 100 is league average — is the best ever by a Yankees starter, better than Ford and Guidry and Clemens. His K/9 is fourth behind only three different Gerr
item.content:encoded:
No one ever said pitching for the New York Yankees was fair.
Cam Schlittler wasn't just the best pitcher in the American League this year; he put up quite possibly the best pitching season in franchise history. If that sounds like recency bias, it really isn't: Schlittler's 215 ERA+ in 2026 — basically, ERA adjusted for ballpark and era, where 100 is league average — is the best ever by a Yankees starter, better than Ford and Guidry and Clemens. His K/9 is fourth behind only three different Gerrit Cole campaigns. His WHIP is second to only Russ Ford back in 1910, the height of the dead-ball era. Oh, and he did all that in his first full season in the Majors, while everybody else in New York's star-studded rotation (not to mention Aaron Judge) was spending time on the IL.
It's hard to overstate the burden he shouldered, or just how brilliant he was in shouldering it. In a just world, Schlittler's legacy would already be secure. But instead, he happens to pitch in the Bronx, which means that his watch is just beginning. With his Yankees in a 1-0 hole against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS — coming off a Game 1 in which his offense nearly got no-hit by Drew Rasmussen — New York will once again ask Schlittler to be nearly perfect to keep its season alive.
If he does it one more time, he'll enter some truly rarefied air in the annals of the most storied franchise in baseball. But if he falters, you'll be shocked by just how quickly his own fan base forgets the last six months.
Fair or not, Cam Schlittler's historic 2026 season will be defined by Game 2 start
Those are the stakes that come with pitching in pinstripes. I say this as a Yankees fan myself, one who is often more than a little embarrassed by the way we treat our own. But there's so much riding on this season. While the rise of youngsters like Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr. alongside Schlittler has the future looking pretty bright, you simply don't know how many more bites at the apple you'll have with Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodon healthy, not to mention the fact that Aaron Judge is only getting older and more injury-prone.
If New York can't get over the hump this year, with the AL as wide-open as it is, it'll be fair to wonder if they ever will, at least with this current core. That sounds like an acute case of third-world problems to 28 or 29 other fan bases around the league, but the tristate area is already on edge about not having won it all since 2009 (gasp, the horror). And it'll be almost impossible to get back to the Fall Classic this year if Schlittler doesn't deliver a win in Game 2 on Monday night.
Of course, the Yankees will still have two home games coming, with Fried and Rodon in some order plus Schlittle looming again in Game 5. But beating this Rays team three times in a row, especially after they just got one over on your soon-to-be Cy Young winner, will feel like a Herculean task.
All of which puts the pressure on Schlittler, who, again, has nothing left to prove to Yankees fans or the baseball world at large. He's already authored not just one but two postseason gems against the Red Sox in his young career, so it's not like he can't hack it in the biggest moments. But this fan base has a nasty habit of forgetting about most everything that doesn't result in a title. Schlittler followed up last year's Wild Card series masterclass against Boston by faltering against the Blue Jays with the season on the line. If he does it again, you can bet the narrative will start to grow.
Cam Schlittler could cement his status as the new face of the Yankees
There is a flip side to that coin, though. If Schlittler does manage to carry the Yankees to a win on Monday — and that'll probably be what it takes, given the state of this offense sans Judge and a seemingly revitalized Freddy Peralta going for Tampa — it will instantly take him into the stratosphere.
He's already a beloved Yankee, the best homegrown pitcher this franchise has seen ... well, maybe ever. (If that sounds like blasphemy, New York doesn't have nearly the track record with Hall of Fame arms as it does with Hall of Fame bats.) Elevate them here, stand tall with Judge on the shelf and the offense floundering and Cole falling short in Game 1, and there's a very real chance that it's a passing of the torch moment.
The Yankees have been Judge's team more or less since 2017, when he first broke onto the scene and led a young, scrappy group to Game 7 of the ALCS after missing the playoffs entirely the year prior. And to be clear, Schlittler has a way's to go over a number of years to reach Judge's stratospheric heights. Then again, Judge's postseason track record needs no further explication, and he isn't around right now. Schlittler has everything in front of him at just 25 years old, the kind of star that even the starriest of franchises has seldom seen. Deliver, and the world is his oyster. No pressure.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Five questions Red Sox must answer at year-end press conference
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Monday morning at 11 a.m. three of the top Red Sox’s top decision-makers — president and CEO Sam Kennedy, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy — will speak to the media in their year-end press conference. The annual gathering typically serves to put a bow on the year while also offering the Red Sox a chance to explain what may have gone wrong and how the club plans to improve going forward. Beyond the usual message about how the organization fell short of its championship
item.content:encoded:
Monday morning at 11 a.m. three of the top Red Sox’s top decision-makers — president and CEO Sam Kennedy, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy — will speak to the media in their year-end press conference.
The annual gathering typically serves to put a bow on the year while also offering the Red Sox a chance to explain what may have gone wrong and how the club plans to improve going forward.
Beyond the usual message about how the organization fell short of its championship goals but how the future is bright, there are a number of specific questions the Red Sox need to answer heading into the offseason. Here are a few the club’s leaders will hopefully address.
How can injury communication improve?
If there was one overarching storyline throughout the 2026 season, it was the club’s communication of injuries that often sounded like no big deal at first but wound up being season-long setbacks.
With both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet, the initial prognosis sounded encouraging. Both players were described as day-to-day and Tracy expressed encouragement that both might avoid stints on the injured list. As it turned out, Anthony’s sprained hand and Crochet’s shoulder inflammation were much more serious, and the mismatch between expectations and reality prompted a lot of blowback upon both the players and the club that could have been avoided if the severity of the injuries were laid out clearly up front.
Did the club really think the injuries were no big deal at first, only to learn later they were serious? If that’s the case, that’s a problem in and of itself. The alternative is the club knew both were looking at long IL stints all along, in which case the club owes its fans an explanation for why the messaging was so off base.
Why didn’t Anthony get imaging before return?
Speaking to reporters after being ruled out for Game 2 on Wednesday, Anthony spoke at length about his hand injury and how it was never 100% even after his return in late August.
But one record scratch moment came when Anthony was asked when the last time he’d underwent imaging was prior to his visit to the hospital earlier that morning.
“It was before I was in Fort Myers,” Anthony said. “So it’s been a while.”
Anthony’s rehab was transferred from Boston to Fort Myers in early July, around which point he also flew to Atlanta to see a hand specialist. If that was the last time his hand was imaged, that means more than a month passed before he began his rehab assignment in Portland on Aug. 18. He then spent almost two weeks ramping up before returning to the big league club on Aug. 30.
Time was of the essence, yes, but with a player as important as Anthony, wouldn’t it make sense to have all the information possible before putting him back on the field and risking a recurrence?
What’s done is done and Anthony will now have somewhere in the ballpark of five months (possibly more) to get his hand right, but it will be interesting to hear the club’s perspective on this.
What is status of coaching staff?
The Red Sox provided needed clarity about their future just prior to the postseason when they announced the interim tag was removed from Tracy’s title and that Breslow’s options were picked up, ensuring the two men will be leading the organization through the remainder of the decade.
But the rest of Tracy’s coaching staff remains in flux.
When Breslow first cleared house, firing former manager Alex Cora and a wide swath of his staff, the Red Sox scrambled to fill all the vacancies midseason. The hitting staff in particular saw wholesale changes. Newly elevated hitting coach John Soteropulos was only a month into his first season on a big league staff and several of his new assistants had limited experience at any level.
Obviously the group made the most of an extremely difficult situation and helped the Red Sox engineer a remarkable turnaround, but should everybody return? A case could be made that the organization would benefit from a proper offseason hiring process, and Tracy and Breslow will hopefully shed light on how they plan to proceed this offseason.
What is club’s top offseason priority?
It should go without saying that the Red Sox’s offense needs to improve, but how?
Will the Red Sox favor a right or left-handed bat? Will the focus be on the infield? The outfield? Would the club consider a full-time designated hitter? How might that impact some of the incumbent players, some of whom the club will inevitably have to move?
And will free agency be the preferred avenue this winter? Or will Breslow continue his trend of aggressively working the trade market?
Don’t expect Breslow to show his whole hand on Monday, but what he does say should be illuminating.
Message to frustrated fans
Right now the Red Sox are in a weird place. They pulled themselves out of a deep hole, gave fans an exciting summer of baseball and fought their way back to the playoffs. But then once the postseason began they got boat-raced by the Yankees in the wild card round, leaving them effectively right back where they left off last year.
This season wasn’t a failure, but it certainly wasn’t a success, and it’s hard to blame fans who feel like the club effectively spent the whole year spinning its wheels.
With a lockout looming and uncertainty hovering over the sport as a whole, those fans deserve real assurances from the Red Sox that better days lie ahead, and concrete reasons why.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox president of baseball operations Sam Breslow said that Roman Anthony (hand) “likely doesn’t need surgery and rest is likely the best path to improvement.”

Normally, we’d be happy that a player doesn’t require surgery; however, Anthony took three months to rest his hand this season and then reaggravated his injury during the final game of the regular season. Hopefully the longer layoff in the offseason will produce more healing, but this will certainly cloud his outlook heading into 2027. If Anthony does return healthy and is able to play a full season for the Red Sox, he could be one of the bigger bargains in fantasy baseball next year.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Brutal Chad Tracy quote on Erik Miller move is exactly what Willson Contreras warned about
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: Red Sox Nation left the Wild Card round with more questions than answers after being embarrassed by the Yankees. Following the Game 2 loss, fans were left heavily questioning manager Chad Tracy's decision-making, especially with regard to his management of the bullpen. The quotes that followed the game didn't help his case. The moment that really got fans riled up was following Sonny Gray's departure in the fifth inning. With two outs and runners on first and third, Tracy handed the ball to Erik
item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Nation left the Wild Card round with more questions than answers after being embarrassed by the Yankees. Following the Game 2 loss, fans were left heavily questioning manager Chad Tracy's decision-making, especially with regard to his management of the bullpen. The quotes that followed the game didn't help his case.
The moment that really got fans riled up was following Sonny Gray's departure in the fifth inning. With two outs and runners on first and third, Tracy handed the ball to Erik Miller in relief. In Game 1, Tracy did the same thing when taking Payton Tolle out in the fifth inning, and Miller immediately gave up a left-on-left home run. In Game 2, with lefty Cody Bellinger at the plate, the scuffling (regressing?) Miller allowed an RBI single, giving New York a 2-0 lead.
Fans were rightfully upset by the decision to trust Miller again. Not only had the lefty struggled down the stretch in the regular season, but he'd just shown the game before that just didn't have it. In the postgame press conference, Tracy tried to justify his move.
Chad Tracy only made himself look worse with his reasoning to use Erik Miller in Game 2 of the Wild Card
"I think, where we were at in today's game, we pretty clearly knew who we were going to throw," Tracy said in response to being asked about bringing on a lefty to face Bellinger, who hits lefties well. "Those are the best ones we have to offer, so it was pretty obvious we were going to be aggressive..."
What it sounds like Tracy is referencing is a game script. That if the Sox were at a certain point in the game, with a certain score, it was predetermined that Erik Miller was going to be the man called upon.
That was exactly what Willson Contreras was talking about in his postgame comments. The veteran first baseman lamented the Sox approach to the games, saying they relied too heavily on analytics and didn't have any feel for the flow of the game.
You can add Sonny Gray's comments in here, too. He mentioned hoping for more trust in the moment he was pulled from the game. He also talked about being one of the best pitchers this season when facing a lineup for the third time (which was true). Anyone who's followed baseball recently knows that analytics-heavy teams don't like pitchers facing a lineup for the third time.
What happened in the game, plus the quotes after, has left Red Sox fans scratching their heads as to what changed. In the middle of the season, it felt like the whole team was running on feel for the game. They pinch-hit in the perfect moments, even if it didn't feel right. They would allow pitchers to work through jams on trust.
Now, Red Sox Nation heads into the offseason questioning the ability of their newly extended manager. They are questioning how much autonomy he actually has from the front office. These questions are going to loom over the entire offseason and into next season.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox insider reveals Willson Contreras drama isn't players' first mutiny of 2026
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: A wild storm of news surrounding the Boston Red Sox, Driveline, and Driveline founder Kyle Boddy has come out in the days following the Red Sox Wild Card Game 2 loss to the New York Yankees. Fans were shocked to hear postgame comments from leaders in the clubhouse pushing back against manager Chad Tracy and CBO Craig Breslow after the team's mentality all season, and reporters who dug further have now revealed this wasn't the first time the fissure affected the club. The quotes started with Will
item.content:encoded:
A wild storm of news surrounding the Boston Red Sox, Driveline, and Driveline founder Kyle Boddy has come out in the days following the Red Sox Wild Card Game 2 loss to the New York Yankees. Fans were shocked to hear postgame comments from leaders in the clubhouse pushing back against manager Chad Tracy and CBO Craig Breslow after the team's mentality all season, and reporters who dug further have now revealed this wasn't the first time the fissure affected the club.
The quotes started with Willson Contreras, who pushed back against the Red Sox heavy use of analytics to drive in-game decisions. Those comments lined up with Sonny Gray pointedly saying he wished he was given more trust to get out of the jam he found himself in in the fifth inning of the game.
After the team seemed so close-knit during the regular season, always hyping each other and Chad Tracy up, to see comments immediately pushing back against the Manager and CBO post-game was a shock. According to MassLive's Sean McAdam, it's not the first time the clubhouse has pushed back against the organization this season
Red Sox players have seemingly been unhappy with the organization for much longer than the fans knew
In a State of the Team article published on October 2, McAdam referenced the fact that pushback from the players in the clubhouse earlier in the season was what led to the team severing ties with Driveline founder Kyle Boddy. There was a big to-do when it was announced that Boddy was no longer a member of the organization, with fans who had lamented the Driveline approach and thought it was ruining the hitting celebrating his departure. McAdam's piece originally referred to the players' push towards "severing ties with Driveline," but was edited to target Boddy specifically.
Boddy pushed back on the article, though.
Posting a reply to Section 10's Tyler Milliken, who posted the passage from McAdam's article to X, Boddy wrote, "This report is inaccurate for several reasons." He referenced that he was never part of Red Sox player development; he was with the Baseball Sciences and Research and Development departments, and that he left Boston due to a conflict of interest with his work with a team in Japan.
Two things can be deduced from this that are likely true in some way. The Red Sox player didn't like Boddy's involvement with the team. Just because he wasn't with player development doesn't mean he wasn't around the players and trying to provide tips they didn't appreciate. Boddy is probably trying to save face. He could have chosen the Japanese team over the Red Sox because he knew the Red Sox may have been trying to get him out the door anyway.
Red Sox Nation will likely never know the true answer as to what happened unless sources from inside the front office decide to shed light on what happened, which would seem unlikely. What is known is that the players have been unhappy with the team's heavy analytical approach.
This seems like something that could start to affect the team. As Milliken pointed out on X, there are still plenty of former Driveline employees working with the team, including John Soteropulos, the Sox's hitting coach. If free agents don't like the approach they are seeing from the team, or have a problem with Driveline, Boston may now be a place free agents stay away from.
