item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Red Sox-Jarren Duran Outlook Just Got Much More Complicated
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have a decision to make with outfielder Jarren Duran this offseason. If you're a Red Sox fan who has been following the club over the last few years, or simply a baseball fan in general who has followed trade rumors, you've likely seen Duran's name a lot. His name was out there as a trade candidate before the 2025 season, ahead of the 2025 trade deadline, before the 2026 season and before the 2026 trade deadline. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have a decision to make with outfielder Jarren Duran this offseason.
If you're a Red Sox fan who has been following the club over the last few years, or simply a baseball fan in general who has followed trade rumors, you've likely seen Duran's name a lot. His name was out there as a trade candidate before the 2025 season, ahead of the 2025 trade deadline, before the 2026 season and before the 2026 trade deadline. In every scenario, the Red Sox kept the speedster.
The offseason is now here for Boston and there surely will be trade chatter again with the Red Sox still having a surplus of talented outfielders. Plus, Duran just had the worst offensive season of his career to this point at the same time. The 30-year-old has two more seasons of team control beyond the 2026 season and arbitration is going to play a big role this offseason in the decision-making process. On Friday, MLB Trade Rumors released its salary estimates for arbitration-eligible players and had Duran at $11.1 million. When it comes to projecting arbitration salaries, MLB Trade Rumors is considered to be among the very best in the business.
What Should Boston Do?
Now, of course, nothing is guaranteed at this exact moment about that $11.1 million number. But if that's the direction Duran's contract is going to go, it's going to make a decision more difficult this winter. In 2026, Duran made $7.7 million and batted .207 with a .266 on-base percentage. Now, of course, his 20 homers, 69 RBIs and 21 stolen bases were good. But those batting average and on-base percentage numbers are almost unplayable.
There's no denying Duran's talent. When he's at his best, he's a five-tool player. But the 2026 season wasn't his best. In 2024, he was a 9.0 WAR player. In 2025, he was a 4.9 WAR player in what was viewed as a somewhat down year. In 2026, he was a 0.4 WAR player. It's going to be hard to argue for the increase to a number in the range that MLB Trade Rumors projected with two straight years of regression. Plus, now Duran is 30 years old.
The deadline to tender contracts is the last Friday before Thanksgiving each November. This year, that day falls on Nov. 20. If the Red Sox non-tender Duran, he would simply enter free agency. If the Red Sox tender him a contract, then that's when this number — or something similar — will come into play. For a club that needs to add more power, shelling out that much cash to Duran would be a lot. Also, a price tag that high could be difficult to trade after he just had a difficult season.
When it comes to Duran, the first decision that's going to come is tendering — or non-tendering — him. If they were to non-tender him, they save the cash but get nothing in return. It's a difficult call, to say the least.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com
Follow patmcavoy

Boston announced that Gasper had a successful repair of his right distal biceps tendon. Dr. Matthew Leibman performed the procedure at Mass General Brigham in Boston.
Red Sox announce: Mickey Gasper underwent a successful Distal Biceps tendon repair. The procedure was performed by Dr. Matthew Leibman at MassGeneral Brigham in Boston, MA.
— Chris Cotillo (@ChrisCotillo) October 2, 2026
Gasper's injury occurred during Boston's Sept. 25 game against the Chicago Cubs. He started behind the plate before leaving in the sixth inning with discomfort in his right biceps.
Looks like something was barking for Mickey Gasper on this swing... not good. pic.twitter.com/WoxWQhDF7F
— Tyler Milliken (@tylermilliken_) September 25, 2026
The injury ended his regular season and kept him off Boston's roster for its American League Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees.
Gasper, 30, enjoyed his most productive major league season to date in 2026. He appeared in 67 games and hit .251 with 10 home runs and 24 RBIs in 225 plate appearances.
He also posted a .357 on-base percentage and .466 slugging percentage.
Gasper is expected to need approximately four to six months to recover from the procedure, per a tweet from Tim Healey. That timeline could make his availability for the start of Boston's 2027 season uncertain.

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox's Wilyer Abreu Gets Shocking Bargain $4.6 Million Contract Update
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason. It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like. There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration. They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitratio
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason.
It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like.
There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration.
They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitration, if they choose to tender them contracts.
One of the biggest names on that list is Wilyer Abreu, and MLB Trade Rumors writer Matt Swartz has projected values for all the Boston arbitration eligible players.
For Abreu, the number comes out to be quite the bargain.
Wilyer Abreu Contract Projection
The MLBTR projection for Abreu’s salary for the 2027 season comes in at $4.6 million.
For a player with the power, glove and throwing arm of Abreu, it certainly seems like a massive bargain.
That doesn’t consider everything that goes into arbitration, though.
Each player that reaches the major leagues via the minor leagues has six years of club control once they reach the majors.
The first three years have a salary based on the collective bargaining agreement, and they’re considered the pre-arbitration years.
Years four through six of a player’s time with a team are the arbitration years. In each of those offseasons, a player is eligible to go to salary arbitration to determine what he’s paid the following season.
The arbitration process features the team submitting a value and the player submitting one, and the independent arbitrator comes to a conclusion on which one wins out.
Teams and players these days often negotiate in advance to avoid actually going to what can be a contentious hearing, but the value they come out with will still end up close to what it would’ve been in arbitration.
All that said, it matters which year a player is in for the sequence — and this is only Abreu’s first arbitration year. Generally, the first arbitration year comes with the lowest salaries, and they rise in each of the two subsequent years, even if the player is viewed as having exactly the same value each season.
So for Abreu, no matter what he did this season, he wasn’t going to end up with a giant arbitration value.
The Red Sox could always look to give him a higher-paying contract extension and buy out some of his eventual free agent years, but for now, Abreu is headed for arbitration.
Other Red Sox in Arbitration
The list of 17 Red Sox heading to salary arbitration is long.
The full list is: Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Jarren Duran, Eli White, Kutter Crawford, Connor Wong, Romy Gonzalez, Triston Casas, Andruw Monasterio, Zack Kelly, Greg Weissert, Wilyer Abreu, Erik Miller, Justin Slaten, Jahmai Jones and Tyron Guerrero.
If a team chooses not to tender a player a contract, they instead go right to free agency.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Craig Breslow started building the 2027 Red Sox in 2026
item.dc:creator: Mike Carlucci
item.description: The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card series against the Yankees was probably the worst way for the 2026 season to end. Everything that was a problem at any point - struggles to score runs, the bullpen, injuries - all happened at the same time and within a matter of minutes. Two games in a row ended the Red Sox season. This wasn’t the plan. As all the Sox players returned from the WBC to Fort Myers, many riding hot streaks, this looked like a team ready to rocket. Yes, there were questions entering the season. But there were answers that hadn’t been fully formed yet.
After the 2025 season, the Sox were desperate for infield help. Trevor Story, not a guarantee of health or success himself, since arriving in Boston, was coming off a tremendous year, his best for the Red Sox. The rest of the infield was a question mark. Third base was more-or-less vacant after Alex Bregman opted out. Second base was going to be a battle with the future potential of Marcelo Mayer as a leading contestant. First base? Triston Casas? Maybe? Catcher, using the more generous definition of infield, was a tandem based on Carlos Narváez hitting in 2025 and Connor Wong, who couldn’t hit at all. There were at least two guys, which was more than could be said about first base.
Craig Breslow looked at the free agent market. He looked at the trade market. He looked at his own farm system. And in two phases he built the roster that he would live or die with.
We know about phase one. Caleb Durbin was acquired from the Milwaukee Brewers. Willson Contreras was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals. Isaiah Kiner-Falefa was signed to platoon (kinda) with Mayer.
On the free agent market, the Red Sox went in the opposite direction. The promise/hope was two bats. And they passed on Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, Bo Bichette etc. Aside from Contreras there were no big bats.
What Durbin would share with Willson, besides become Mini Bowser to his Bowser, was control. Contreras was guaranteed to be in town through 2027 with an option for 2028. Durbin will not hit free agency until the 2030s. The same with Mayer. Ranger Suarez, on the other side of the ball, also was signed long-term.
As it would turn out Willson Contreras would not even sniff competition from Triston Casas, who would face a series of injuries that would cost him the season. Not that anyone was worried about having too many first basemen. Caleb Durbin would start off slow with the bat, glacial even, but provide solid defense. He’d go on to set a new career high in home runs while, likely, competing for a Gold Glove.
Marcelo Mayer would underperform and then get hurt. Carlos Narváez would revert to his reputation as a bat-second player. While Connor Wong would provide some offense in a bounce-back season, the catcher tandem as a whole was underwater.
Phase two would be at the deadline. With Durbin rounding into form as The Durbinator, Breslow and his team set their sights on second base and catcher. Turning Connelly Early into Curtis Mead gave them another second baseman with control for years to come. And while the sample size is small, Mead hit 17 home runs in just 87 games. Adding a 30-homer threat to second base would be a tremendous pillar of the offense. Mayer would be traded separately, Mead would get hurt, but the plan was in place.
Similarly, the massive all-in prospect trade for Adley Rutschman was for 2026 and 2027. Connor Wong isn’t a free agent until after the 2028 season so catcher is set for another year and they have time to evaluate Rutschman or find a replacement before 2028. For Breslow’s plan through this summer, when he didn’t know he’d be extended, that’s all that mattered. Build then best team for what could be his last season if they struggled.
Entering 2027 the Red Sox have two catchers. They have an entire starting infield, plus top prospect Franklin Arias. They have Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu (plus control of Jarren Duran, and Masataka Yoshida, and Kristian Campbell) in the outfield.
The rotation has Payton Tolle, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suarez, and Jake Bennett. Boston holds an option on Sonny Gray that he can opt out of, but potentially the entire rotation is headed back for 2027. Starters 6-10 might be a concern, but for a healthy Opening Day major league roster, Breslow took care of that already.
We never actually got to see this team assembled together in 2026. Even if Curtis Mead came into the last game of the season while Garrett Crochet was on the mound, Roman was out. This year, unless there is a big trade to accommodate a move, the Hot Stove season won’t be the same. The roster is basically set. Did Breslow see the lockout as an obstacle? Maybe! He might have been thinking that teams would scramble to make moves before and after and he’d be set. For a team that was seeing it’s window open in 2025, it seems too intentional to put together the whole thing one year in with really only the Story to Arias transition as a big roster move to facilitate.
The performance of the team in 2026 was up and down, but overall we saw a number of good years from this group - Tolle, Abreu, Contreras, Rafaela, and Durbin all provide reasons to be optimistic. Roman Anthony had a good run around the hand injury. Six months off sure would be nice to let that heal. There’s reason to think 2027 can be fun. Maybe distributed a little better too.
Your Opening Day 2027 Boston Red Sox:
C: Rutschman, Wong
1: Contreras
2B: Mead, Sogard
SS: Story, Arias
3B: Durbin
OF: Roman, Rafaela, Abreau, Duran (if he’s not moved/non-tenderd), Campbell
DH: Yoshida

item.description: Los Medias Rojas de Boston fueron barridos en la serie de comodines ante los Yankees de Nueva York, luego de una temporada que parecía para el olvido. Pero entre las cosas a destacar de este equipo fue la incorporación de Willson Contreras para el 2025 desde los Cardenales de San Luis. El criollo, que se adueñó de la primera base, demostró su capacidad ofensiva y logró dejar su huella siendo la bujía del equipo. Lee también: Willson Contreras, contundente tras la eliminación El oriundo de Puerto
item.content:encoded:
Los Medias Rojas de Boston fueron barridos en la serie de comodines ante los Yankees de Nueva York, luego de una temporada que parecía para el olvido.
Pero entre las cosas a destacar de este equipo fue la incorporación de Willson Contreras para el 2025 desde los Cardenales de San Luis. El criollo, que se adueñó de la primera base, demostró su capacidad ofensiva y logró dejar su huella siendo la bujía del equipo.
Lee también: Willson Contreras, contundente tras la eliminación
El oriundo de Puerto Cabello lideró dentro del conjunto el departamento de cuadrangulares (27) y empujadas (81), fue segundo en promedio de bateo (.275) y tercero en anotadas (68). Contreras fue el bateador más constante y completo de la organización, siendo esta, incluso, su mejor campaña en los 11 años que tiene en el “Big Show”.
Además, en el juego dos del comodín ante los Yankees lo volvió a demostrar con un cuadrangular solitario a la altura del sexto capítulo, aunque no fue suficiente para darle la victoria a los patirrojos.
«Hay muchas cosas que mejorar en cada área», comentó Contreras. «Ves el juego, y tenemos que mejorar corriendo las bases, controlando a los robadores. Tenemos que hacer muchas cosas diferentes y no es suficiente cuando tienes talento o tienes datos o tienes computadoras diciéndote qué hacer».
Esas fueron las palabras del inicialista de Boston luego de ser eliminados.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Was Red Sox manager Chad Tracy right to remove Sonny Gray from Game 2 against the Yankees?
item.dc:creator: Jacob Roy

item.content:encoded:
Baseball is a game of numbers. It’s played on the field, with balls and bats and gloves, but every action, decision, and outcome is measured by a number. Those numbers are presented to us during broadcasts, in gambling ads, and by people like me on Twitter and in pieces here on OTM. Most of the numbers we see are presented without context.
Just this week, there was plenty of chatter about how Payton Tolle has reverse splits and performs better against righties than he does against lefties. If you say that Tolle stats against righties are superior to those against lefties, you are correct. If you claim that opponents should start lefties against Tolle for that reason, citing that stat as evidence, you’d be a little bit off base.
In short, Tolle’s stats against lefties were worse than those against righties because he only throws to the best left-handed hitters. If he faced a lineup of nine lefties, he’d rack up strikeouts and groundball outs because of the pitches he has at his disposal. Tolle isn’t the point of this piece, though, so I digress.
Another example of this came after the final game of the season. The Red Sox bullpen got caved in by the Yankees, and the season ended in embarrassing fashion. During the postmortem, Sonny Gray, who was pulled after just 4.2 innings and 70 pitches, expressed his displeasure at not being allowed to continue. He said that he’s the best pitcher in the American League at facing a lineup for a third time.
His numbers facing hitters for a third time are in fact excellent: .515 OPS against, 21.6% strikeout rate, 6.8% walk rate, and a .180 batting average in 162 plate appearances across 28 games this season. Despite this, Gray wasn’t allowed to see Cody Bellinger for a third time; Erik Miller came in and gave up a run, and the game snowballed from there, ending the Red Sox season.
If you read my work, you know I like numbers. I do my best to provide context and try to blend the stats with on-field applications, but I admit that I tend to believe what the numbers say even if they go against conventional wisdom. Those choices that go against conventional wisdom have come to be known as “analytics”. If people don’t agree with something, they blame “analytics” without knowing what information was actually used in that decision.
In this case, the consensus was that Gray was removed because “analytics” say that seeing a lineup for the third time is a disadvantage. The numbers presented above disagree with that sentiment, but the Boston Red Sox, who pay people to research these types of things, aren’t making decisions based on slash lines in 150 plate appearance samples. Still, the decision was, at least in some part, motivated by statistics.
This piece is not in defense of Chad Tracy, Craig Breslow, or anyone else who might have had a hand in the decision-making process or game planning. In fact, I’ll go as far as to say that I staunchly disagree with the decision. I didn’t have a suite of statistics at my disposal at the time, but I thought Gray had a better chance of getting the out than Miller. I actually messaged the rest of the OTM staff and said: “So this is insane, right?” Before the game, I published a piece on how the Red Sox needed Sonny Gray to go deep into the game, for the sake of both Game 2 and a potential Game 3. Even after looking at the numbers that I’ll share momentarily, I disagree with the decision, although that’s easy to do in hindsight.
Instead of supporting or tearing down the decision, what I’m trying to do here is reverse-engineer the thought process and provide some context, because despite what sports talk radio or faceless Twitter accounts might tell you, it is much more nuanced than “third time through the order bad”. Let’s do it.
I’ll set the scene. It’s the fifth inning with the Yankees leading, 1-0. Trent Grisham has reached on a single to start the inning, and swapped places on the bases with Austin Wells, who grounded out to second base but beat the throw from Trevor Story to break up the double play. Ryan McMahon struck out on a good sweeper, and Ben Rice singled on a hard ground ball through the infield to move Wells up to third base. After 70 pitches and one earned run, Gray walked off the mound.
The first thing I’ll look at is Bellinger’s other at-bats against Gray. In his first trip to the plate, he roped a first-pitch sinker to Nick Sogard, who made a great pick to get the out. His second time up, he grounded out again, this time after fouling off three two-strike pitches and spitting on a good sweeper to his back foot. If you’re judging based on those two matchups alone, I could understand the decision to not give Bellinger a third crack at Gray. Bellinger looked like he was seeing the ball well.
Next, let’s look at how Gray approached the lineup to that point.
Against the eight lefties in the Yankees’ lineup, Gray used his four-seam and sinker a combined 59% of the time. The rest of his arsenal was made up of 12 sweepers, 10 curveballs, and three changeups. The fastballs were in the zone (~60% zone rate on both the four-seam and the sinker), while all three of his secondary pitches returned zone rates between 20% and 33%. While that might seem intuitive — fastballs in the zone, putaway pitches below it — that’s not always the case for Gray. He’s usually willing to flip his curveball in for called strikes, and occasionally does the same with his sweeper. On Wednesday, the plan was clearly to attack with fastballs for strikes, and breaking balls below the zone.
The Yankees’ lefties had the second-highest hard-hit rate against in-zone breaking balls from righties this season, as well as the seventh-highest barrel rate. They had the second-highest whiff rate, but Gray’s breaking balls didn’t miss bats in the zone this season. With those statistics in mind, it’s likely that Gray wasn’t going to change his game plan.
Now let’s look at the fastballs. The third time through the lineup, their performance seriously suffers. Entering the postseason, he threw his four-seam and sinker each about 18% of the time. He also used his cutter 15% of the time, but didn’t throw a single cutter to lefties on Wednesday and used it sparingly in his final start of the regular season, so it appeared to be removed from his game plan. The fastballs that he did use weren’t nearly as effective as they were early in games. The shape and velocity held, but the results did not. His four-seam ideal contact rate jumped from 40% to 56%, as the pitch found the middle of the plate often.
The sinker returned weak contact, but that was likely because the zone rate dropped from 60% the first two times through to 40% the third time through. Because of this, the called strike rate plummeted, and the strike rate fell to near 50%.
His breaking stuff wasn’t much better. The curveball had a huge swinging strike rate and chase rate, but when hitters did connect, it was hammered to the tune of a 67% ideal contact rate. The sweeper, his best whiff pitch, saw its chase rate drop 15% the third time through, thanks to bigger misses off the plate.
Bellinger is an excellent breaking ball hitter. Gray’s fastballs lose effectiveness later in games, and hitters don’t expand the zone as frequently against his sweepers. If those are your cards, you probably want to fold that hand in favor of another. The card that Tracy chose to play is a whole other can of worms, but there was a case for Gray to be removed.
If you read this and thought, “the analytics have gone too far, who cares that Gray’s sweeper is less effective the third time through the order it’s playoff baseball you pitch with your nuts not your arm blah blah blah”, I don’t blame you. As I wrote this, I questioned if I was too in the weeds myself, and still would have probably rolled the dice with Gray. Regardless of whether you agree or disagree with Gray’s early exit, I hope this provided some insight into what the team might have been thinking, because it really is deeper than blanket truths discovered by “analytics” that have been parroted 1,000 times by people who think Billy Beane ruined baseball.

item.content:encoded:
After beginning the season 32-46, the Boston Red Sox went on a 32-5 run over the summer to go from the bottom of the American League standings to safely in a wild-card spot.
However, after that streak, the Red Sox struggled in the second half of August and September. They ended up being swept in the AL wild-card series by the New York Yankees. For Boston to go on the run they went on with the injuries they had, they needed some players to step up, and that was the case.
One of those players was right-handed pitcher Sonny Gray. When Garrett Crochet went down in April with an injury, he became the de facto ace for manager Chad Tracy. However, as well as how Boston played as a team, there were some players who were disappointments. Joel Reuter of Bleacher Report listed each MLB team’s biggest surprise and disappointment. For Boston, their biggest disappointment is not a surprise.
Jarren Duran Tabbed as Boston Red Sox Biggest 2026 Disappointment
One player who took a step back was outfielder Jarren Duran. It was just two years ago that he was the All-Star Game MVP. This season in 151 regular season games, he slashed .207/.266/.361 with 20 home runs and 69 runs driven in. He stole 21 bases, but his WAR was eye-opening for a 20/20 player.
“There have been 527 individual 20/20 seasons in MLB history, and Duran’s 0.4 WAR this year is tied for 519th among them. The counting statistics still point to some offensive value, but his overall production and defensive value declined sharply. He has fallen well short of both his 9.0-WAR peak two years ago and his 4.9-WAR campaign in 2025,” wrote Reuter.
Against the Yankees in the wild-card round, Boston’s offense struggled. Duran went 0-for-3 combined in both games with a walk. Given the logjam of outfielders the Red Sox have and the potential of adding one through free agency, trading Duran is a real possibility this offseason.
Jarren Duran’s Future With the Boston Red Sox is in Doubt
Changes are coming this offseason for the Red Sox. Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow has some decisions to make. One of them is Duran. He has two years of team control remaining, and Zachary D. Rymer of Bleacher Report thinks that could be a selling point for a team to put a package together to take him off Boston’s hands.
“It just feels like it’s time for the Red Sox and Duran to break up, doesn’t it? He’s been a regular in trade rumors for two years, and the energy he brings to the team isn’t always positive,” Rymer wrote. “The Red Sox can market him as an All-Star outfielder with two years of club control before free agency.”
Many questions remain about what the offseason will look like with a potential work stoppage looming. However, plenty of rumors will surround players before December. Duran’s name will be out there, and it would be surprising if he were moved before a stoppage, should it happen. However, when it comes to Breslow, expect the unexpected.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Sonny Gray and 3 other Red Sox who won't be back after embarrassing Yankees series
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: As paintul as it is to lose to the New York Yankees in the playoffs (for the second year in a row, no less), it hurts more to know that the Boston Red Sox's loss was more self-inflicted than anything. Boston's offense fell apart in September and the complete lack of momentum cursed it when it mattered. Pitching has been the Sox's single-biggest strength all season but Chad Tracy trusted the wrong arms at the wrong times. The moves could've cost the Red Sox any chance they had at a reunion with i
item.content:encoded:
As paintul as it is to lose to the New York Yankees in the playoffs (for the second year in a row, no less), it hurts more to know that the Boston Red Sox's loss was more self-inflicted than anything.
Boston's offense fell apart in September and the complete lack of momentum cursed it when it mattered. Pitching has been the Sox's single-biggest strength all season but Chad Tracy trusted the wrong arms at the wrong times. The moves could've cost the Red Sox any chance they had at a reunion with impending free agent Sonny Gray, who was vocal about his disappointment following his 4.2 inning outing.
“I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact,” Gray said. “I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am, and yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way."
The veteran has recently dropped hints that he might retire after this season, but after the Sox's loss he changed his tune, saying he's "got a lot of baseball left in [him]." Despite Boston's need for a right-handed pitcher next season, it's hard to foresee a reunion with Gray now.
The Sox have another impending free agent who likely won't want to come back after some explosive postgame comments, as well as some other players who could be moved after a disappointing loss.
Sonny Gray and 3 other Red Sox who won't be back after embarrassing Yankees series
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
Isiah Kiner-Falefa is yet another veteran who came to the Red Sox organization and revealed issues with the club's internal workings. Before the Red Sox went off on their tear over the summer, Kiner-Falefa called out some outside distractions that kept them from performing. He called the Sox's Wild Card loss "unacceptable" after Game 2.
Falefa didn't appear in the Wild Card series against the Yankees and he doesn't have a place in the Red Sox's infield next year — Trevor Story is under contract for one more season, Franklin Arias should be in the big leagues on Opening Day, Curtis Mead should be healthy and Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler will be options off the bench. But Kiner-Falefa has also called out the behind-the-scenes drama in the Red Sox organization and most likely prefers to play for a better-run team next year.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval didn't make the Red Sox's Wild Card roster, and there's a good reason for it. The lefty posted a 5.12 ERA and a 1.68 WHIP over 70.1 innings this year. He struggled in August and September with a 5.79 ERA between the two months. Seven of his eight decisions were losses.
The Red Sox certainly don't need another lefty starter in their rotation given the group they'll carry into next season. Boston's post-UCL surgery rebound projects have largely been unsuccessful and Sandoval did not change that.
Jarren Duran
The Red Sox hoped to rely on Jarren Duran as a veteran presence and an offensive threat this season and he was neither. He finished the season with a .207/.266/.361 slash line and 165 strikeouts in 151 games, the worst marks of his career so far.
Boston was already past the point of getting a good trade return for Duran last season, but the return doesn't matter at this point. The Red Sox need right-handed power and consistency and it makes the most sense to add it in the outfield.

item.content:encoded:
Happy Friday, everyone. I know this week hasn’t gone the way we had hoped, and that October baseball is now over for the Cubs, but the postseason rolls on, and we’ll still be keeping an eye on its progress as the month goes on. Today, we look at how the Astros fans turned on their own club as the disappointment of being swept out of the postseason got the best of them. We see how the Yankees proved they could win even without Aaron Judge, and how their ability to avoid rigid lineups might have helped them best the Red Sox. We also share takes from several players who were none too pleased with how the postseason turned out for them.
So let’s just get right into it.
- Jay Jaffe looks at how the Yankees bested the Red Sox to advance to the ALDS.
- Michael Baumann explains why the Yankees were the only ones constructing their Wild Card roster correctly.
- Brendan Gawlowski shares how the Padres advanced to the NLDS, but we might not want to relive that one just yet.
- Eric Longenhagen assesses how the White Sox were able to push past the Astros and onto the ALDS.
- Karl Rasmussen had some key takeaways from the White Sox series sweep of the Astros.
- Torey Lovullo will be sticking around as the Diamondbacks manager. (ESPN)
- Andy McCullough looks at how the ABS system is already changing October baseball. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Katie Woo explains why this might be the final year of the Dodger dynasty. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Willson Contreras has some feelings about Big Data.
- Davy Andrews explains why the Orioles will have some tough times ahead due to injury.
- Henry Palettella looks at the best moments from Wild Card history.
- Ryan Phillips and Tom Verducci draft the ultimate postseason pitching roster.
- Tom Verducci looked at how the Yankees proved they could win, even without Aaron Judge.
- Astros fans weren’t afraid to share how they really felt after the team was swept from the Wild Card series. Story by Karl Rasmussen.
- Sony Gray shared his displeasure at being pulled from the Wild Card game after only 70 pitches. (AP)
- It’s very hard not to like this guy.
- Cole Jacobson looks at which parks have the best home-field advantage for the postseason.
- Keegan Matheson shares how the Blue Jays are feeling about Guerrero Jr and what their focus is for this offseason.
- Andy Nesbitt looks at how things actually got worse for the Red Sox once they got back to their clubhouse after their Wild Card loss.
- How to watch SI’s original Shohei Ohtani documentary. (SI)
- Tyler Kepner explains why a rigid bullpen blueprint ultimately sank the Red Sox. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Get ready to feel very old.
And tomorrow will be a better day than today, Buster. Make it so.

item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox young star outfielder Roman Anthony found himself in one of the toughest positions in Major League Baseball this season, dealing with injuries throughout much of the campaign.
Anthony played in just 55 games, eventually returning later in the season. He finished with just a .735 OPS, hitting five home runs, 11 doubles, and driving in 15 RBIs.
By his standards, this season clearly didn't go as planned, but injuries were the reason.
There was hope and expectation that Anthony was going to be good to go in the postseason, though after the first two at-bats of the Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees, it was evident that something was still wrong with his hand.
Speaking to reporters after he didn't play Wednesday night when the Red Sox were eliminated by the Yankees, Anthony said his hand problems flared up and, for much of the season, he was never as healthy as he wanted to be.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," Anthony said, per CBS.
"But I think for me, it was to a point where it was tolerable, and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy but was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately, I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn't the case."
With the next few months off during Major League Baseball's offseason, Anthony will have time to come back next year and be ready to go. With Major League Baseball expected to be in a lockout, he could have even more time to get healthy. Only 22 years old, the biggest focus for the Red Sox is ensuring that he's ready to play for a long time.
That was clearly part of why they decided to sit him in Game 2.

item.content:encoded:
Finally, Caleb Durbin can figure out what to do with that pinkie.
He played with a crooked, painful left little finger for three-plus months, and along the way consistently downplayed what specifically was wrong — and whether it might need surgery.
Now, with the Red Sox’ season ending Wednesday, he can give it the care it needs.
“We were kind of putting it off to the end here, and I guess this is the end,” Durbin said. “So we’ll find out these next couple days, and we’ll get it fixed up. It’s been stuck in that certain position for a little while now. So I’m hoping they can put it back to normal.”
Durbin initially partially dislocated the pinkie on June 24, which turned out to be the day before the start of the Red Sox’ turnaround. He messed it up again on Aug. 6, the day before the Sox’ hot stretch ended.
In 82 games after the first episode, he hit .272 with a .377 on-base percentage and .391 slugging rate.
Among the reasons Durbin played through: He wasn’t alone.
“Some guys were grinding through stuff near the tail end here, but everyone’s going through something, so you try to keep that in mind,” he said. “Would have liked to have a couple more weeks in the tank, but it is what it is.”
Gasper to have surgery
Mickey Gasper will have surgery Friday to repair a distal biceps tear, an injury suffered in the third-to-last game of the regular season.
“There’s a little bit of tendon left,” he said. “Doctor said that that’s good for pinning it down. But yeah, they just got to repair it, reattach the biceps.”
Gasper said after 6-8 weeks he should “start feeling really good,” at which point “I’ve just got to not go too crazy.” It’ll take 4-6 months until he is game-ready again. That would bring him to sometime between early February and early April.
“My plan is to be ready to go March 1,” Gasper said. “That’s my mentality. March 1, be playing in that game.”
A Merrimack, N.H., native and Bryant University alumnus, Gasper had a whirlwind year, beginning when he was claimed off waivers by the Nationals in January and the Red Sox in February. He had several stints in the big league and starting in mid-August hit eight home runs in 16 games, his first taste of immense success at the highest level — at age 30.
Does he feel he proved anything with that showing?
“No, you never arrive in this game,” Gasper said. “One thing I always heard multiple guys say [on the 2025 Twins] was you can never arrive in this game. That’s in the past. It goes on your baseball card, but you’ve got to do it tomorrow.”
Banged up
Among other kinda, sorta injured Sox: Willson Contreras had a lot going on. “I’m sore all over,” he said. “My hammy is tight, my right hand is sore, my right hip is tight. But you play the whole season just to be in the playoffs, and I couldn’t miss it. I was not going to miss the playoffs.” … Garrett Crochet (left shoulder injury) deemed himself “100 percent” healthy and headed toward a normal offseason after making it back for a four-batter, zero-out appearance in the playoffs. “It was definitely nice to [pitch] again,” he said. “I felt like I was in control as much as you can be when you’re getting the [expletive] beat out of you.” … Isiah Kiner-Falefa hit .143/.265/.167 in September after returning from a left forearm stress reaction. On Wednesday, he referred to wanting to “just let this wrist get fully healthy” so he could resume his Driveline-based hitting training methods, with which he found much success before getting hurt in June. “I’m excited for what’s to come,” said Kiner-Falefa, a pending free agent … Perhaps the straightest straight-shooter on the team, Kiner-Falefa did not mince words on the Red Sox’ “unacceptable” Wild Card Series loss to the Yankees. “Doesn’t feel good. Obviously, not what any of us expected. An uncompetitive two games. Got boatraced. I guess the better team won,” he said. “You play in this market, you’ve got to win. We didn’t get the job done.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [dairylandexpress.com] Ranking the 5 defining moments of the Milwaukee Brewers' historic 2026 season
item.dc:creator: Dylan Carter
item.description: The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers cemented their place as one of the most exciting teams in franchise history, setting a new record with 103 regular-season wins while reaffirming one of the strongest cultures in the MLB, let alone American professional sports as a whole. They not only secured the No. 1 seed in the National League and an NL Central title, but also finished with the best record in the MLB as the only team to top 100 wins. But what are the moments that will stand out most when you look ba
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers cemented their place as one of the most exciting teams in franchise history, setting a new record with 103 regular-season wins while reaffirming one of the strongest cultures in the MLB, let alone American professional sports as a whole. They not only secured the No. 1 seed in the National League and an NL Central title, but also finished with the best record in the MLB as the only team to top 100 wins.
But what are the moments that will stand out most when you look back on this team? From broken records to walk-offs, home runs, stolen bases, strikeouts, clutch wins, and devastating losses, there are quite literally dozens of moments to choose from.
However, several moments stand out from the rest and will linger in Milwaukee Brewers fans' minds for the rest of their lives. These are the top five moments that defined the 2026 Brewers season.
5. May 10, 2026: Brice Turang completes Mother's Day Miracle with a walk-off home run for Brewers' first sweep of the Yankees since 1989.
The 2026 season will be remembered as the year Brice Turang solidified himself as one of, if not the single best second baseman in the MLB. But no moment encapsulates his rise quite like the walk-off home run that completed Milwaukee's first sweep of the New York Yankees in 37 years.
With two outs in a tie game, Turang hit a miraculous solo shot off reliever David Bednar in the bottom of the ninth inning to complete the series sweep and once again confirm that the Milwaukee Brewers are not a team to be trifled with. It was one of the first true indications that this Brewers crew was bound for greatness this season, and that Turang would be key to that rise.
4. September 8, 2026: Luis Lara's first career walk-off seals Brewers' back-and-forth extra-inning battle vs. the Cubs.
Resiliency is one of the key traits that stands out most from this year's Milwaukee Brewers team, and there were few moments that exemplified this better than the Brewers' Sept. 8 matchup with the rival Chicago Cubs.
Tied at 1-1 from the first inning to the ninth, Jacob Misiorowski allowed just one run in six innings, tallying nine strikeouts, including a record-setting 104.5 MPH pitch to start things off. Unfortunately, Trevor Megill couldn't hold onto that momentum in the ninth inning, loading the bases and allowing Carson Kelly to put the Cubs ahead 3-1 heading into the bottom of the ninth.
Pinch-hitting in the final frame, Christian Yelich hit a crucial single, setting up Jackson Chourio for the game-tying home run blast deep into left field. In the 10th inning, Garrett Mitchell made a spectacular catch-and-toss to David Hamilton at third base, retiring both Alex Bregman and Seiya Suzuki. On offense, Sal Frelick hit a pop-up single that evaded two Cubs in left field, setting up a bases-loaded situation for rookie Luis Lara to hit his first career walk-off RBI deep into left field, securing a crucial win that made a serious dent in Chicago's race to catch up to the Brewers in the NL Central race.
Spoiler alert: They never caught up, and your Milwaukee Brewers won the division handily.
3. August 18, 2026: Brewers achieve the largest shutout since 1887 with a 22-0 rout of the Mariners in Milwaukee.
This historic 22-0 rout of the Seattle Mariners was an achievement we've never seen in Milwaukee. 11 players logged hits, seven with multiple hits, and Seattle failed to earn a single run in response. Among those batters, Yelich, David Hamilton, and Luis Lara each had four RBIs, contributing to the largest rout in recent MLB history.
Not only did this tie the Brewers' franchise record for runs scored in a game, but it was the first rout by such a margin since 2004. And flying under the radar was starter Kyle Harrison, who allowed just two hits in five innings before handing the reins over to Shane Drohan, Grant Anderson, and even catcher Gary Sánchez. It was a sight to behold and one that cemented its place in Milwaukee sports history.
2. August 13, 2026: Brewers make a statement with their comeback victory at Dodgers Stadium, leading to a win in the season series.
Trailing 4-2 entering the ninth inning, the Milwaukee Brewers knew they desperately needed a bounce-back after being swept by the San Diego Padres and, for the first time this year, felt the seams starting to come undone on their historic win trajectory.
Following the resilient spirit embodied by the franchise, the Brewers hit five singles in six at-bats, including RBI singles by Jackson Chourio, Garrett Mitchell, and Jake Bauers to take the lead at the top of the ninth frame. Now with a 5-4 lead in the ninth inning, Trevor Megill entered the game and put the Dodgers away, earning his 22nd save of the season.
Although this wasn't as flashy a moment in what's been an outstanding season for the Brew Crew, it was certainly one of the most meaningful, because this is the moment they knew there was nothing that could stop them but themselves.
1. June 12, 2026: Jacob Misiorowski throws his first-career complete-game shutout vs. the Phillies.
For all the wonderful moments we've experienced, the story of the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers' season has to be the presumptive Cy Young Award-winning campaign by homegrown superstar pitcher Jacob Misiorowski. And no moment stands out from his season as much as the complete-game shutout he posted with 15 strikeouts, the most by any pitcher in the 2026 season.
He allowed only one hit in the entire game, throwing 74 strikes in 95 pitches to decimate the Philadelphia Phillies in front of the Milwaukee faithful at American Family Field. He recorded a 104.5 MPH fastball, breaking his own previous record for the fastest recorded pitch by a starter in the pitch-tracking era. This was also the most strikeouts in a Maddux, or a sub-100-pitch complete-game shutout, and he threw more than 55 pitches at 100 MPH in the contest.
Some games are cemented in Brewers history. This one is cemented in professional baseball history, and for that, it has to top the charts of the greatest moments of Milwaukee's epic 2026 campaign. Let's just hope they can add to the list as their playoff run begins this October.

item.title: [New York Post] What MLB had to say about Sonny Gray’s neck during Red Sox loss to Yankees
item.dc:creator: Christian Arnold
item.description: Major League Baseball did in fact look into the substance that many people seemed to notice on Sonny Gray’s neck during the Red Sox’s Game 2 wild-card series loss to the Yankees, sports talk host Craig Carton said on WFAN on Thursday. While the Yankees walloped the Red Sox to complete the sweep, plenty of baseball fans noticed what appeared to be a strange substance on Gray’s neck when he was on the mound, raising plenty of questions. Gray appeared to touch it at various times while on the mound
item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball did in fact look into the substance that many people seemed to notice on Sonny Gray’s neck during the Red Sox’s Game 2 wild-card series loss to the Yankees, sports talk host Craig Carton said on WFAN on Thursday.
While the Yankees walloped the Red Sox to complete the sweep, plenty of baseball fans noticed what appeared to be a strange substance on Gray’s neck when he was on the mound, raising plenty of questions.
Gray appeared to touch it at various times while on the mound, and baseball fans were quick to point out the discoloration on the right side of his neck.
However, Carton said he was told by Major League Baseball that it was on top of the situation and that the umpires had checked his hat, glove and hands after every inning he pitched.
“He was checked after every inning. The spin rate was not up at all compared to his starts throughout the regular season,” Carton said. “They did a full check because, obviously, if you’re watching the game, like we all are, you saw the right side of his neck was discolored.”
An MLB spokesperson did not immediately reply to a request for comment from The Post on Thursday.
Gray pitched 4 ⅔ innings and allowed only a solo home run to Luis Garcia Jr. before he was pulled from the game at 70 pitches.
The veteran right-hander seemed to question the decision to pull him from the game.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact. I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am,” he told reporters. “You can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. I felt strong. I felt confident.
“I felt convicted. What can you do? You know.”

item.title: [The Boston Globe] Sonny Gray says there’s ‘a lot of baseball left in me,’ but is undecided about what’s next - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Tim Healey
item.description: NEW YORK — In the first moments after the end of another season, Sonny Gray was right where he wanted to be: with his kids. Brothers Gunnar, 11, and Declan, 8, were periodic presences around the Red Sox since the start of spring training. They hung around with their father and his teammates in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium late Wednesday, a cheerful, youthful salve for the wound of sudden elimination from the postseason. It illustrated the position Gray finds himself in after 14 year
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — In the first moments after the end of another season, Sonny Gray was right where he wanted to be: with his kids.
Brothers Gunnar, 11, and Declan, 8, were periodic presences around the Red Sox since the start of spring training. They hung around with their father and his teammates in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium late Wednesday, a cheerful, youthful salve for the wound of sudden elimination from the postseason.
It illustrated the position Gray finds himself in after 14 years in the majors. On the mound, he remains eminently capable, having just turned in another high-end season, with a 2.72 ERA across 29 starts. Away from the field, he feels the pull of family, well aware of what it would mean to be a full-time dad back home in Tennessee.
In the immediate aftermath of a season-ending loss to the Yankees, Gray was noncommittal about pitching in 2027. As he mulls retirement, though, he emphasized that he needs time to figure it out.
“I don’t know what the future holds for me,” he said. “I do know that I walked off of that mound with my chest back and my chin up, and I can definitely be proud that I left it all out there until the ball was taken out of my hand.”
Gray, who turns 37 in November, is due to become a free agent, and is a virtual lock to decline his mutual option for next season and get a $10 million buyout instead.
If he does play next season, would the Red Sox be a destination?
“I don’t know,” he said.
Gray was sour after manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of an eventual 9-2 loss — a 1-0 game at the moment Gray exited.
“I would’ve liked to have been trusted in that moment,” he said.
Cognizant of the emotion surrounding that managerial call, as well as the end of the season, Gray emphasized patience.
“I do know that in moments like this, it’s never beneficial for any party involved to make rash decisions,” he said. “You’re a train going down the tracks, and it just gets stopped immediately. I know step No. 1 is to not make any rash decisions. I think I just try to take it one thing at a time for now. And No. 1 would be getting my bags packed, getting in the shower, getting some food, getting back to the hotel, seeing my family, and getting back to Boston, and then we’ll go from there.”
After coming off the field, Gray went around the room hugging teammates, a parade that “just felt right” and was “not a planned thing,” he said.
Acquired from the Cardinals via trade last November, Gray was supposed to be the Red Sox’ No. 2 starting pitcher, solidifying the rotation behind Garrett Crochet. Instead, he led it, emerging as a stabilizing force as Crochet missed more than five months because of a shoulder injury.
“I was telling him that a second ago: Whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year,” Crochet said. “I still think he’s got a lot to give the game, but there’s something to be said about going on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that’ll be something that — us as a team — that we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston.”
Gray told the Globe recently that “I’ll be done in a heartbeat” when his family makes it clear he’s wanted back home.
Does he still have baseball left in him?
“I think that’s an easy answer,” he said, breaking into a smile. “I got a lot of baseball left in me.”
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.title: [puckettspond.com] Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz takes shots at Willson Contreras, Red Sox after early exit
item.dc:creator: Jackson Kruse

The Yankees swept the Red Sox in two games, winning 9-0 on Tuesday and 9-2 on Wednesday. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were completely embarrassed by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series this week. The Yankees swept the Red Sox in two games, winning 9-0 on Tuesday and 9-2 on Wednesday. Boston is now eliminated from the postseason, while New York will play the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series.
With two outs in the bottom of the second inning in Wednesday's game, Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. hit a ball up the middle that Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story smothered on a nice diving play. There appeared to be a play at first base, but Contreras wasn't covering the bag, allowing Chisholm to reach. Luckily for the Red Sox, Contreras' misplay didn't come back to haunt him.
It's one thing for a player to make a defensive mistake once in a game. It's a whole other story if the player makes two defensive gaffes. That's exactly what Contreras did.
Red Sox's Willson Contreras makes defensive mistakes in Wild Card Game 2 loss to Yankees
Boston left-hander Garrett Crochet entered the game in the bottom of the sixth inning with the Yankees leading 2-1. Crochet got the first batter he faced, Spencer Jones, to strike out swinging. However, Jones swung at a ball in the dirt that got away from catcher Adley Rutschman, who was notably slow to retrieve the ball and throw it to first base, allowing Jones to reach first despite striking out.
Contreras was covering first base, but he was positioned on the back of the bag. It wasn't completely Contreras' fault that Jones reached first, but if he had his foot on the front of the bag and stretched to catch the ball, Jones likely would have been out.
Jones stole second base and reached third on a throwing error from Rutschman. He scored on an RBI single from George Lombard Jr. The Yankees scored five more runs in the inning, increasing their lead to 8-1.
It's worth noting that Contreras did his job at the plate Wednesday, going 2-for-2 with a home run and two walks. Unfortunately, his defensive gaffes are what's gaining more attention after Boston's rough loss.
After the loss, Contreras essentially told the media that he believes the Red Sox rely too much on data. Notably, the Red Sox pulled right-hander Sonny Gray from Wednesday's game after he allowed two runs on just 70 pitches over 4 2/3 innings.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."
Former Twins fan favorite Doug Mientkiewicz, a member of the Red Sox's 2004 World Series team, took a shot at Contreras and the Red Sox after the Boston first baseman's comments.
"How about cover first- or maybe one of your 15 coaches should say something," Mientkiewicz wrote on X. "Oh but they will shoot balls out of a tiny machine on a slab of turf though during pregame. Embarrassing."
Mientkiewicz played for the Twins from 1998-2004. The Twins traded the first baseman to the Red Sox at the 2004 trade deadline.
During his seven years with the Twins, Mientkiewicz hit .275/.367/.408 with 43 home runs and 266 RBI. After his stint with Boston in 2004, Mientkiewicz played for the New York Mets, Kansas City Royals, New York Yankees, Pittsburgh Pirates and Los Angeles Dodgers. He retired after the 2009 season.

Anthony's wrist and finger ailments made it hard for him to help save the Red Sox's season Wednesday night, with the New York Yankees eliminating them. But one writer grabbed the attention of Boston fans by adding more context in
item.content:encoded:
Writer's take on Roman Anthony injury situation will catch Red Sox fans' attention appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox dealt with a battered Roman Anthony before their MLB Playoffs elimination game. Anthony's wrist and finger ailments made it hard for him to help save the Red Sox's season Wednesday night, with the New York Yankees eliminating them. But one writer grabbed the attention of Boston fans by adding more context into the severity of his injury.
Boston Globe Red Sox insider Tim Healey provided new details on his appearance with Foul Territory Thursday. Included if Anthony should've sat a long time ago amid his MLB Injury.
"It sounds like he was never fully healed," Healey explained. "He had dealt with troubling swings for six weeks. If we count backwards, six weeks goes back to his rehab assignment."
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
So Anthony's injury should've placed him on IL. Granted, Anthony flashed at the bat while navigating through the injury. But the swings started to hurt him in late August and September, Healey adds.
"The tendon and the ligament never fully healed," Healey said. "He kept swinging and kept playing almost everyday. Now other parts of his hand are strained as well."
Healey became blunt about what happens next for Anthony.
"He's going to need a hard reset on that hand this offseason," Healey said.
It sounds like Roman Anthony was never entirely healed, says @TimBHealey.
"He's going to need a hard reset on that hand this offseason." pic.twitter.com/vcLqtqiDph
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 1, 2026
Boston mustered only two runs in the two games against its longtime nemesis. New York piled the runs and reached nine in both victories.
The Red Sox will now reset plus evaluate the 2026 roster following their late playoff charge. Including resting Anthony in all likelihood.

Related: Why Red Sox fan Dave Portnoy called out Yankees after AL Wild Card Series

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Insider Weighs in on Red Sox, Sonny Gray Substance Speculation
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Boston Red Sox's season is over. With two blowout losses to the New York Yankees in the American League wild card series, they were swept out of the playoffs and now will look towards 2027. Plenty of moments stood out in the loss, specifically when Sonny Gray was pulled in favor of Garrett Crochet, which resulted in the Yankees blowing the game open. However, some fans on social media took it a step further, suggesting that when the right-hander tapped his neck before throwing a pitch during
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's season is over. With two blowout losses to the New York Yankees in the American League wild card series, they were swept out of the playoffs and now will look towards 2027. Plenty of moments stood out in the loss, specifically when Sonny Gray was pulled in favor of Garrett Crochet, which resulted in the Yankees blowing the game open.
However, some fans on social media took it a step further, suggesting that when the right-hander tapped his neck before throwing a pitch during the game, he had a substance there and was trying to doctor the baseball.
However, neither the umpires, nor the Yankees seemed to take any issue with it. On Thursday, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic appeared on Foul Territory and shared that he doesn't think it's a big deal.
"That is something the umpires would have needed to catch and address, and they did not, so I don't know that retroactively, MLB is going to step in simply by looking at video when you can't touch Sonny Gray's neck anymore and see what's going on," Rosenthal said.
"I know what the videos look like, I know we live in a conspiratorial kind of society right now where we all think something's up all the time. But if the umps didn't flag it, the Yankees didn't flag it, I think we've got kind of a non-issue."
"If the umpires or Yankees didn't flag it, I think we've got kind of a non-issue."
– @Ken_Rosenthal on the speculation about a substance on Sonny Gray's neck. pic.twitter.com/GlMXQmTxXa
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 1, 2026
Ken Rosenthal Doesn't Believe Sonny Gray Substance Rumors
In this day and age, umpires are all over pitchers who use substances. They have been cracking down on that for several years now, so in truth, if they thought there was an issue, they likely would have flagged it and checked Gray. It's important too to remember that ever since the league cracked down on spider tack and other substances, umpires have been checking pitchers as they walk off the mound each inning.
The Yankees likely would have noticed as well, and at no point did they suggest that there was something off about what Gray was doing or ask the umpires to check him.
Even if there was a concern at all during last night's game, it's too late for the league to do anything to punish Gray. The Red Sox lost the game and are eliminated, and Gray has even hinted at retirement at the end of this season, so there isn't anything that can really be done about it.
Sonny Gray's Future With Boston Red Sox
Gray was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals in November to stabilize the Red Sox's rotation. In 29 starts, the 36-year-old veteran went 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA over 169 innings of work. The right-hander also struck out 149 batters and posted a 4.3 WAR.
If this is the end for Gray, he at least will finish his career on a high note, having posted one of the best seasons of his career. It will be interesting to see if he decides to keep pitching or chooses to retire once the postseason comes to an end.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Insider Weighs in on Red Sox, Sonny Gray Substance Speculation appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [fansided.com] What the number say about Pete Crow-Armstrong's postseason failures
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: Regardless of how his career turns out, Chicago Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong may already have Mike Trout beat in one key category: playoff games. Both are still seeking their first Championship Series appearance, but at least PCA had another opportunity this week. Any hopes the Cubs had of advancing beyond the Wild Card Round ended fairly quickly, though, with the presumptive NL MVP being held hitless in eight at-bats against the Padres. Crow-Armstrong’s dreadful two-game performance follo
item.content:encoded:
Regardless of how his career turns out, Chicago Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong may already have Mike Trout beat in one key category: playoff games.
Both are still seeking their first Championship Series appearance, but at least PCA had another opportunity this week. Any hopes the Cubs had of advancing beyond the Wild Card Round ended fairly quickly, though, with the presumptive NL MVP being held hitless in eight at-bats against the Padres.
Crow-Armstrong’s dreadful two-game performance follows him hitting .184 with 12 strikeouts over eight playoff games last year.
“You can look at the scoreboard, you can look at the stat sheet, wherever you get your numbers from, and it is clear to see that I didn’t contribute,” he told reporters. “None of it feels good. Pretty disappointed in myself, but that’s for me to work on.”
Given the current state of baseball’s labor crisis, he’ll likely have plenty of additional time to reflect on what went wrong.
Should Chicago Cubs fans be concerned by Pete Crow-Armstrong’s playoff struggles?
Some of the more generous PCA-related social media posts have involved questioning his MVP status or accusing him of being overrated. Right, because someone who just put up nearly 10 bWAR and joined the 40-40 club is overrated.
This will sound crazy, but Crow-Armstrong is still only 24. He’s already become one of the sport’s premier faces to the point that we wouldn’t be shocked if he’s on the cover of next year’s MLB The Show game. We talk so much about New York and Los Angeles that we forget he’s thrived in the Chicago media market, which isn’t exactly a bunch of villages and huts in the middle of nowhere.
Anyone who blames Crow-Armstrong for the Cubs’ playoff loss is deliberately being lazy. Alex Bregman, Dansby Swanson and Ian Happ all went hitless in the series themselves. They managed one run over 18 innings.
Credit to the Padres for keeping Crow-Armstrong off the basepaths, which should sound obvious enough. But he drew walks in nearly 12 percent of his plate appearances during the regular season yet only managed a single free pass this week.
Analysts constantly referenced Trout’s 1-for-12 showing in the 2014 ALDS — still his lone postseason appearance — because he and the Angels still haven’t returned to the playoffs. That’s why no one even bothers bringing it up anymore; we’ve just collectively gotten used to the Angels finishing in or near last place.
Do you remember who else had a reputation as a poor postseason performer? Alex Rodriguez, a narrative that vanished when the Yankees won the 2009 World Series. The talk surrounding Aaron Judge’s October struggles will vanish if he catches the final out of the Fall Classic.
Let’s give Crow-Armstrong some more time. Besides, the Cubs are only 10 years into a title drought rather than 108. Things could be far worse.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] MLB insider reveals Orioles' 'steep' asking price from Yankees for Adley Rutschman | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Conor Liguori
item.description: The New York Yankees targeted several catchers at the trade deadline. Ultimately, they did not acquire a right-handed hitter to platoon with Austin Wells, who received trade interest from another AL East team. On Wednesday, the New York Post's Jon Heyman reported that the Baltimore Orioles inquired about Wells and a few other Yankees players in a potential deal for catcher Adley Rutschman. "The Orioles had a request to the Yankees on the table for star catcher Adley Rutschman at the deadline: pi
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees targeted several catchers at the trade deadline.
Ultimately, they did not acquire a right-handed hitter to platoon with Austin Wells, who received trade interest from another AL East team.
On Wednesday, the New York Post's Jon Heyman reported that the Baltimore Orioles inquired about Wells and a few other Yankees players in a potential deal for catcher Adley Rutschman.
"The Orioles had a request to the Yankees on the table for star catcher Adley Rutschman at the deadline: pitching prospect Elmer Rodriguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena plus one of two young starters - either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers," Heyman wrote.
That would have been quite the price for the Yankees to pay for a year and a half of Rutschman, who has dealt with injuries in recent seasons.
The Yankees value Wells' pitching-calling abilities and his work with their pitching staff.
Warren and Weathers could be key contributors to New York's bullpen in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. Both pitchers are under team control through at least 2028 (Weathers).
Plus, Rodriguez is an intriguing arm, and Pena hit .323 with six home runs in 23 games at Single-A Tampa.
Did the Yankees need Rutschman that badly? As it turns out, not really.
Wells caught fire at the plate during the later months of the regular season and has continued that trend into the postseason.
For now, Ali Sanchez is a perfectly competent backup.
The Yankees can readdress their catching situation in the offseason.
Not trading four players for Rutschman, who posted a .688 OPS in 32 games with the Boston Red Sox, seems like the correct decision.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What to Know About Roman Anthony's Injury After Red Sox Playoff Exit

item.content:encoded:
The offseason is now here for the Boston Red Sox and the health of Roman Anthony is going to be a massive question mark that hangs over this organization for months.
Boston won't play another real game until late March, unless the collective bargaining agreement negotiations mess things up and impact the 2027 season. That is over five months away after Boston was knocked out of the wild-card round by the New York Yankees on Wednesday night.
Anthony unfortunately was forced to exit Game 1 after aggravating his hand/wrist injury that forced him to miss roughly three months of time earlier in the season. After Anthony left Game 1, he went for imaging back in Boston and it revealed "new strains to different muscles in his wrist" while also "exacerbating" the old injury. The injury that knocked Anthony out for months was a partially torn ring finger CMC ligament.
So, now what? Well, the best thing about the offseason is time to recover. If everything goes as planned and there are no issues with the 2027 campaign, Spring Training will begin in February. That's four months away. Even if Anthony suffered the exact injury again, he has more time right now to recover than it took between when he first got hurt and when he returned to the field.
Roman Anthony's Bad Luck
Unfortunately, it's a freak injury. Back in June, Alex Speier of The Boston Globe quoted Dr. Mark Cohen of Midwest Orthopaedics at Rush University, who said he hadn't heard of an injury like Anthony's in 32 years of practicing medicine. Sometimes, there is just bad luck involved. But that doesn't mean the process to get Anthony back was wrong. Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow spoke about the process on Wednesday, as transcribed by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo.
"As far as I know, the rehab and the return to play was the appropriate one. Last night in the game, he did something where things changed, things worsened and we needed to take a fresh look at it," Breslow said.
Anthony spoke about the injury himself on Wednesday and whether his elite swing speed is the cause.
“I’ve had above-average bat speed I think for a while before this has been a problem,” Anthony said, as transcribed by MassLive.com's Christopher Smith. “Maybe it’s something to do with it, but I don’t think that’s the reason. I think it’s just an injury that happened and maybe wasn’t 100%. I wish I had that answer, but I think it could be a bunch of different things, to be honest."
Again, sometimes guys just get unlucky. When you suffer an injury that a doctor says they haven't heard of in 32 years, that's a pretty big sign of bad luck. Barring further setbacks, there should be enough time between now and Spring Training for Anthony to work his way back. The exact severity of the injury hasn't been revealed yet, but even if it was as bad as his previous injury, there is more than three months to go until Boston returns.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Scout affirms what Willson Contreras was hinting at after embarrassing Red Sox ending
item.dc:creator: Pat Ragazzo

After Boston got eliminated on Wednesday night, first baseman Willson Contreras hinted that there is too much reliance on data within the organization. item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's season is officially over after they were embarrassed by the American League East rival New York Yankees, getting swept in two games in the Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium. After Boston got eliminated on Wednesday night, first baseman Willson Contreras hinted that there is too much reliance on data within the organization.
In back-to-back games, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy lifted his starting pitcher after just 4.2 innings. First it was Payton Tolle who only threw 83 pitches and was cruising in Game 1, and then it was Sonny Gray after just 70 pitches last night. Both moves ultimately backfired as Boston's bullpen, which led baseball with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season, imploded in each contest.
Red Sox relief pitchers were charged with 15 runs across two games. This mark was very unorthodox for this unit based on what occurred during the regular season, but Boston should've gone with its starters longer.
Why one scout agrees with Willson Contreras' critique of the Red Sox
One National League scout who spoke with FanSided seemed to concur with what Contreras had to say during his postgame availability about the Red Sox's decision making.
"The Red Sox were beleaguered by injuries, but their mid game pitching decisions made the series a laugher," the scout said. "Seems like they are leaning so hard on the large sample size that they are ignoring what their eyes were telling them. In a must win game, the choice to never use (Aroldis) Chapman until the series was over, has had people fired for less."
Regarding Chapman, the Red Sox didn't put the closer, their best reliever, into the game until it was already out of hand in Game 2, with Boston trailing 9-2 in the eighth inning. Despite having a 1.92 ERA this season, Chapman only appeared in one of two games in the series once things were out of reach. He struck out the side in his lone low-leverage appearance.
In the postseason, teams often go to their closer earlier than the ninth inning in order to pitch them in high-leverage spots to help preserve the game. If the Red Sox had taken this approach with Chapman, they might have been able to keep themselves in the game in one or both of these contests.
Instead, the Yankees blew the Red Sox out in both games. The Red Sox were outscored 18-2 across these two games, which resulted in a series sweep. Beyond its bizarre pitching management, Boston's bats didn't show up in the Wild Card series either. The team and organization will now have a long time to think about the way their season ended now that it's officially over.

item.content:encoded:
In 1969, the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers — who were the Seattle Pilots for one season — were founded as MLB expansion teams.
Now, 58 short years later, the perennial National League contenders are meeting in the postseason for the first time.
On Saturday, Oct. 3, the best-of-five NLDS will get underway at Milwaukee’s American Family Field with the Brewers’ ace and Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski (16-5, 1.80 ERA) on the hill.
Following a two-game stint in the Cream City, the series will move to SoCal for a pair of contests at San Diego’s PETCO Park. They’re slated to take place:
Game 3
Tuesday, Oct. 6
Game 4
Wednesday, Oct. 7
If you’d like to be there, tickets are available for both high-stakes hypothetical San Diego showdowns.
At the time of publication, the lowest price we could find on tickets for either game was $121 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $99 including fees for the three potential meetings in Milwaukee.
Before this series, the Padres got revenge against the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card round, sweeping MVP hopeful Pete Crow-Armstrong’s club at home after losing to them in three games to open the playoffs last year.
“They’re playing great baseball right now,” San Diego manager Craig Stammen said about his club.
Next up, they have a tall task taking on MLB’s winningest team in 2026.
Oddsmakers project the Brewers are -180 favorites going into the NLDS.
Yet, it should be factored in that San Diego took four of their six meetings over the course of the regular season including a clutch 4-3, eleven-inning victory on Aug. 12.
Is this the year that one of these two clubs finally gets over the hump and returns to the World Series?
While we can’t say for certain we do know that their first-ever postseason meeting with some of the game’s hardest flamethrowers in Misiorowski and Mason Miller should be downright electric.
Don’t miss this one. We just might have an instant classic on our hands.
For more information, our team has everything you need to know and more about the Padres vs. Brewers 2026 NLDS below.

Starry-eyed fans looking to get ahead of themselves can procure potential NLCS and World Series tickets before the NLDS even begins.
To grab seats for the game of your choosing, all hypothetical Padres playoff tickets can be found here.
How to watch the Padres in the 2026 playoffs
Fans that prefer to watch on the tube, you can catch Padres playoff contests on FOX, which can be found on DIRECTV.
Huge 2026-27 San Diego shows
The Yankees aren’t the only huge attraction in America’s Finest City these next few months.
Here are just five of the biggest acts headed to San Diego in the near future.
