item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’s Willson Contreras Takes Shot at Chad Tracy for Controversial Sonny Gray Move
item.dc:creator: Owen Crisafulli
item.description: The Boston Red Sox's 2026 campaign officially came to a close on Wednesday night, as they suffered a 9-2 loss at the hands of the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their wild-card series. Once again, the Sox got virtually no production on offense, while their bullpen fell apart down the stretch thanks to a bevy of head-scratching moves from manager Chad Tracy. The most consequential decision from Tracy was his controversial decision to remove Sonny Gray from the game after 4.2 innings of work in fav
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox's 2026 campaign officially came to a close on Wednesday night, as they suffered a 9-2 loss at the hands of the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their wild-card series. Once again, the Sox got virtually no production on offense, while their bullpen fell apart down the stretch thanks to a bevy of head-scratching moves from manager Chad Tracy.
The most consequential decision from Tracy was his controversial decision to remove Sonny Gray from the game after 4.2 innings of work in favor of Erik Miller, who had just given up a crucial home run in Game 1 of this series the day before. Gray made it very clear after the game that he was not a fan of Tracy's decision to pull him, and it seems like All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras agrees with his teammate.
Willson Contreras Makes Thoughts Clear on Chad Tracy's Sonny Gray Move
In Game 1 against the Yankees, Tracy removed Payton Tolle after 4.2 innings of work and turned to Miller to face Ben Rice. Tolle was at 83 pitches on the night, but he had generally pitched well. The move immediately backfired, as Miller gave up a solo home run to Rice that woke up the rest of New York's lineup.
Tracy's decision to remove Gray in Game 2 was even more jarring, though. While a pair of runners were on first and second base, Gray had largely cruised through his outing, and this time, he was only at 70 pitches on the night. Tracy once again went to Miller out of the bullpen, and he quickly got burned again, with Miller giving up an RBI single to Cody Bellinger.
Gray did not hold back after the game when discussing Tracy's decision to pull him, saying he would have liked to be trusted in that situation after putting together such a successful season with the team. When asked about Tracy pulling Gray out of the game prematurely, Contreras didn't say anything, and instead pantomimed himself zipping his mouth shut and throwing away the key.
Red Sox Finish 2026 Campaign With Dispiriting Series vs. Yankees
So much went right for the Red Sox in their mid-summer turnaround that resulted in them finding their way to the postseason. At the end of the day, though, this team's weaknesses were too much to overcome. The lineup, which has been a weakness all year, did nothing aside from a pair of solo home runs from Contreras and Nick Sogard in Game 2, the bullpen faltered, and the lights were clearly too bright for Tracy, as every single move he made proved to be the wrong one.
Boston finds itself in the same exact spot it was in last offseason, as it clearly needs to make sweeping upgrades to its lineup in order to take the step forward it appears capable of taking. You'd think the front office would have figured this out after being subjected to the same fate in last year's playoffs, but if it puts together another weak offseason of work, the Red Sox could quickly find themselves stuck in the purgatory of being a consistently mediocre team.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox's Willson Contreras Takes Shot at Chad Tracy for Controversial Sonny Gray Move appeared first on HEAVY.

item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa. The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the post
item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The Boston Red Sox were eliminated from the MLB postseason after getting swept embarrassingly by the AL East rival New York Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series. During this series loss, the Red Sox saw Garrett Crochet make some MLB history- just not the kind of history anyone wants to set. The Athletic's Jayson Stark revealed how Crochet made some seemingly impossible history in the Wild Card loss, with Crochet getting one strikeout but not recording a single out in a brutal outing coming out of
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were eliminated from the MLB postseason after getting swept embarrassingly by the AL East rival New York Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
During this series loss, the Red Sox saw Garrett Crochet make some MLB history- just not the kind of history anyone wants to set.
The Athletic's Jayson Stark revealed how Crochet made some seemingly impossible history in the Wild Card loss, with Crochet getting one strikeout but not recording a single out in a brutal outing coming out of the bullpen.
How Garrett Crochet made seemingly impossible MLB history
"Crochet became the only pitcher in postseason history to have an outing with: One strikeout, But... No outs!" Stark shared.
In Game 2 of the AL Wild Card round in the Red Sox vs. Yankees series, Crochet came into the game out of the bullpen and had a brutal outing.
Crochet went 0.0 innings of work, allowing three hits and four runs while walking no batters but getting one strikeout.
The issue for Crochet is that his strikeout of Spencer Jones didn't actually result in an out. He struck him out, but on a wild pitch that went past the catcher, letting Jones scamper to first base and reach safely.
That kick-started a disastrous inning, featuring multiple hits, misplays, and eventually Garrett Whitlock coming into the game to take over for Crochet, before he, too, had a blowup outing.
When it was all said and done, the Yankees scored six runs in the inning, capped off by a Cody Bellinger grand slam to blow the game wide open, effectively ending the Red Sox's season.
Thanks to Crochet's poor outing, the Red Sox were eliminated. But his poor outing might've been a clean inning had the first batter he faced not resulted in a strikeout turning into a base runner.
There has not been a pitcher in MLB postseason history to get a strikeout but not record an out in that same appearance. Crochet's line is one-of-a-kind, and it might never happen again in the history of Major League Baseball.

But with the game in extra innings, the Phillies got an incredibly clutch solo homer to right field from Alec Bohm to put the Phillies up 4-3. That extra-inning, go-ahead HR from Bohm made some incredible MLB history. According to Jayson Stark of The Athletic, Bohm's homer has made him the third player ever to hit a go-ahead home r
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies hit two clutch home runs during Game 2 of the NL Wild Card, with Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper going back-to-back to tie the game up late.
But with the game in extra innings, the Phillies got an incredibly clutch solo homer to right field from Alec Bohm to put the Phillies up 4-3. That extra-inning, go-ahead HR from Bohm made some incredible MLB history.
According to Jayson Stark of The Athletic, Bohm's homer has made him the third player ever to hit a go-ahead home run in extra innings in an elimination game during the postseason, joining David Ortiz and Carlton Fisk.
Alec Bohm joins David Ortiz, Carlton Fisk with all-time clutch HR
"Tie-breaking extra-inning HR by cleanup hitters in postseason elimination game: Carlton Fisk, 1975, WS Game 6; David Ortiz, 2004, ALCS Game 4; Alec Bohm, 2026, WSC Game 2," Stark shared.
There is no other player in MLB history other than these three hitters to have a go-ahead home run in extra innings when their team was facing elimination.
This incredibly clutch homer kept the Phillies' season alive, and it has now made Bohm a part of some of the most iconic home runs in MLB postseason history.
Although it doesn't feel like it at all right now, this homer from Bohm is in some very rare air, with Fisk's '75 homer and Ortiz's '04 homer two of the most legendary in MLB history.
If the Phillies can go on a run to win the 2026 World Series, this Bohm home run will be the moment that sparked this Phillies team to greatness.
But even if the Phillies don't win it all, Bohm's clutch home run is still one of the craziest of all time. On the brink of elimination, Bohm hit a clutch homer in extra innings to save the season. It doesn't get a whole lot better than that.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox were swept by the New York Yankees in the American League Wild Card Series, and Sonny Gray now faces a decision on his future.
Earlier this year, the 36-year-old pitcher noted that he is open to retiring if his family wants him to hang it up. He had a great year and revealed after the game that he thinks he has a lot of baseball left in him. However, he needs to decide if playing is what's best for him and his family.
"I was telling him that a second ago, whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year," ace Garrett Crochet said after the loss to the Yankees, per MassLive's Chris Cotillo. "I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
Even if Gray continues to play, his postgame comments open the door for him to leave the Red Sox. He has a $30 million mutual option, which will likely be declined by the Red Sox. He could re-sign as a free agent, but when he was asked if Boston was a destination he would consider after the year he had, he said "I don't know."
Gray stepped up big time for the Red Sox this year. They needed the entire rotation to play better with Crochet hurt. Having him and Crochet together in the rotation, along with Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez, would be great for the Red Sox.
More MLB: White Sox Finally Win Playoff Series For First Time In Decades

item.content:encoded:
When the Chicago White Sox traded Garrett Crochet to the Boston Red Sox on Dec. 11, 2024 for four players, Boston initially won the trade.
Crochet finished second in AL Cy Young voting last season, boasting an 18-5 record with a 2.59 ERA and 255 strikeouts across 32 appearances. But with the White Sox's surprising turnaround this season, their young core has shifted the perception of the trade over the last year.
The young talent they possess has helped carry them into their first postseason berth since 2021. Three of the players acquired from the Crochet trade (Chase Meidroth, Kyle Teel, & Braden Montgomery) have been solid contributors to the team.
They were also productive in the AL Wild Card Series, helping the White Sox sweep the Houston Astros. Meidroth went 2-for-3 with a home run, three RBI and a run in Game 2 while Teel went 2-for-5 with an RBI and a run. Montgomery went 2-for-4 with a run in Game 1.
The White Sox have advanced to the AL Division Series and will face the Cleveland Guardians.
The White Sox traded Garrett Crochet to the Red Sox for 4 players, 3 of whom played every inning of the Wild Card Series:
Chase Meidroth (2-3, HR, 3 RBI, R in Game 2)
Kyle Teel (2-5, RBI, R in Game 2)
Braden Montgomery (2-4, R in Game 1)
Chris Getz, take a bow.@MLBNetwork
All things considered, the Crochet trade was at the very least a win-win for the clubs involved.
Crochet struggled through an injury-riddled 2026 season and gave up for runs in a playoff appearance out of the bullpen. Considering that he hadn't pitched in five months, his rocky outing is somewhat understandable.
This season is one that Crochet will want to put past him. The 27-year-old southpaw will be looking to return to form and bounce back with the Red Sox.
Boston transformed its 2026 season after early-season struggles. However, the grit that was present in their late-season surge was nowhere to be seen in the postseason. The Yankees humiliated the Red Sox in the ALWCS, outscoring them 18-2 across two games.
Overall, the Crochet trade has provided both Sox teams with success. But it will be captivating to see how far the White Sox's young core will take them this postseason, and how this trade is viewed a few years down the line.

item.title: [fansided.com] Regrading the Garrett Crochet trade after White Sox beat Boston to the ALDS

item.content:encoded:
When the Boston Red Sox acquired Garrett Crochet from the Chicago White Sox in December of 2024, it felt like a tale of two teams heading in very different directions. Boston had a generational crop of homegrown talent banging down to the door, headlined by Roman Anthony, Marcelo Mayer and Kristian Campbell, with Crochet as the final piece of a potential championship puzzle. As for Chicago ... well, they'd lost 100-plus games for two years in a row, and it didn't seem like that streak would end any time soon. If you were forced to bet on which team would be the first to win a playoff series, you would've put your life's savings on the Red Sox.
Turns out we all would've lost a whole bunch of money. Boston is headed home after the Wild Card Round for the second straight year, and this elimination was even more humiliating than the last. The White Sox, meanwhile, are still very much alive, sweeping the Houston Astros on the road to punch their ticket to the ALDS this weekend.
Pretty much everything we thought we knew about these teams has been flipped on its head over the last two years. How much should that change how we view the Crochet deal in hindsight? FanSided originally had the trade about even, giving the White Sox a B and the Red Sox a B- at the time. Now, though, things look a whole lot different.
White Sox' Garrett Crochet trade regrade
The Crochet return centered around three players: catcher Kyle Teel, outfielder Braden Montgomery and infielder Chase Meidroth. Teel and Montgomery were the headliners, two consensus top-100 prospects that the White Sox hoped would be the foundation for their next competitive window.
Instead, Meidroth might be the biggest win of all. He might not have the most upside, but with his contact skills and slick glove at second base, he's got an awfully high floor that should make him a big-league regular for a very long time. Meidroth posted a 115 OPS+ and 4.5 bWAR in his sophomore season, one of the biggest reasons why the White Sox are where they are right now.
But he's far from the only building block Chicago was able to acquire. Teel has had a hard time staying healthy since the trade, but when he's been on the field he's looked the part of a legit two-way catcher, solid behind the plate with elite barrel and walk rates as a hitter. If he can just avoid injury for a full season, there's no reason he can't become a top 10-15 catcher in the sport — at a minimum.
Montgomery is admittedly a bit behind the other two, a good athlete who needs to figure out how to either make more contact or pull the ball in the air more if he's going to pan out as a Major League hitter. Still: All signs point to both Meidroth and Teel becoming mainstays in Chicago's lineup for years to come, and that's a home run given the question marks around Crochet at the time — question marks that are still swirling despite the success he's had in Boston.
White Sox regrade: A
Red Sox' Garrett Crochet trade regrade
It's pretty ironic that, given the roller-coaster ride Crochet's been on across two years with the Red Sox, Boston's grade in this trade winds up pretty much right where it started.
At the time, we thought that Crochet was a high-risk, high-reward proposition, a lefty with obvious ace stuff who was dogged by workload an injury concerns. Sure enough, we've seen both sides of that coin play out so far: Crochet was one of the very best pitchers in the sport in 2025, finishing second to Tarik Skubal in AL Cy Young voting, but he managed just 30 innings of a 6.30 ERA this year before landing on the IL with a shoulder issue.
Crochet did manage to get back on the field in October, making a relief appearance in Boston's Game 2 loss on Wednesday night. And he could well have a healthy offseason and get back to making good on the six-year, $170 million extension the Red Sox gave him last March. But the fact is that he's cracked 100 innings in a season exactly twice in his baseball career; he's only cleared 150 innings once, and the very next year his shoulder started barking. Can he be a year-in, year-out ace? That remains to be seen, and that means the jury is very much still out for Boston here — especially as they struggle to find upgrades at the exact positions where Meidroth and Teel are thriving.

item.content:encoded:
One of two National League Wild Card Series wrapped up on Wednesday night when the San Diego Padres completed their two-game sweep of the Chicago Cubs.
The series win for San Diego means it will hit the road and travel to the Midwest for an NLDS showdown against the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers.
The two teams met six times in the regular season, with the Padres taking four of six games from the Brewers. Let's dive into who performed well from each side in those six games.
Offensively for San Diego, it was a bit of an unlikely hero in the regular season series. First baseman Ty France was outstanding against the Brewers, slashing .389/.421/.556, good for an OPS of .977 with a homer and three walks.
Wednesday's playoff hero Gavin Sheets also was stellar against Milwaukee, slashing .308/.471/.589, good for an OPS of 1.009 with four walks and a game-winning home run early in the season.
The San Diego bullpen arms were also solid, especially Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller, who combined for five shutout innings across five appearances.
Ty France drills a solo home run to left field and cuts the Padres' deficit to 2-1 in the bottom of the 2nd!
Brewers @ Padres#MLB #ForTheFaithful pic.twitter.com/fzfv1Pd9GQ
GAVIN SHEETS 9th-INNING HEROICS
Down to their last out, the @Padres have rallied! pic.twitter.com/yO0CxqvN33
Milwaukee did not have much offensive success against San Diego, averaging just 3.5 runs per game. There were still encouraging signs, though, especially from the first base duo of Jake Bauers and Andrew Vaughn.
Bauers had 18 at-bats against the Padres, slashing .278/.381/.444 with three doubles and three RBI. Vaughn hit .294 with two RBI in 17 at-bats.
NL CY Young frontrunner and Game 1 starter Jacob Misiorowski made one start against the Padres in the regular season and it was excellent. Misiorowski tossed seven shutout innings with zero walks and 10 strikeouts. Left-hander Kyle Harrison was also good against the Padres, posting a 2.79 ERA across two starts and 9 2/3 innings.
10 strikeouts for Jacob Misiorowski
He completes 7 IP for the first time in 2026! pic.twitter.com/nsJoZX3DVp
Milwaukee has a slight advantage in the starting pitching department, but the two bullpens may be the deciding factor in the series.
They ranked first and third in the National League in ERA this season and the ultimate deciding factor may be which bullpen blinks first and lets a late lead slip away.

item.content:encoded:
Will Red Sox' Sonny Gray retire? Garrett Crochet hints at very real possibility appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox entered the offseason with one question hanging over Sonny Gray. Garrett Crochet acknowledged that retirement is a real possibility after Boston's Wild Card sweep by the New York Yankees. Gray, who joined the Red Sox from the St. Louis Cardinals last offseason, delivered an ace-level season. He finished 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA and 4.3 WAR. Now, his next move remains uncertain.
Boston Globe reporter Tim Healey asked Gray whether Boston could remain a destination if he pitches in 2027.
"I don't know," Gray said.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
That answer leaves the Red Sox staring at a rotation decision. Gray turns 37 in November, but his production suggests he can still help a contender. His future may come down to something bigger than numbers. Family, timing, and the chance to walk away on his own terms could matter just as much.
Red Sox' Garrett Crochet offers emotional Sonny Gray message
Red Sox beat writer Chris Cotillo shared Crochet's reaction as Gray weighs retirement.
"I was telling him that a second ago, whatever him and his family decide, it was a joy to watch this year. I still think he's got a lot to give the game, but there's something to be said about going out on your own terms, I suppose. Whatever he ultimately decides, that'll be something that as a team, we support him on. But it was a pleasure having him here in Boston."
Crochet's message captured the mood after a painful ending. Boston's season ended quickly, with the Yankees sweeping the Wild Card series and sending the Red Sox home.
Still, Gray gave Boston stability all season. He became one of the club's most reliable starters and finished with some of the best numbers of his career. Under the postseason lights, his final appearance may have become his final MLB start.
If so, Sonny Gray would leave on his terms. If not, could one more season with the Red Sox be waiting?
Related: Red Sox most to blame for embarrassing AL Wild Card Series sweep by Yankees

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

item.title: [NBC Sports Boston] Sonny Gray not happy with Chad Tracy's bullpen decision in Red Sox' season-ending loss

item.content:encoded:
Having been in the big leagues since 2013, Sonny Gray has accumulated a lot of stats in his career. He certainly can't be aware of all of them, but there's one this year that he clearly knew by heart.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, after the Boston Red Sox were swept out of the Wild Card Series against the rival New York Yankees. "I think that's a fact."
Indeed, the 36-year-old was great when facing a lineup for a third time this year, holding hitters to a .180 average while posting a 1.99 ERA.
Yet, while the crafty veteran was aware of his effectiveness the third time through the batting order, his manager was either unaware or not interested in letting Gray pitch out of a miniature jam with Boston's season on the line.
After Gray allowed two singles with the Yankees leading 1-0 in the fifth, first-year manager Chad Tracy strode to the mound and inexplicably called upon lefty reliever Erik Miller for the second straight night at the same exact point in the game.
That move backfired immediately in Game 1, when Miller replaced Payton Tolle and surrendered a home run on his third pitch. And it failed again in Game 2, with Miller giving up two hits to the only batters he faced. The first was Cody Bellinger, who ripped an RBI single off Miller's slider to double the Yankees' lead to 2-0.
Gray, who will finish in the top three of AL Cy Young voting this year, felt he should have been given the chance to at least finish the fifth inning.
"I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. I think you could probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way," Gray said. "I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted. But what can you do?"
Gray added: "I would have liked to been trusted in that moment."
Certainly, Gray's work both this season and throughout his career earned him a start in the playoffs over Ranger Suarez, who's one of the best postseason pitchers in baseball history. And at just 70 pitches, and after getting proper rest down the stretch, Gray was far from being on the ropes when Tracy made his call.
More Red Sox Coverage
Even though the decision to go to Miller allowed the Yankees to instantly double their leads in both games of the sweep, Tracy defended his decisions.
"[Tolle and Gray] are great, yeah. Our bullpen's been great all year, too," Tracy said. "It's a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room we have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to [keep the starters in the game]. But trying to be aggressive and create tough matchups, and it just didn't work out."
Tracy's assertion that the bullpen has been great all year is true overall, but it doesn't apply to Miller specifically.
After joining the Red Sox as the return in the Marcelo Mayer trade, Miller made a strong first impression, posting a 0.63 ERA and 1.047 WHIP in his first 14 appearances. He struck out 25 batters and walked just six in that span, earning a trusted spot for high-leverage, late-game situations for Boston.
But his effectiveness nosedived late in the year, when he posted a 12.46 ERA and 2.538 WHIP over his final five appearances, walking six batters while striking out just four.
Those struggles clearly continued in Game 1, when Miller gave up a home run and an infield single in his one-third of an inning, but Tracy — with his full complement of high-leverage bullpen arms available — went right back to Miller in Game 2. For a second straight night, Miller could not deliver.
Tracy and the Red Sox felt comfortable giving the ball to Tolle in Game 1 on the road in Yankee Stadium. Yet with two outs and nobody on in the fifth, and with Tolle at just 83 pitches, Tracy took that ball away and gave it to a reliever in whom the manager should have lost trust.
Tracy and the Red Sox then felt comfortable giving the ball to Gray in Game 2, this time with the season hanging in the balance. Yet with two outs and two runners aboard in the fifth, Tracy again took the ball out of the hand of the trusted starter to place it in the shaky left hand of Miller.
Both times, the move did not work. And though the correlation may not be strictly scientific, both bullpen moves led to Game 1 and Game 2 spiraling out of control from that point forward.
Gray, who's set to become a free agent this offseason unless he retires, said that Tracy did not give him an explanation for the move. Gray was also asked if Boston would be a "destination" if he does choose to pitch again next year.
"I don't know," he answered.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Red Sox Paid a Massive Price for Adley Rutschman to Win in October. Then They Went 0-2
item.dc:creator: Gary Adornato
item.description: Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October. Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman. item.content:encoded:
Boston was already headed toward the playoffs when it surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for Rutschman. The Yankees reportedly rejected Baltimore’s asking price — then swept the Red Sox out of October.
Let’s be clear about why the Boston Red Sox acquired Adley Rutschman.
They didn’t need him to save their season.
They didn’t need him to drag them into postseason contention.
And they certainly didn’t surrender four prospects and their starting major-league catcher simply to hang a Wild Card banner.
Boston was already one of baseball’s hottest teams when it acquired Rutschman from the Baltimore Orioles at the Aug. 3 trade deadline. The Red Sox had transformed their season with a remarkable summer surge and were firmly positioned to reach the postseason.
Rutschman was supposed to provide something more.
October.
The Red Sox paid an enormous price to a division rival because they believed adding a three-time All-Star catcher could help turn a playoff team into a championship team.
Instead, their postseason lasted two games.
The New York Yankees completed an embarrassing two-game sweep Wednesday night, beating Boston 9-2 after a 9-0 demolition in Game 1.
Final aggregate score: Yankees 18, Red Sox 2.
Boston managed only seven hits in 18 innings and batted .117 in the series. The Yankees did all of it without three-time American League MVP Aaron Judge, who was sidelined by a calf injury.
And Rutschman?
The expensive deadline addition Boston acquired specifically to make a difference at this time of year couldn’t make one.
Making matters considerably worse, the Yankees reportedly had their own opportunity to acquire Rutschman.
They decided Baltimore’s price was too high.
Then they sent Boston home.
Boston Didn’t Need Adley Rutschman to Reach the Playoffs
This is the most important context when evaluating the trade.
The Red Sox weren’t desperately chasing the final Wild Card position when chief baseball officer Craig Breslow made the deal.
Boston had gone 23-3 beginning July 2, establishing itself as one of baseball’s hottest teams and putting itself firmly on a postseason trajectory before Rutschman ever put on a Red Sox uniform.
That’s why simply pointing out that Boston reached the postseason after acquiring him misses the point.
Reaching October wasn’t supposed to justify the trade.
Winning in October was.
The Red Sox ultimately finished 87-75 and secured a Wild Card berth. Then the Yankees eliminated them in two games.
So what exactly did Boston’s massive deadline investment change?
Not its playoff destination and certainly not its playoff result.
Adley Rutschman Didn’t Deliver When Boston Needed Him Most
This was the stage for which Boston acquired Rutschman.
Instead, the Red Sox scored two runs in two games.
Rutschman finished the series 1-for-8 with three strikeouts and did not drive in a run as Boston’s offense was overwhelmed by Cam Schlittler and Max Fried.
And one of his most consequential moments came defensively during Boston’s disastrous sixth inning Wednesday.
With the Red Sox trailing 2-1 and desperately trying to keep their season alive, Spencer Jones reached first after swinging at a third strike from Garrett Crochet that got away from Rutschman.
Jones then stole second and advanced to third when Rutschman’s throw sailed into center field.
George Lombard Jr. followed with an RBI single.
The inning disintegrated from there.
By the time Boston finally recorded the third out, New York had scored six runs and transformed a one-run elimination game into another rout.
It would be ridiculous to blame Rutschman for Boston’s elimination. The Red Sox were comprehensively outplayed, their offense disappeared and their pitching couldn’t contain New York when the series was on the line.
But that’s precisely why the trade deserves scrutiny.
Boston didn’t surrender a collection of valuable young players for another complementary piece.
It paid for a difference-maker.
When the difference needed to be made, it wasn’t.
Look at What Boston Gave Baltimore
The price looks even more jarring now.
Baltimore received five players:
RHP Anthony Eyanson: Boston’s No. 2 prospect at the time of the trade and a top-50 prospect in baseball. He immediately became Baltimore’s top-ranked prospect.
RHP Kyson Witherspoon: Another highly regarded pitching prospect who immediately became one of the better prospects in Baltimore’s system.
OF Enddy Azocar: A promising young outfielder who added another high-upside asset to Baltimore’s farm system.
C Carlos Narváez: Boston’s starting major-league catcher, giving Baltimore an immediate replacement behind the plate.
OF Harold Rivas: The 18-year-old outfielder eventually sent to Baltimore as the player to be named later.
Boston received Rutschman, catcher Jake Rogers and cash.
Four prospects and a starting major-league catcher.
Sent directly to an American League East rival.
That’s not a routine deadline upgrade.
That’s a significant transfer of organizational value made specifically because Boston believed Rutschman could help it win immediately.
The immediate payoff?
Thirty-two regular-season games and a postseason that lasted two losses.
The Yankees Were Offered Adley Rutschman, Too. They Walked Away.
This is where Boston’s decision becomes even harder to swallow.
The Red Sox weren’t the only AL East contender that discussed Rutschman with Baltimore.
The Yankees reportedly explored acquiring him before the deadline.
According to the New York Post, Baltimore’s asking price from New York included pitching prospect Elmer Rodríguez, catcher Austin Wells, outfield prospect Yostin Pena and either Will Warren or Ryan Weathers.
The Yankees decided it was too much.
Boston decided its own massive prospect package wasn’t.
Two months later, the teams met in October.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox.
That alone doesn’t prove New York made the correct long-term decision. Prospects fail. Rutschman could return to All-Star form. The careers of the players Boston and New York retained or surrendered will ultimately determine how these decisions age.
But the immediate comparison couldn’t be much uglier for Breslow.
New York kept its catcher.
It kept its prospects.
It kept its young pitching.
And it eliminated the team that paid Baltimore’s price.
Ben Rice Made the Comparison Even More Painful
There is another piece of this that Boston probably doesn’t want to think about.
The Yankees didn’t merely decline to acquire Rutschman.
They watched one of their own young players become the kind of offensive weapon Boston hoped it was acquiring.
Ben Rice erupted for 41 home runs during the regular season.
Then he opened the postseason by destroying the Red Sox.
Rice went 4-for-5 with two home runs and six RBIs in New York’s 9-0 Game 1 victory.
Six RBIs.
Boston scored two runs in the entire series.
The Yankees didn’t need to surrender a massive package to Baltimore to find an impact bat.
They developed one.
Boston went shopping for an established star.
Then Rice helped send its expensive new catcher and the rest of the Red Sox home.
Boston Didn’t Even Get the Superstar Version of Rutschman
Boston can at least point to Rutschman’s impressive résumé.
He was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2019 MLB Draft, became the centerpiece of Baltimore’s rebuild and developed into one of baseball’s most recognizable catchers.
But the Red Sox weren’t trading for his résumé.
They were trading for what he could do in 2026 and 2027.
That’s an important distinction.
Rutschman was already on the injured list with wrist inflammation when Boston acquired him.
Once healthy, he played 32 regular-season games for the Red Sox and hit .222 with a .278 on-base percentage and .410 slugging percentage.
His OPS was .688.
He hit five home runs and drove in 13 runs.
His 92 OPS+ meant he was eight percent below league average offensively after adjusting for league and ballpark conditions.
Boston surrendered four prospects and its starting catcher for an immediate upgrade and received below-average regular-season offense.
Then came October.
No transformational performance.
No postseason victory.
No series win.
Craig Breslow Made a Win-Now Trade. Boston Didn’t Win.
There is nothing inherently wrong with trading prospects.
Contending organizations sometimes become too protective of players who have never taken a major-league at-bat. Windows close. Players get hurt. Rosters change.
When an organization has an opportunity to win a championship, there are times when being aggressive is exactly the right approach.
But here’s the other side of that philosophy:
If you’re going to make a win-now trade, eventually you have to win now.
Breslow pushed a significant portion of Boston’s prospect capital into the middle of the table.
The Red Sox responded by finishing 87-75.
Then they arrived at Yankee Stadium and were outscored 18-2 in two games.
That’s not an October run.
That’s barely an October appearance.
The Yankees advanced. Boston went home before October was two days old.
And the player Breslow acquired as his blockbuster deadline upgrade produced neither the offensive impact nor the postseason difference Boston was paying for.
Meanwhile, Baltimore Gets to Keep All Five Players
This is the part that could hurt Boston considerably longer than Wednesday night’s loss.
Baltimore doesn’t need all four prospects to become stars for this trade to sting the Red Sox.
It doesn’t even need two of them to become stars.
If Eyanson develops into a quality major-league starter, or Witherspoon reaches his upside, or Azocar or Rivas eventually develops into an everyday player, Boston could spend years watching a division rival benefit from its deadline gamble.
Narváez is already a major-league catcher.
The Orioles essentially converted one player approaching his final season of club control into five assets.
Boston acquired the short-term star.
Baltimore acquired years of potential value.
And the Orioles didn’t have to wait long to see the first part of their gamble work.
Rutschman’s first postseason with Boston lasted two games.
Now Boston May Have to Pay for Rutschman Again
That’s what makes this more than simply a failed 2026 deadline gamble.
Rutschman can become a free agent after the 2027 season.
Boston therefore has another major decision coming.
The Red Sox can attempt to sign him to a lucrative extension, committing significant long-term money to a catcher whose offensive production has declined from his early-career peak and who has dealt with injuries.
They can let him play out 2027 and risk watching him depart as a free agent roughly 17 months after surrendering four prospects and Narváez to acquire him.
Or they can eventually trade him and attempt to recover some of the organizational value they sent Baltimore.
None looks particularly attractive this morning.
And Boston should be especially careful about allowing the enormous acquisition cost to influence its next decision.
The prospects are gone regardless.
Paying Rutschman a huge extension because Boston already paid dearly to acquire him would be classic sunk-cost thinking.
The next decision has to be based on what Rutschman is likely to provide going forward, not what Boston surrendered to get him.
He could make this entire discussion look foolish next season. Rutschman is talented enough to rebound, produce another All-Star season and become an important part of a championship contender.
But that’s a 2027 argument.
We know what happened in 2026.
Boston was already headed toward the postseason.
Baltimore put an enormous price on Rutschman.
The Yankees looked at that price and walked away.
The Red Sox paid it.
Then those two teams met in October.
New York outscored Boston 18-2, swept the Red Sox in two games and advanced without Aaron Judge.
Boston went home.
And Baltimore still has all five players.

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray sends frustrated message to Red Sox manager Chad Tracy over early pull in elimination game originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox suffered the most ignominious of results during their AL Wild Card series, seeing their postseason hopes dash in just two matches against the Yankees.
The contests weren't all that competitive. New York blanked Boston in the opener before advancing courtesy of a 9-2 win on Wednesday.
The Red Sox's bats failed to muster much of a murmur when confronted with the Pintstripers' pitching. And yet, it was Chad Tracy's decision to relieve ace Sonny Gray of the ball after with one out left in the fifth inning that proved especially disorienting to those cloaked in Boston regalia.
Gray spoke out about his premature exit after the game ended. Suffice to say, he was less than pleased.
Sonny Gray reacts to Chad Tracy's early pull in elimination game
Gray was left dismayed by Tracy's decision to hand him his walking papers before the end of the fifth inning. Speaking with media following the contest, Gray reaffirmed that he was feeling confident about his ability to deliver from the mound when Tracy took the ball from him.
"I felt crisp, I felt sharp, I felt like I was just out there, competing," Gray said. "I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do."
The 36-year-old acknowledged that he surrendered more contact than he would've liked across his 4.2-inning appearance, citing Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run, as well as a gaggle of singles. Nevertheless, he tends to get better the deeper he goes into contests — a fact he made sure to highlight during his post-game presser.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said. "I think that's a fact. Yeah, I mean, I would have liked to deliver with me in that moment. But that's the competitor that I am.
"I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way."
Gray held hitters to a .515 OPS when facing them the third time in the order in 2026. His 38 split OPS+ was comfortably better than the league's average. Hitters posted a .515 OPS when facing Gray the third time in an order, the third-worst mark in baseball (and worst in the American League) among pitchers to face at least 100 batters in that situation.
In other words, if there was ever a candidate to stay in the game for longer than conventional wisdom might suggest, it was Gray.
"I would have liked to been trusted in that moment," Gray said.
He's not the only one to think so. Willson Contreras blasted the organization for prioritizing data over intangibles in its postseason run. According to Mass Live's Chris Cotillo, Gray's premature exit was at the heart of the catcher's frustrations.
""It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There's a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I'll state it like that."
None of this is what those of a Red Sox disposition would want to hear at the end of the season. At 36, it's unclear what Gray's future plans are. He has a year left on his contract with Boston, but has an out should Boston attempt to exercise its club option. Garrett Crochet suggested that retirement is a possibility for the aging hurler, who posted some of the best numbers of his career in 2026.
Regardless, Tracy's decision to pull him is certain to leave a sour taste in Gray's mouth, something that could prove difficult to grapple with when it's time to figure out if he'd like to return to Fenway in 2027.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Another unsuccessful Red Sox season ends with early exit, leaves players venting about Sonny Gray's early hook
item.dc:creator: Julian McWilliams

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For the second year in a row, the Red Sox season ended where it began: at Yankee Stadium.
On Wednesday night, before September officially turned to October, marking the true beginning of the postseason, the Red Sox were sent packing, again, by the Yankees. Unlike last year in this round, there was no need for a third game. No need for Aaron Judge. No need for Giancarlo Stanton. The Red Sox lost 9-2 on Wednesday night, a day after getting blown out 9-0 in the opener.
Instead, only embarrassment lived. Only quietness existed inside a clubhouse that will have to chew on two humiliating losses in the American League Wild Card Series.
There will be plenty from this season worth pointing to.
The Red Sox were once 14 games under .500. Then came the midsummer streak when they rattled off 15 straight wins and went 27-3 from the start of July through the beginning of August. Willson Contreras's season was vital to this club's success. Caleb Durbin's toughness and grit helped set the tone. The offense showed some malleability, deviating from its pull-side approach and becoming less one-dimensional.
All of that happened. All of it mattered.
But don't let any of it obscure the reality. Don't let the front office twist this. Don't let it off the hook too easily. The front office pivoted to Durbin only once it missed out on Alex Bregman.
And when October arrived -- pardon, the end of September -- the Red Sox finished their season with one fewer postseason win than they had a year ago.
It has now been five years since postseason baseball was last played at Fenway Park, the longest October drought for the ballpark since 1976-85.
Don't be fooled by the summer surge. Don't be fooled by the progress.
This season wasn't a success.
"Uncompetitive." Isaiah Kiner-Falefa said afterward. "We got boat-raced. To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable."
"I mean, right now it's, regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series," manager Chad Tracy said. "And that ended for us tonight."
'I would have liked to have been trusted'
Frustration mounted in the clubhouse afterward, too. For a second straight night, Tracy pulled his starter early for Erik Miller, and it immediately backfired.
This time, it was Sonny Gray, who had allowed just one run, a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the top of the fourth. In the fifth, Gray worked around a Trent Grisham leadoff single, recording two outs on a force out and a groundout. Yet, after a Ben Rice single put runners at first and third, Tracy inexplicably ended Gray's evening at just 70 pitches with Cody Bellinger looming.
Instantly, much like Tuesday night, the Yankees capitalized. Bellinger laced a single to right, extending the lead to 2-0.
Forced to piece together the rest of the game with a bullpen that included appearances from Garrett Crochet and Garrett Whitlock, the Red Sox watched the Yankees pour on eight runs against their relievers.
A disgruntled Gray didn't hold back his sentiments following the outing.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League the third time through the order," Gray said. He then paused for a moment. "I think that's a fact. I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Gray was spot-on. He, indeed, was the best starter in the American League the third time through the order, carrying a 1.99 ERA in 45 ⅓ innings pitched, a large enough sample size.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball and the data is here to help us," Contreras said. "But at the end of the day, we're going to need experienced and veteran guys to win games."
That points to a larger issue that has followed lead executive Craig Breslow.
The April firing of manager Alex Cora and his staff might have been the right decision. Tracy (who was named the full-time skipper last week), ideally, is the manager that Breslow envisioned at the helm. But don't let their torrid summer misconstrue the split in the clubhouse. Some players remain convinced the new coaching staff had little to do with their success.
That might have been Gray's last time in a Red Sox uniform -- or in any uniform, as the 36-year-old has contemplated retirement. Asked if he would want to return next season to the Red Sox if he decided to play:
"I don't know," Gray responded.
Roster questions looming
Roman Anthony needs to prove he can stay healthy. He was pulled from Game 1 after re-aggravating the same right hand that kept him out for 101 games. Anthony went for an MRI in Boston early Wednesday morning before returning that afternoon. It's still unclear if he needs surgery.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," he said. "But I think for me, it was to a point where it was tolerable, and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy but was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately, I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn't the case."
Remember the Big Three? Anthony, Kristian Campbell and Marcelo Mayer were supposed to represent the next wave of the Red Sox.
What do the Red Sox do with Campbell, who was stuck in Triple-A all season and put up subpar numbers? Mayer was supposed to be the heir apparent to Trevor Story. He was traded to San Francisco.
Surely, Story has aged out of being an everyday shortstop.
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela and right fielder Wilyer Abreu are proven everyday players. But if Anthony isn't healthy, the Red Sox will need to patch up left field. Jarren Duran might have played his last season in a Red Sox uniform, with many suspecting he will be traded in the offseason.
And, despite the offense coming alive this summer, that could be viewed as fool's gold. During their 37-game surge, the Sox hit .258 with a .445 slugging percentage and their run creation was 15% better than league average. Over their final 47 games, those numbers fell to a .236 average, .382 slugging percentage and they created runs 6% below the league-average mark.
Their late-season woes looked much more like the offense from the first 78 games, when the club hit .244 with a .385 slugging percentage, than the one that transformed its season.
"Obviously disappointed," Story said on getting bounced from the postseason. "A lot of thoughts, but proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the hate and everything going around, the way this team came together, we really turned the season around to get back into this position. It was something that was special."
The summer run was special, yes.
But don't let this club off the hook.
The season wasn't a success.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox players miffed by Chad Tracy’s decision to pull stater early
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo

But with two outs in the bottom of the fifth, with his team clinging to a 1-0 lead and runners at the corners after Yankees slugger Ben Rice tagged him for a single, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy decided to take the ball from his starter and go to Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger, opting for a lefty-on-lefty matchup e
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Sonny Gray has been one of the top pitchers in the American League all season, and for much of Wednesday night he did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
But with two outs in the bottom of the fifth, with his team clinging to a 1-0 lead and runners at the corners after Yankees slugger Ben Rice tagged him for a single, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy decided to take the ball from his starter and go to Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger, opting for a lefty-on-lefty matchup even though Gray was only at 70 pitches and Miller has been shaky to close the season.
The move didn’t work out. Bellinger hit an RBI single and the Yankees ultimately went on to score eight runs against the Red Sox bullpen, winning Game 2 by a lopsided score of 9-2 to complete the Wild Cad Series sweep.
Following the game Gray was candid about his displeasure with getting the hook.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact. Yeah I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment but that’s the competitor I am,” Gray said. “I think you can probably ask the guys and they feel the same way. I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted, but what can you do?”
“I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment,” Gray continued, adding later that he hasn’t spoken with Tracy yet and wasn’t sure if there would be any point.
Gray wasn’t the only Red Sox veteran miffed about the decision. Asked for his thoughts shortly afterwards, first baseman Willson Contreras responded only by zipping his lips.
Tracy explained that he decided to go to Miller because they had fallen behind and he felt he had to be aggressive, especially given how much the offense was struggling to score runs. The Yankees had already gotten a couple of hits against Gray in the inning, and with how reliable the bullpen has been throughout the season he decided to play the matchup in hopes of putting out the fire.
“We’re trailing. We’re struggling to score runs. And when you get in spots where struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go,” Tracy said.
“Our bullpen’s been great all year,” Tracy continued later. “It’s a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room you have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to do that. But trying to be aggressive and create tough match-ups, and it just didn’t work out.”
Tracy also went to the bullpen early in Game 1 as well, pulling Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings in Boston’s eventual 9-0 loss. Tolle’s pitch count was a relatively modest 83 pitches at that point, and though the rookie took a much more charitable view than his older teammates, he admitted any starter would rather keep going in that spot.
“As a competitor as you want to go as long as you can. I think for me I see it as there’s people that are going to – I trust our bullpen and the way they’ve gone about this year, I think they’ve been incredible, they’ve picked me up more times than I can count,” Tolle said. “It’s the postseason, you’ve got to limit as much as you can so whenever those situations happen, for me, ok, this is what’s going to be best for the team.”

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.
Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said (h/t SNY). "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
When asked if he felt the Red Sox relied too much on data, Contreras nodded as he said, "If you watch the game."
Tracy, who had also pulled Game 1 starter Payton Tolle early, called Gray off the mound with two runners on base, one out remaining and the Red Sox trailing by one run in the bottom of the fifth.
Gray was replaced by Erik Miller, who on his third pitch of the game allowed a two-RBI single from Cody Bellinger.
Tracy then turned to Garrett Crochet for the sixth inning. Crochet allowed a run and loaded the bases until he was removed for Garrett Whitlock, who allowed five more runs before he was able to close out the frame.
Tracy said after the elimination loss he used the same reasoning to pull Gray as he had to remove Tolle from a Game 1 shutout loss to the Yankees.
"We're trailing. We're struggling to score runs, and when you get into spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive," Tracy told reporters Wednesday night.
The Yankees will now advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, while the Red Sox will concede their second Wild Card loss in as many years. Ranger Suárez, who was slated to start a potential deciding Game 3, will not pitch this postseason.
The Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora and turned to Tracy following a 10-17 start to the season. Tracy lost his interim tag and inked a three-year extension after leading the club to clinch a postseason berth.
Tracy will now be tasked with helping his club find a way to respond next fall to scoring two runs across their two postseason games.

item.title: [thebiglead.com] Red Sox get brutal Roman Anthony injury update immediately before Game 2 vs. Yankees

The specifics were revealed Wednesday—and they aren’t good. Tracy said that Anthony reaggravated the same injury that knocked him out for almost six months earlier in the season. U
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy essentially ruled outfielder Roman Anthony out of the postseason in his pregame remarks to reporters on Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Anthony was removed from Game 1 of the Red Sox’s American League wild-card series against the New York Yankees on Tuesday with an unspecified right-hand injury. The specifics were revealed Wednesday—and they aren’t good.
Tracy said that Anthony reaggravated the same injury that knocked him out for almost six months earlier in the season. Unfortunately, imaging performed Tuesday night also revealed multiple new strains in his hand. Anthony was immediately removed from Boston’s 26-man roster, leaving him ineligible to return for the American League Division Series should the Red Sox advance.
Andruw Monasterio replaced Anthony after the 22-year-old outfielder checked his swing in separate at-bats, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. Following the game, Tracy told reporters that Anthony’s hand was “uncomfortable” and “flared up” on one of the check swings.
Facing elimination
Having won Game 1 by a 9-0 score, the Yankees can eliminate the Red Sox in their best-of-three series Wednesday night.
The Red Sox can extend the series with a victory in Game 2. A winner-take-all Game 3 would happen at Yankee Stadium Thursday night.
Boston clinched the AL’s second wild-card berth—forcing them to play this round on the road—largely without Anthony, who slashed .245/.339/.396 over just 55 regular-season games. He finished third in AL Rookie of the Year voting in 2025, slashing .292/.396/.463 in 71 games.
Now, with Anthony’s season likely over, the Red Sox will try to forge ahead without their young star as they look to come back against their archrivals.

item.title: [New York Post] Willson Contreras takes veiled shot at Red Sox front office after brutal sweep: ‘Computers telling you what to do’
item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description: Willson Contreras provided one of the few good Red Sox swings in this embarrassing showing against the Yankees and then took another postgame whack at his team. The first-year Red Sox slugger seemingly took aim at the organization’s analytics philosophy after their 9-2 Game 2 loss to the Yankees in a wild-card sweep. “There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game. If you watch the game, we have to get better at the game running, we have to get better at taking care of the ste
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras provided one of the few good Red Sox swings in this embarrassing showing against the Yankees and then took another postgame whack at his team.
The first-year Red Sox slugger seemingly took aim at the organization’s analytics philosophy after their 9-2 Game 2 loss to the Yankees in a wild-card sweep.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game. If you watch the game, we have to get better at the game running, we have to get better at taking care of the stealers, we have to do a lot of different stuff,” said Contreras, who homered off Max Fried in the sixth inning. “It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball.
“The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
If there was any confusion about who Contreras, 34, was throwing under the bus, the line “you have computers telling you what to do” clears that all up.
The Red Sox, like any team that thrives in baseball, rely on analytics to help them.
There will always be a debate about how much of the human element should be blended into games versus specifically relying on data to make decisions.
Contreras received a follow-up question about whether the Red Sox rely too much on data, and provided a cryptic decision.
“If you watch the game,” he said, “if you watch the game.”
His shot at the “computers” is notable since it came after two seemingly analytics-driven decisions for the Red Sox backfired, one in each game.
First-year manager Chad Tracy pulled Payton Tolle in a 1-0 game to have lefty reliever Erik Miller face Ben Rice in the fifth inning in Game 1 and Rice promptly homered.
He tried a similar move Wednesday in yanking Sonny Gray in the fifth for Miller to face Cody Bellinger in a 1-0 game and the Yankees outfielder laced an RBI single.
When asked his thoughts on pulling Gray, Contreras did not verbally answer but said all he needed to say by instead pretending to sow his mouth shut.
Contreras also provided an interesting answer about what happened to the team’s once-scorching lineup, with Boston tearing the cover off the ball during its 32-5 run that saved its season and then slumping to end the regular season before this two-run showing over 18 postseason innings.
“That’s a good question,” he replied. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer. We got eliminated, that’s the bottom line.
Contreras is under contract with Boston for the 2027 season and the team holds a $17.5 team option for 2028, and he produced a career-best .901 OPS this past season.
Boston surely will aim this offseason to build a deeper lineup around him and Roman Antony and if the team value his two cents, it seems he’ll be telling them to forget the data and use their eyes.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Roman Anthony’s Hand Injury Reveals Darker Truth For Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Spencer Rickles
item.description: The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes. Scans Show Worse Damage Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results we
item.content:encoded:
The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes.
Scans Show Worse Damage
Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results were grim. "We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exasperating the old injuries. It's not great," Tracy told reporters, per ESPN.
This isn't a minor tweak. The 22-year-old missed 101 games earlier this year with a torn ligament in his right ring finger. He only played 55 regular season games before this latest setback. His stats dropped from a .292 average last year to .245 this season. The Red Sox signed him to a massive $130 million extension hoping for a star. Now that deal looks like a gamble on a broken body.
A Brutal Playoff Rule
There is a cruel twist in the rulebook that fans need to know. If a player gets removed from a playoff roster during a series, he cannot play in the next series either. This means Anthony won't just miss Game 2 against the Yankees. He will be ineligible for the entire ALDS if Boston advances. The team replaced Anthony on the roster with Curtis Mead, according to MLB Trade Rumors.
Tracy tried to frame it as a common issue for players coming off long layoffs. "He's obviously coming off that. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it's fine, it goes away," Tracy said. But the reality is different today. "Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," he added, per ESPN. The hope is gone. The pain is real.
The Cost of a Broken Star
The Red Sox are one loss from elimination. They need every bat they can get. Jahmai Jones is set to hit leadoff as the designated hitter. The lineup includes Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu. Sonny Gray will start on the mound against a former team. But the lineup is missing its most promising young hitter.
Anthony was supposed to be the centerpiece of the next decade. His wrist issues have already cost the team almost four months of the regular season. Now they lose him in the playoffs too. The $130 million contract is secure, but the on-field value is gone for now. Boston has to hope Mead or Seigler can step up immediately. The clock is ticking, and the scans say time is not on their side.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras Sound Off on Red Sox's ALWCS Loss vs. Yankees
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
