item.title: [Boston.com] Curtis Mead to join Red Sox playoff roster in place of Roman Anthony
item.dc:creator: Conor Ryan
item.description: Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories. With Roman Anthony’s availability in doubt this postseason, the Red Sox are turning to another slugger to add pop to the lineup. The Red Sox and MLB announced Wednesday evening that Boston completed a playoff roster substitution, with infielder/DH Curtis Mead joining the Red Sox in place of Anthony, who suffered another hand injury during Boston’s Game 1 loss to the Yankees in the Wild Card series. It remains to be see
item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
With Roman Anthony’s availability in doubt this postseason, the Red Sox are turning to another slugger to add pop to the lineup.
The Red Sox and MLB announced Wednesday evening that Boston completed a playoff roster substitution, with infielder/DH Curtis Mead joining the Red Sox in place of Anthony, who suffered another hand injury during Boston’s Game 1 loss to the Yankees in the Wild Card series.
It remains to be seen just how much Mead can offer a Red Sox lineup that was completely befuddled by Cam Schlittler in Game 1.
Mead — acquired by Boston in a one-for-one swap with Connelly Early as part of a trade with the Nationals in July — has not appeared in a game since July 27 after suffering a fractured wrist.
He will not be in Boston’s lineup to open a do-or-die Game 2 in the Bronx on Wednesday, but the 25-year-old Mead said that he’ll be ready to contribute if called upon during this series — likely in a pinch-hitting spot in this upcoming bout with the Yankees.
“I think I feel 100 percent,” Mead told reporters at Yankee Stadium, including MassLive’s Sean McAdam. “I feel like I’m ready however the team needs me. I’m excited to hopefully get the opportunity tonight or tomorrow.”
Despite Mead’s comments, the Red Sox infielder hasn’t had much of a ramp-up before potentially getting thrown into the middle of a high-stakes playoff game on Wednesday or Thursday.
Mead broke his wrist in his Red Sox debut, taking a fastball near his hand off a check swing in just his second plate appearance with his new team. He couldn’t take part in any rehab games before Boston’s minor-league campaigns wrapped — and only faced live BP earlier this week down in Florida.
“Obviously, it’s not ideal, right?” Mead told McAdam of his accelerated return to game action. “But I think with the injury to Roman and even Mickey [Gasper] and just some guys being banged up, I feel like in as good a spot if not better than some of those guys. So I definitely feel like I can put together some good at-bats.”
With Mead replacing Anthony on Boston’s playoff roster, Anthony will be ineligible to play until at least the ALCS — although it’s unclear if the Red Sox get that far, and whether Anthony will be cleared to play by then.
“Sore,” Tracy said of Anthony’s status on Wednesday afternoon. “He was sent back last night after leaving the game. We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exacerbating the old injuries. It’s not great. I know there’s enough there, and enough new stuff there, where [Anthony] is not gonna be able to play.”
Mead might be a wild card this postseason due to that injury and his limited time facing live pitching. But the young slugger was once viewed as a sizable upgrade for Boston’s lineup this summer before his untimely injury.
Mead was in the middle of a breakout season with the Nationals before arriving in Boston in July, with the Australian-born infielder batting .256 with 17 home runs, 48 RBI and an .852 OPS over 87 games in Washington.
If the Red Sox do extend their season for at least another game with a win in Game 2, Mead said that he’s not sure if he’ll be called into the lineup for a decisive Game 3 on Thursday.
“I’m not sure,” Mead told McAdam. “That’s up to [Tracy] and the coaching staff. If they asked if I would be ready, yeah, I would absolutely be ready. I think the goal is to just get through the night and then assess where we’re at tomorrow.
“Probably two weeks ago, if you had asked if I thought I’d be in this position, the answer would probably be ‘no.’ It’s definitely exciting.”

item.title: [mlb.com] Anthony 'sick to my stomach' after aggravating hand injury
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne
item.description: NEW YORK – The news worsened for Red Sox outfielder/designated hitter Roman Anthony on Wednesday when he was taken off the roster for the remainder of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees after imaging back in Boston showed additional strains in his right wrist. The fact that Anthony was taken off the Wild Card Series roster means he would be ineligible to play in the AL Division Series against the Rays, should Boston advance. “I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much,
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The news worsened for Red Sox outfielder/designated hitter Roman Anthony on Wednesday when he was taken off the roster for the remainder of the American League Wild Card Series against the Yankees after imaging back in Boston showed additional strains in his right wrist.
The fact that Anthony was taken off the Wild Card Series roster means he would be ineligible to play in the AL Division Series against the Rays, should Boston advance.
“I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much,” said Anthony. “It doesn't really feel real, to be honest. There's so many different emotions and feelings throughout the course of this rehab process this year that to kind of get to this same news again, and even worse, it's just like, I don't know. It's hard to have an answer to anything right now.”
Mead has turned a corner of late with his hitting progression, recently taking live batting practice. His ramp-up to postseason action was accelerated due to Anthony’s injury, and several others (Mickey Gasper, Masataka Yoshida and Romy Gonzalez) also being unavailable due to health reasons.
“There are times when you accelerate timelines and compress things,” said Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow. “You still want to make sure you have the interests of the player and the team in mind. We’re not going to do anything that’s reckless or irresponsible, but medically, Curtis is cleared.”
Losing Anthony was tough timing for the Red Sox, who took a 9-0 loss in Game 1 of this best-of-three series. Sensing immediately it was more than a minor setback, the team hired a car to drive Anthony back to Boston after the game, and he had imaging taken on Wednesday morning.
“He is sore,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “He was sent back last night after leaving the game. Sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging, which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist, in addition to exacerbating the old [finger] injury. So it's not great.”
The sensation Anthony felt in his at-bats in Game 1 was familiar in a nauseating way.
“Basically the same thing that happened early on in the year in addition to other strains in a few muscles in other areas in the hand. So, to shorten it up, it's the same thing with more added on,” said Anthony. “Yeah. It’s brutal. It’s confusing. There’s a lot of different emotions going on that I don’t know. It’s tough to put into words, and I feel like I grinded all year throughout something to get to where I am right now and to get to play in a game last night. And for that to happen, it’s confusing and it sucks.”
The Red Sox were equally confused by the recurrence.
“As far as I know, the rehab and the return to play was the appropriate one,” said Breslow. “Last night in the game, he did something where things changed, things worsened and we need to take a fresh look at it.”
Other than feeling occasional “zingers” on swings since his return to action on Aug. 30, Anthony hadn’t felt anything close to the discomfort that took place in Game 1, when he exited the game in the sixth inning after striking out in his first two at-bats.
The best-case scenario is that rest and rehab help Anthony recover, and that surgery won’t be necessary.
“I think we're still trying to figure out exactly what happened and what the prognosis will be,” said Breslow. “It’s still so recent that we’re collecting information, and I'm sure we'll examine all of those things.”
The 22-year-old left-handed hitter has had mixed results since returning to action, slashing .262/.321/.476 with four homers and 10 RBIs in his final 103 regular-season at-bats.
“I’ve been experiencing some things with the swings and check swings over the past six weeks, and last night just felt a little more intense than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones that I had before, so it was super alarming,” Anthony said. “It got to a point where it was tough to grip a bat, so I knew this was similar to the one earlier on in the year, and that’s why we decided to go get imaging.”
And now, the Red Sox will try to win without Anthony, which they did earlier in the season, most notably during that 32-5 stretch from June 25-Aug. 8. For that to happen, players will have to heat up. Boston’s offense has been cold as a unit for weeks.
“I think he's a special talent. He's a special guy,” said Breslow. “Right now we're focused on making sure that we put ourselves in a position to win the game tonight and figure out everything that's going on with Roman's wrist. I think to talk beyond that is probably foolish at this point.”

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series
The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
The Sox won't have the services of Roman Anthony, who appeared to reaggravate his hand injury during the team's 9-0 loss in Game 1.
"We actually sent him back to Boston last evening to get there so he could be early in the morning and re-image the hand, which shows additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "So he's sore and obviously not in the lineup."
Anthony will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist during his debut with the Red Sox on July 27. Anthony would eligible to return to the lineup for the American League Championship Series.
The Sox will have long odds to beat to continue their playoff run. Teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game wild-card series have gone on to win that series 21 out of 24 times, 17 times with a sweep.
Home teams have won all nine series in which they have won the first game.
On Tuesday, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and the rest of the pitching staff held the Sox to just three hits.
Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle might have been the team's best player, but manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of a 1-run game. Reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up a homer to Dartmouth College graduate Ben Rice, and it was all downhill from there.
On Wednesday night, Gray will pitch opposite Yankees starter Max Fried.

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony is out for the foreseeable future and is no longer on the Wild Card roster after he left with a right hand injury Tuesday night.
Batting leadoff as the Red Sox designated hitter in his playoff debut, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing 2-0 in the sixth inning. New York took a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three series with a 9-0 victory.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand. Tracy said it doesn't appear the latest injury is necessarily related, as it involves muscles in the wrist.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," Anthony told reporters on Wednesday. "Last night just felt a little more intense, little bit more harsh than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones I was used to had. So it just was super alarming and got to the point where it was tough to grip a bat."
The manager said that after the game, Anthony returned to Boston for imaging on his hand, which found "additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before."
Anthony is not in Wednesday night's lineup, when the Red Sox must win to extend their season. Jahmai Jones is leading off at DH in Anthony's absence.
Wednesday night, the team announced that infielder Curtis Mead replaced Anthony on the Wild Card roster. That means that if the Red Sox advance to the ALDS, Anthony would be out for that round as well.
One of baseball's premier prospects when he arrived in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 regular-season games this season.
"He's a really good player. Certainly not something we wanted to happen and having him in there is important. But can't reiterate enough, we've dealt with things like this all year. But the show goes on, you've got to play tonight and be able to win a ballgame," Tracy said.
The manager added that it is not yet known if Anthony will need surgery.
Sonny Gray is on the mound for the Red Sox in Game 2, which is scheduled to start at 8:15 p.m.

item.content:encoded:
For the first time since July, Curtis Mead will put on a Red Sox uniform. The team hopes his hot hitting returns tonight during Game 2 of the Wild Card series against the Yankees.
Mead, a righty, replaces Roman Anthony on the roster.
This move comes after Anthony left Boston’s Game 1 loss on Tuesday after experiencing right-hand discomfort. Anthony missed nearly four months this season due to a partially torn ligament on his right ring finger.
It’s a massive opportunity for Mead, looking to help tie the series after the Yankees decimated the Red Sox in Game 1.
Wednesday will be Mead’s first time on the Red Sox roster since being placed on the IL in July. After being traded to Boston from the Nationals, Mead was hit on his left wrist in his second plate appearance in a Red Sox uniform and sustained a fracture.
Mead called the process “challenging” (per MassLive) a few weeks ago, but remained optimistic he could play. He’s available off the bench and could pinch hit, per manager Chad Tracy.
Mead was in the middle of a career season, posting 17 home runs and 48 RBIs and slashing 254/.352/.500 with an .852 OPS before being traded. His contract has him with the Red Sox through 2030.

item.title: [trentonian.com] JAY DUNN: From the Phillie Phanatic to Fireworks to the Hot Pants Patrol, Bill Giles wanted to entertain
item.dc:creator: Jay Dunn
item.description: Bill Giles died last week and every obituary I saw focused on the Phillie Phanatic. Giles is best remembered as the Phillies executive who, in 1978, oversaw the introduction of the sports world’s most famous mascot. But the obituaries shouldn’t have stopped there. item.content:encoded:
Bill Giles died last week and every obituary I saw focused on the Phillie Phanatic. Giles is best remembered as the Phillies executive who, in 1978, oversaw the introduction of the sports world’s most famous mascot.
But the obituaries shouldn’t have stopped there.
Giles was the one who once hired a circus performer to walk a tight rope that was strung from one foul pole to the other.
Giles is the one who introduced “Kiteman” and promised that on Opening Day he would fly from centerfield to home plate with the season’s first ball. He sputtered twice before getting it right the third time.
Giles is the one who made Independence Day fireworks spectacles an annual tradition. Not only did each show sell out the ballpark, but it created traffic jams all around the park as people without tickets jockeyed for vantage points.
Giles first came to Philadelphia in 1969. He was assigned to change the team’s tattered image and that was a formidable job.
The team was due to move into a new ballpark and Giles sought to make everything else new as well. He introduced new uniforms and brought a new broadcaster (Harry Kalas) as well. He hired an organist who could not only entertain the crowd but enliven it as well.
And there was the Hot Pants Patrol.
Yes, you read that right. The new stadium’s ushers were usherettes, and they were clad in uniforms that included short shorts. Giles even made ballgirls out of a few of them and stationed one down each foul line.
The introduction of The Phanatic was probably his most significant accomplishment, but he refused to take any of the credit for it.
“The costume,” he said, “is 25 percent of it. The other 75 percent is the man inside the costume.”
David Raymond was that man. He was working as an intern in the ticket office when he agreed to climb into the Phanatic suit. His father was the head football coach at the University of Delaware, but his mother was probably the one who had the greatest influence on his career as an entertainer. She was deaf, so Raymond had grown up practicing non-verbal communications — exactly what was needed for The Phanatic’s hi-jinx. He became a national sensation almost overnight.
In a perfect world Giles would have basked in the glory and ridden off into the sunset, but that’s not what happened.
Giles’ father, Warren Giles, had been a successful general manager in Cincinnati, building pennant winners in 1939 and 1940. His son yearned to do the same and in 1981 he got the opportunity. He put together an ownership group that purchased the Phillies. He names himself the general manager.
At best the results were mixed.
Almost immediately he made a horrible five-for-one trade that fizzled badly. Eight months later he fired his manager even though the club was in first place at the time.
Some aging free agents carried the team to a pennant in 1983, but everything went downhill very quickly after that. Before long the other members of his ownership group grew restless and relieved him of any meaningful authority.
The saga deserves a happy ending, but there is none.
Like an old soldier, Bill Giles just faded away.
***
I’ve been lucky enough to visit Grand Teuton National Park more than once. I’ve breathed the mountain air. I’ve climbed to the top of Inspiration Point. I’ve fished for brown trout and dined on the harvest. After dark I’ve enjoyed staring at the Milky Way. I think it’s an excellent place to enjoy the outdoors.
Now I read that somebody has suggested that a baseball stadium should be built there.
All I can say is somebody must be out of his cotton-pickin’ mind.
2026 BY THE NUMBERS: Colson Montgomery of the White Sox struck out 227 times, which is a record. His final whiff came when he swung at a pitch that hit him … Pete Alonso of the Orioles led the AL in RBIs with 113. In so doing he became the first player ever to lead both leagues in that statistic … Bryson Stott of the Phillies was originally ruled out on a stolen base attempt on Sunday, but the call was reversed after an appeal. Because of that Stott finished the season 27-for-27 on thefts … Jake McCarthy of the Rockies hit six triples in September. He finished with 13, which was second in the majors … Mackenzie Gore of the Rangers was the only pitcher to make 34 starts. He finished with an 8-11 record … The NL compiled a 384-336 edge in interleague play …The Yankees were 4-11 in extra-inning games and 17-22 in games decided by one run … Mason Fluharty of the Blue Jays appeared in 83 games as a pitcher. He produced a 7-1 record with one save … Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno went 16-for-40 in his final 10 games and became the first catcher since Buster Posey to win the NL batting crown … The Padres were 51-30 at home, but 40-41 on the road … Anthony Kay of the White Sox hit 26 batters in 158 innings. No other pitcher hit more than 17 … Eight players appeared in every one of their team’s games, but Matt Olson of the Braves is the only one to start every game and play in the field every time … Chandler Simpson of the Rays had 153 singles, which is 14 more than anyone else … Geraldo Perdomo of the Diamondbacks finished with nine sacrifice bunts and eight sacrifice flies. He was among the top 10 in the majors in both categories … Wilyer Abreu of the Red Sox led AL outfielders in assists with 13. He also led in errors with nine … Nasim Nunez of the Nationals batted only .209. but led the majors in stolen bases with 49 … Derek Hill of the Phillies and Michael Conforto of the Cubs each hit four pinch homers … Alec Burleson of the Cardinals batted .279 overall. but with runners in scoring position he hit .358. No wonder he led the majors in RBIs … Kevin Kelly of the Rays and Tyler Rogers of the Blue Jays each recorded 33 holds … Opposing batters hit .236 against Yankees pitching. Four teams posted better figures, but none of those four qualified for the postseason.
Former Hall of Fame voter Jay Dunn has written baseball for The Trentonian for 58 years. Contact him at jaydunn8@aol.com

item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: Once again, the Boston Red Sox will be without Roman Anthony for the playoffs. After being removed from the game in the sixth inning of Game 1 against the New York Yankees, the Red Sox sent him back to Boston overnight for more imaging on the hand he injured earlier in the season. The results showed aggravation of his precious injury, as well as new strains in his wrist. Reports from the Red Sox today said that this injury will keep Anthony out for the foreseeable future. The Red Sox officially
item.content:encoded:
Once again, the Boston Red Sox will be without Roman Anthony for the playoffs. After being removed from the game in the sixth inning of Game 1 against the New York Yankees, the Red Sox sent him back to Boston overnight for more imaging on the hand he injured earlier in the season. The results showed aggravation of his precious injury, as well as new strains in his wrist.
Reports from the Red Sox today said that this injury will keep Anthony out for the foreseeable future. The Red Sox officially removed Anthony from the playoff roster, meaning he is done for the Wild Card and division series, at least. If he is healthy, he could be added to the ALCS roster if Boston makes it.
Because Anthony was removed due to an injury, the Red Sox are allowed to replace him on the roster. Speculation early in the day was between two players, and ultimately, the Sox chose Curtis Mead.
Red Sox hope Curtis Mead continues early season breakout to keep them alive against Yankees
The Red Sox acquired Mead a week before the trade deadline, sending back a highly touted young pitcher, Connelly Early. Mead was in the midst of a breakout season when Boston acquired him. After bouncing around a few franchises, he settled in with the Washington Nationals this season.
Mead batted .254 with an .852 OPS in 87 games with the Nationals. He logged 17 doubles, 17 home runs, and 48 RBI. He had an almost 12% walk rate with a strikeout rate under 20%; he was one of just 22 hitters with more than 300 at-bats to do that this season. While some were wary that the infielder's breakout wasn't sustainable, his underlying metrics suggested what was happening was real.
The 25-year-old was supposed to add major pop to the Sox lineup. Unfortunately, just two at-bats into his Red Sox career, he was hit on the wrist with a pitch, causing a fracture. The injury cost him the rest of the regular season. Most of Red Sox Nation assumed it was going to be a "see you next year" scenario, but he worked his way back to health, and now the team is calling on him to step in for Anthony.
Mead has not been substituted into the lineup for Game 2 of the Wild Card, and according to MassLive's Chris Cotillo the Red Sox aren't expected to add him. Although he's not in the starting nine, it's very likely Red Sox Nation will see him pinch hit in the win-or-go-home game.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Red Sox removing Roman Anthony from postseason roster due to recurring injury
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: NEW YORK – The 2026 Red Sox season could come to an end on Wednesday night, but Roman Anthony’s year is already officially over. The 22-year-old outfielder/designated hitter was not in the Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of the Wild Card round, and will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead. Anthony not only reaggravated the right hand injury that sidelined him for over three months of the regular season, but sustained new muscular damage in his wrist, manager Chad Tracy announced pregame
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The 2026 Red Sox season could come to an end on Wednesday night, but Roman Anthony’s year is already officially over.
The 22-year-old outfielder/designated hitter was not in the Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of the Wild Card round, and will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead.
Anthony not only reaggravated the right hand injury that sidelined him for over three months of the regular season, but sustained new muscular damage in his wrist, manager Chad Tracy announced pregame.
“(Imaging) showed additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren’t there before,” Tracy said.
Tuesday’s series-opener was Anthony’s first career postseason game, as he missed last year’s Wild Card round at Yankee Stadium due to an oblique strain in early September of his rookie year. But his Game 1 as leadoff man and DH lasted all of two at-bats, both strikeouts, before Andruw Monasterio pinch-hit for him in the top of the sixth.
Anthony was not made available to the press in the visitors’ clubhouse following Tuesday night’s 9-0 Game 1 loss, and Red Sox media relations said he had already departed Yankee Stadium. Tracy explained Wednesday that they sent Anthony to Boston for testing after the previous night’s game, but that he was already on his way back to New York to be with the team for Game 2.
“He’s upset; mentally, going through it,” Tracy said of his conversations with Anthony. “It was grinding on him, for sure. He’s upset. He wants to be out there with the guys, and obviously, everything he’s gone through this year, dealing with all these different things, it’s been tough for him.”
Tracy did not have many concrete answers on next steps, after receiving the news “just midday” on Wednesday. The Sox skipper said he did not know yet if surgery is necessary, or who would replace Anthony on the roster. Speedy minor league outfielder Braiden Ward would have been a likely candidate, as he was originally with the Red Sox when they arrived in New York, but Tracy said Ward was no longer on-site.
“I just know that the imaging shows more than what was originally there,” Tracy said. “We’re trying to replace him, we have paperwork in on that (to the league office), but it’s enough there that we’re not going to have him.”
An hour later, MLB communications announced the approval of Mead as Anthony’s roster replacement.
There’s an element of brutal irony to this swap. Anthony’s hand sidelined him between May 5 and Aug. 29, and Mead has not played since suffering a wrist fracture on a hit-by-pitch in his second at-bat after the Red Sox acquired him from the Washington Nationals in late July.
But the Red Sox did not have time to dwell on any of it. Wednesday is win-or-go-home.
“Can’t reiterate enough, we’ve dealt with things like this all year,” Tracy said, “and show goes on.”

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Red Sox must hope Sonny Gray justifies their choice with Ranger Suarez's playoff pedigree looming
item.dc:creator: Brian Burrows
item.description: It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game. They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. item.content:encoded:
It's do-or-die for the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card series. Game 1 was a disaster — while Payton Tolle was able to hold the New York Yankees to one run in his 4 ⅔ innings, it really didn't matter because the offense couldn't get anything going the entire game.
They now head into Game 2 with one thing in mind: put runs on the board. The offense will need to find something against Max Fried, and they are going to need the pitching staff to keep them in the game as best it can. Sonny Gray will take the bump for the Sox in the pivotal matchup, but he may be the wrong choice.
Over the offseason, the Red Sox made two big pitching acquisitions: Gray and Ranger Suarez. Gray was a veteran who was essentially in the last year of his deal, meant to be a mid-rotation arm. Suarez was meant to be the No. 2 behind Garrett Crochet, and his playoff excellence was supposed to help after what the Red Sox starters struggled (besides Crochet) in the Wild Card last year.
Recency bias is influencing the Red Sox's starter decision for Game 2 of the Wild Card
Suarez is one of the best playoff pitchers in baseball ever. His 1.48 ERA in the postseason is the sixth-lowest for any pitcher with 40 or more playoff innings pitched. He has held hitters to a .201 batting average while striking out over nine per nine innings. His numbers in the regular season are great, but the selling point was what he could do in October.
Now, of course, the regular season played a part in the decision to start Gray in Game 2. The righty was dominant all year and could finish in the top five in Cy Young voting. Gray had a 2.72 ERA this season over 169 innings. It's hard not to guarantee a pitcher who performed so well in the regular season a start in the postseason when he was so influential in getting the team there. But Suarez is on the team for this exact moment.
In a win-or-go-home scenario, it's hard not to hand the ball to the pitcher who slows his heartbeat in the playoffs. If the Sox can win this game, it will be great to have Suarez pitching Game 3, but the Red Sox need to keep themselves in the game. Gray could be the one to do it, but the track record says Suarez is the better choice.

item.title: [fansided.com] Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox injury report with star OF banged up again
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air. Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the
item.content:encoded:
Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air.
Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the fan base won't like it, with Anthony on the bench.
Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox's lineup gives answer
Here's a look at Boston's Anthony-less lineup against Yankees left-hander Max Fried.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 7. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 8. Trevor Story | SS |
| 9. Nate Eaton | LF |
Yeah, the Red Sox are going to miss Anthony dearly. Sure, there's the makings of a decent lineup here. Jahmai Jones has done nothing but crush lefties since the Red Sox acquired him. Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras are proven stars. Wilyer Abreu has broken out against left-handers this season, in particular. Ceddanne Rafaela is having his best offensive year. Still, there's no replacing Anthony.
He only appeared in 55 regular-season games and didn't look great in his two at-bats on Tuesday, but nobody in Boston's organization has a higher ceiling than Anthony. Being without him makes the already daunting challenge of rebounding from an 0-1 deficit in the best-of-three series that much more difficult.
Red Sox's growing injury report makes it tougher to believe in dream run
What makes Anthony's injury that much more difficult is that he's far from the only one. The Red Sox have a slew of notables on the IL, and that's making achieving their ultimate gol tough to believe in.
| Player | Position | Injury | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mickey Gasper | C/INF | Right biceps strain | 2027 |
| Tyron Guerrero | RHP | Right shoulder strain | 2027 |
| Eli White | INF/OF | Ligament damage in right foot | 2027 |
| Curtis Mead | INF | Left wrist fracture | Postseason or 2027 |
| Kutter Crawford | RHP | Right flexor irritation | 2027 |
| Johan Oviedo | RHP | Right flexor strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Anthony Siegler | INF | Right wrist discomfort | Postseason or 2027 |
| Justin Slaten | RHP | Right elbow inflammation | 2027 |
| Masataka Yoshida | DH | Left hamstring strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Triston Casas | 1B | Left abdominal strain | 2027 |
The list is lengthy and littered with quality talent. Lineup-wise, the Red Sox sure could use Mickey Gasper, who was one of their hottest hitters before suffering his injury, right about now. They could also use Curtis Mead, a player who crushes left-handed pitching. Even Masataka Yoshida's bat would really come in handy with Anthony out.
Pitching-wise, Boston's depth has taken a hit. Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten are two of the most important members of their bullpen, and perhaps they would've been able to keep the game closer on Tuesday had they been healthy. Guys like Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo are proven back-end starters who could've eaten innings this October.
Perhaps the Red Sox can get Mead and a few others back if they can get past the Yankees, but with Anthony now joining the laundry list of injured players, it's getting tough to believe in them making a comeback.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are hoping to eliminate the Boston Red Sox on Wednesday night in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series.
To end the best-of-three series early, the Yanks will have to hit well against Red Sox starting pitcher Sonny Gray.
The good news for the Yanks is that some of their lineup has a positive history against Gray.
The bad news for the Yankees is that Gray had an 18-5 record this season with a 2.72 ERA. Even at 36 years old, he's still one of the most effective pitchers in baseball.
Boston has to feel good about giving Gray the ball with their season on the line. It's do-or-die for them.
The Yankees will have confidence, too, coming off a 9-0 win in Game 1.
This rivalry rarely disappoints, and it shouldn't on Wednesday night, either.
Yankees vs. Sonny Gray
The Yankees' current roster as a whole has faced Gray for 161 at bats.
In that sample size, they've got 37 hits — for a .230 average — with a .642 OPS.
So all told, it's not a great look for the Yankees.
This is the hitter-by-hitter breakdown:
- Jose Caballero: 3-for-9
- Luis Garcia Jr.: 4-for-10, 1 double, 1 HR, 1 K
- Spencer Jones: 3-for-6, 1 double, 3 Ks
A couple things stand out.
First is that Goldschmidt line — he's one of the best hitters in this era of baseball and somehow has just one hit in 26 at bats against Gray.
The lines of Grisham, Garcia, Rice and Rosario are all encouraging, though. It'll be interesting to see how manager Aaron Boone might deploy them on Wednesday.
Sonny Gray Stats With Yankees
It's worth noting that Gray also spent time pitching for the Yankees.
He was traded to the Yanks from the A's midway through the 2017 season.
In the back half of the 2017 season while with the Yankees, Gray had a 3.72 ERA in 11 outings.
He then pitched 30 times for the Yanks in 2018 and had a 4.90 ERA.
There was concern that the small-statured Gray might not hold up over the long haul, and the Yankees didn't keep him around any longer.
But then he went to the Reds, and the Twins, and the Cardinals, and now the Red Sox — and Gray is still going strong.
Even if the Yankees had kept Gray longer, he likely wouldn't still be wearing the pinstripes by this stage. So he's trying to hand New York a loss on Wednesday night that would send this one to Game 3.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees vs. Sonny Gray: Batter-Pitcher Stats for Game 2 appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are in danger of watching their season come to a close in Yankee Stadium for the second consecutive year. The offense showed zero signs of life as the Yankees cruised to a 9-0 victory headlined by 10 strikeouts from growing Red Sox killer Cam Schlittler. Payton Tolle did enough on the mound as the Game 1 starter. His team was clearly just unable to do their part around them.
Now, the Red Sox fall into the need of a historic response given that just 3 of 24 teams to lose the opener in the Wild Card round have come back to win the series. For starters, Boston sends 18-game winner Sonny Gray to the mound. He flirted with a no-hitter the last time he faced New York in June and tallied a 1.98 ERA against the Yankees in 2026.
The Yankees counter with Max Fried, who has battled some inconsistencies in his ramp-up period from an injury return. The southpaw does have a sparkling 1.93 career ERA against the Red Sox in addition to a brilliant start in Game 1 last year with 6 1/3 scoreless innings, which his bullpen ruined in Boston's 3-1 victory. To best combat the talented lefty, Jahmai Jones slots in leading off as the designated hitter. Caleb Durbin moves up to the sixth spot and Nate Eaton – another right-handed bat – gets the nod in left field.
After being shut out in consecutive postseason games, the Red Sox must find a way to score runs and now do so without Roman Anthony, who will come off the ALWC roster with new and aggravated injuries in his right hand. It's an uphill challenge undoubtedly, though it's one Boston must be ready for in order to extend the season.

Pedro Martinez Reflects on Red Sox's Historic Comeback vs. Yankees, 2004 World Series in B/R Video
Twenty-two years after the Boston Red Sox ended the Curse of the Bambino in the most dramatic way possible, one of the key figures involved in the series joined B/R to share new insights into how it happened.
Baseball Hall of Famer Pedro Martínez appeared on The Run to discuss Boston's 3-0 comeback against the New York Yankees in the ALCS and riding the wave of momentum into the World Series when the Red Sox swept the St. Louis Cardinals.
The 2004 season saw the Red Sox end the 86-year curse that was believed to have stemmed from Babe Ruth being sold by Boston to the Yankees.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Póker de ases en Octubre, los virtuales MVP y Cy Young chocan en los playoffs de la MLB
item.dc:creator: Alejandra González Centeno
item.description: El beisbol de octubre siempre ofrece el espectáculo más puro y dramático del deporte, pero la postemporada de 2026 ha elevado la apuesta a un nivel histórico. Además de disfrutar de la máxima tensión que caracteriza a los playoffs, los aficionados están siendo testigos de un fenómeno pocas veces visto: los cuatro mejores jugadores de la temporada regular están activos y compitiendo simultáneamente por el campeonato. Hablamos de los dos virtuales ganadores del premio al Jugador Más Valioso (MVP),
item.content:encoded:
El beisbol de octubre siempre ofrece el espectáculo más puro y dramático del deporte, pero la postemporada de 2026 ha elevado la apuesta a un nivel histórico.
Además de disfrutar de la máxima tensión que caracteriza a los playoffs, los aficionados están siendo testigos de un fenómeno pocas veces visto: los cuatro mejores jugadores de la temporada regular están activos y compitiendo simultáneamente por el campeonato.
Hablamos de los dos virtuales ganadores del premio al Jugador Más Valioso (MVP), Yordan Álvarez y Pete Crow-Armstrong, junto a los dos favoritos unánimes al premio Cy Young, Cam Schlittler y Jacob Misiorowski.
Este póker de superestrellas buscan traducir su brillantez individual en éxito colectivo en el escenario más exigente de las Grandes Ligas.
Yordan Álvarez, Astros de Houston
En la Liga Americana, Yordan Álvarez construyó una temporada que coqueteó seriamente con la mítica Triple Corona. El bateador designado de los Astros se adjudicó el título de bateo con un promedio de .316, convirtiéndose en el campeón de bateo general de la MLB con el promedio más bajo desde Dick Groat (.325) en 1960, y en el Joven Circuito desde Carl Yastrzemski (.301) en 1968.
A esto sumó 42 cuadrangulares y 106 carreras impulsadas, quedándose a un solo paso de liderar también esos departamentos.
El despliegue de poder del cubano de 29 años fue absolutamente aterrador para los lanzadores rivales. Álvarez lideró las Grandes Ligas con un estratosférico OPS de 1.033 y la métrica avanzada de Statcast registró velocidades de salida máximas de hasta 115.9 millas por hora en sus cuadrangulares.
Su producción ofensiva fue tan abrumadora y determinante que, en la práctica, cargó por sí solo a unos Astros vulnerables que lograron ganar la División Oeste con un inusual y modesto récord de 81-81.
Sin embargo, el inicio de los playoffs ha sido un duro golpe de realidad para Álvarez y su equipo. En el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines ante los White Sox, los Astros cayeron 6-3 en casa.
Enfrentando una estrategia diseñada de forma quirúrgica para evadir su zona de poder, Yordan se fue de 4-1 (.250 AVG) sin lograr conectar extrabases ni remolcar carreras.
Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs de Chicago
Por el lado de la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong protagonizó una campaña que redefinió los límites atléticos del jugador de cinco herramientas. El prodigioso jardinero central de los Cubs ingresó al elitista club 40-40, convirtiéndose en apenas el séptimo jugador en toda la historia de la franquicia y de la MLB en alcanzar 40 jonrones y 40 bases robadas en una misma temporada.
Sus 45 vuelacercas y 41 estafadas cimentaron una actuación que será recordada por décadas.
Más allá de los números redondos, PCA registró un fWAR de 10.6, el más alto de todo el beisbol y una cifra que en el presente siglo solo había sido alcanzada o superada por las mejores versiones históricas de Barry Bonds y Aaron Judge.
El joven de 24 años combinó un OPS de .942 con 119 carreras anotadas (líder de MLB) y 107 remolcadas, además de exhibir una defensiva élite en los jardines y una velocidad de sprint que lo ubica en el percentil 95.
A pesar de su grandeza en el maratón de 162 juegos, su debut en la postemporada 2026 resultó amargo.
Los Cubs se cruzaron en la Serie de Comodines con unos encendidos Padres de San Diego, quienes propinaron una aplastante blanqueada de 8-0 a Chicago en el Juego 1. Crow-Armstrong fue silenciado por el pitcheo californiano, yéndose de 3-0 en el encuentro.
Cam Schlittler, Yankees de New York
En cuanto al montículo, Cam Schlittler fue el cirujano que mantuvo con vida a los Bombarderos del Bronx. El diestro de 25 años es el virtual Cy Young de la Liga Americana tras registrar una brillante efectividad de 1.95, un récord de 14-6 y 239 ponches a lo largo de 193.2 entradas de labor inmaculada.
Su campaña lo unió a la realeza, al ser apenas el cuarto lanzador en la extensa historia de la franquicia neoyorquina en terminar con una efectividad inferior a 2.00.
La precisión de Schlittler rozó la perfección, logrando permitir una o ninguna carrera en 21 de sus 31 aperturas, estableciendo un nuevo récord absoluto para los Yankees en una sola temporada.
Lideró la liga con un minúsculo WHIP de 0.90 y su capacidad para limitar el daño compensó con creces las lesiones en la rotación, guiando a Nueva York al boleto de comodín con 93 triunfos.
Su impacto se trasladó de inmediato a la postemporada, donde Schlittler entregó una obra maestra en el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines ante sus archirrivales históricos, los Red Sox de Boston. Los Yankees aplastaron 9-0 a Boston gracias a que su joven as lanzó 6.1 entradas en blanco, permitiendo solo dos inofensivos hits, regalando un boleto y recetando 10 ponches. Arropado por ensordecedores cánticos de "¡MVP!" en el Yankee Stadium, Schlittler modificó su plan de juego y sorprendió con el uso de la curva para desarticular por completo los bates rivales.
Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers de Milwaukee
El inmenso as de los Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski, tuvo una campaña superlativa al liderar todas las Grandes Ligas en efectividad (1.80), ponches (252) y WHIP (0.80).
Estas cifras de videojuego lo convirtieron en el primer serpentinero desde 1950 en dominar simultáneamente los departamentos de ERA, abanicados y promedio de bateo en contra (.157).
Lo verdaderamente asombroso del lanzador de 24 años fue la velocidad extraterrestre y sostenida de sus envíos.
Misiorowski destrozó los radares al realizar 1,115 pitcheos a 100 mph o más durante la temporada, aniquilando de manera absurda el récord histórico previo de 673 lanzamientos centenarios que pertenecía a Jordan Hicks.
Con una tasa de 12.98 ponches por cada nueve entradas, corrigió sus problemas de descontrol del pasado y lideró a los Brewers a la mejor temporada regular de toda su historia con 103 victorias.
A diferencia de Álvarez, Crow-Armstrong y Schlittler, Misiorowski aún no ha hecho su aparición en los playoffs de este año.
Gracias al nuevo formato de postemporada, el arrollador dominio de su equipo les otorgó un codiciado pase directo que los exime de jugar la desgastante Serie de Comodines.
Actualmente, Miz aguarda pacientemente su turno para subir a la loma en el Juego 1 de la Serie Divisional, donde desatará su brazo completamente descansado ante el rival que logre sobrevivir a la primera ronda de la Liga Nacional.

item.title: [mlb.com] Ex-Yankee Gray takes ball in Game 2 with Red Sox on the brink
item.dc:creator: Max Ralph
item.description: Sonny Gray didn’t mince words when he joined the Red Sox via trade this past offseason. item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray didn’t mince words when he joined the Red Sox via trade this past offseason. Needing to waive a no-trade clause for the deal to go through, Gray said one factor in the decision was that it felt good to “go to a place now where it’s easy to hate the Yankees.”
“I never wanted to go there in the first place,” said Gray, who spent the end of 2017 and all of 2018 with the Yankees after a trade from the A’s. After struggling to a 4.90 ERA in 2018, the Yankees shipped Gray to the Reds, where he became an All-Star in 2019.
Now, the 36-year-old righty will get another up-close taste of The Rivalry.
Gray will get the start Wednesday as the Red Sox face elimination at Yankee Stadium in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series. The Yankees won Game 1, 9-0, behind a dominant Cam Schlittler start.
“As far as reception, this or that, it will be what it will be,” Gray said before Tuesday’s game. “I'm not going to sit here and try to control something that I can't control because I ultimately have no control over that.
“It will be what it will be, and I'll just do my part to be ready to go out there and compete and to pitch and to go win a game.”
Gray described his time in New York as a “snowball” with “a lot of outside this, outside that, unfamiliarity with me and my situation and my family.” He added that it took time and a different environment to reflect on what happened.
“But I do know that playing here [New York] made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband,” Gray said. “Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that's kind of what I take from my time here.”
Gray got back to his best self in his first year in Boston after two seasons with the Cardinals. Leading MLB with 18 wins in 29 starts, the 14-year veteran turned in a 2.72 ERA. He owned a 2.79 ERA in 2023 for the Twins, when he finished as the AL Cy Young runner-up.
Gray faced the Yankees twice in the 2026 regular season. The Red Sox won both games, one at Yankee Stadium and one at Fenway Park. Gray turned in 6 1/3 innings of three-run ball his first time and 7 1/3 scoreless frames the second, striking out nine and flirting with a no-hitter.
The Red Sox will need that version of Gray on Wednesday with their backs against the wall. After all, teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game Wild Card series have gone on to win the series 21 of 24 times (88%), including 17 two-game sweeps. Home teams have won all nine series in which they have gone ahead 1-0, including eight sweeps.
“I feel good,” Gray said. “I think the atmosphere will be a high-level, high-energy, intense playoff atmosphere, which, as a player that's played for a while, who's been around, that's what you want, right? For me, that's what keeps you wanting to continue to come back and play.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Red Sox season hinges on Sonny Gray
item.dc:creator: Jacob Roy
item.description: The Red Sox are up against the wall. Cam Schlittler, once again, shoved against the Red Sox in game one, throwing 117 pitches in a 6.1-inning shutout before handing it over to the bullpen. Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber shut the door, keeping the Red Sox off the scoreboard to win game one, 9-0. item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are up against the wall. Cam Schlittler, once again, shoved against the Red Sox in game one, throwing 117 pitches in a 6.1-inning shutout before handing it over to the bullpen. Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber shut the door, keeping the Red Sox off the scoreboard to win game one, 9-0. Coming into this season, the winner of game one has won 15 of 16 Wild Card series since playoff expansion. The only exception is the Yankees over the Red Sox last season.
If the Red Sox want to keep their season alive, it comes down to Sonny Gray. Let's think about it in innings. The Red Sox used five relievers on Tuesday night: Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Alec Gamboa, Wyatt Olds, and Brayan Bello.
Erik Miller was excellent immediately after being acquired, but his September, as well as his career-long control issues, should reduce him to only low-leverage spots. Greg Weissert can potentially provide an inning, but he's not an arm to trust on back-to-back days in a sticky spot. Alec Gamboa and Wyatt Olds were both late additions to the roster, and neither looked particularly up to the job in game one, while Brayan Bello has never pitched two days in a row in the major leagues.
That leaves Ranger Suarez, Garrett Crochet, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman, and Jake Bennett as the unused pitchers, alongside today's starter Sonny Gray.
Ranger Suarez is set to start game three. Garrett Crochet is a complete unknown. He hasn't pitched since April, and he was ineffective when he was on the mound. If he's healthy, I'd expect him to be able to get outs, but who knows where he's truly at health-wise. Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best relievers in baseball, but his longest outing of the season is 1.1 innings. He's only thrown more than 30 pitches once this season, and it came in an outing in which he walked two hitters. Extending him for more than one inning could be a tricky proposition. And then there's Aroldis Chapman. Chapman, like Whitlock, has been fantastic, but hasn't got more than three outs in a game this season. If you put those three arms together and assign two innings to Crochet, that's four innings. Of course, given the stakes, they could extend Whitlock or Chapman, but their effectiveness after three outs is a relative mystery. If you want to give Jake Bennett an inning or two, you could, but he doesn't seem like an arm they'd go to unless they were trailing, and there's no need to eat innings in a do-or-die game.
The offense was, at least in terms of scoring, the worst in baseball in September. Roman Anthony was lost in the middle of game one, and the rest of the lineup couldn't touch Schlittler. If I were a betting man, I wouldn't put money on them putting a lot of runs on the board against Max Fried. If they want a chance to win the game, they'll need to keep the Yankees off the board, and with the lack of quality innings in the bullpen, that means getting length out of Sonny Gray.
Gray has been the Red Sox best starter by ERA this season. He's gone at least six innings in 22 of his 29 starts. In two starts against the Yankees, he's allowed three earned runs over 13.2 innings pitched with 12 strikeouts and 3 walks. Despite a 14-year career, Gray has only thrown in six postseason games. In those six games, he has a 3.26 ERA, but has only pitched more than five innings once (an 8-inning shoutout for the Athletics against the Tigers in 2013). For the Red Sox to win today, they need Sonny Gray to turn in one of the best postseason performances of his career.
Fortunately, Chad Tracy can unload the clip in game two, because in playoff baseball terms, game three might as well be in six months. The Red Sox need to play every card they have to keep the season alive, but Sonny Gray keeping the Yankees off the scoreboard for as long as possible is the key.

The Red Sox hit some bumps in September, but their hope was that they would be the healthiest they have been all season by the time the postseason rolled around. That's easier said than done. item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony's early exit is major cause for concern for Red Sox originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox hit some bumps in September, but their hope was that they would be the healthiest they have been all season by the time the postseason rolled around.
That's easier said than done. While Garrett Crochet is back and Boston's Game 1 lineup against the Yankees featured Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, Contreras is believed to be playing at less than 100 percent — and Anthony is now dealing with an ailment of his own.
The young Red Sox outfielder exited Game 1 in the sixth inning, and manager Chad Tracy's postgame update was concerning to Boston fans.
Here's the latest on Anthony's status.
Roman Anthony exits Game 1
Anthony was pinch-hit for in the sixth inning of Game 1, a move that raised a few eyebrows. After the game, Tracy made it clear that it wasn't just a strategic decision,
Tracy told reporters that Anthony's hand, which forced him to miss most of the season, "flared" during the game. While Tracy said Anthony has felt occasional pain in his hand since returning, this instance was "more serious" and uncomfortable."
Chad Tracy said Roman Anthony had experienced the occasional "zinger" in that hand in the month since he returned.
"Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," Tracy said. https://t.co/MkBoWPP4AD
Anthony previously winced after a check swing during the Red Sox' final game of the regular season, indicating he was dealing with some pain in the hand.
Here's what we know about Anthony's status for Game 2.
MORE: How Cam Schlittler became enemy No. 1 for Red Sox fans
Roman Anthony injury update
Anthony left Yankee Stadium before the Red Sox' postgame media availability and did not speak to reporters Tuesday night.
Asked directly whether Anthony would be available for Game 2, Tracy told reporters, "It's hard to say right now. It's one of those things where he obviously was in a lot of discomfort."
The Red Sox were shut out in Game 1, raising the level of urgency all-around in the clubhouse. Losing Anthony's bat would be a blow to Boston's lineup, though the former No. 1 prospect struggled down the stretch after a red-hot first week back from his months-long absence.

item.title: [CBS Sports] The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to stay alive vs. Yankees, but a nagging hand injury keeps derailing his season
item.dc:creator: Julian McWilliams
item.description: NEW YORK -- There was no sighting of Roman Anthony late Tuesday night. Inside the clubhouse, his locker sat vacant. His Red Sox teammates sat nearby, too, coping with the aftermath of in Game 1 of this best-of-three AL Wild Card Series. Yet the night carried an even deeper concern. Anthony's vacancy in the clubhouse mirrored his absence on the field. In the top of the sixth inning, the Red Sox's prized 22-year-old was removed from the game with the same hand and finger injury that cost him 101 g
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- There was no sighting of Roman Anthony late Tuesday night. Inside the clubhouse, his locker sat vacant. His Red Sox teammates sat nearby, too, coping with the aftermath of in Game 1 of this best-of-three AL Wild Card Series.
Yet the night carried an even deeper concern. Anthony's vacancy in the clubhouse mirrored his absence on the field. In the top of the sixth inning, the Red Sox's prized 22-year-old was removed from the game with the same hand and finger injury that cost him 101 games this season.
"The hand," Boston manager Chad Tracy said about Anthony in a low tone after the loss. "He took a check swing and then another swing and his hand flared on him. And it got uncomfortable, so we had to make a move there."
The hand.
It's bugged Anthony all season during a diluted second year in the majors. Boston didn't expect Anthony to miss much time. But the injury never responded -- not to treatment, nor to the swing that had made him one of the best young players in the game. One the Red Sox were certain could carry a load, even as he continued growing into his slender shoulders.
The hand created so much dialogue. So many opinions over the course of this season. The partial tendon and ligament tear had some within baseball circles questioning Anthony's toughness. The Red Sox even tried a change of scenery, sending Anthony to Fort Myers, Fla., in early July to continue his rehab at their spring training complex. Maybe that would push him along.
It didn't. The hand continued to bother him.
And so much changed in his absence.
The Red Sox even ripped off a 15-game winning streak without him. But for all they accomplished while Anthony watched, they knew there would come a point when they would need him.
And on Tuesday, with the Red Sox trailing just 2-0 in the sixth, that moment arrived. Only it was Andruw Monasterio, not Anthony, who stepped to the plate against the dominant Cam Schlittler
"It's difficult," Tracy said. "Obviously, it flares up on him and becomes uncomfortable, and you have to make a move there. So we'll see what the next steps are, but yeah, it was difficult."
In truth, Anthony's absence late in this contest wasn't the difference-maker. Schlittler had too much to do with suppressing Boston's offense, tilting the scale firmly in his club's favor.
His 6 ⅓ innings were dominant, adding to his postseason lore against the team he grew up cheering for. He struck out 10 and induced 24 whiffs. Schlittler, known for the three variations of his fastball that continued to smother Red Sox hitters, added another headache Tuesday: a devastating curveball that generated eight swings and misses on its own.
"He used his curveball a little bit more than usual, and obviously it worked," Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story said. "We did a good job of making him work and getting his pitch count up, but just didn't do enough to have a big moment or gather any extra-base hits or put any runs on the board."
"He dominated every pitch," said Wilyer Abreu, who had one of the two hits off Schlittler. "He made really good pitches"
Facing Schlittler on the road at Yankee Stadium was about as unforgiving a matchup as the Red Sox could draw. Fans bellowed chants of MVP. They chanted his name. The crowd never had to question his outing. The pressure never amounted to pressure. The angst never consumed the moment.
Because Schlittler -- a second-year player, just like Anthony -- imposed his will, toying with Red Sox hitters, announcing, for a second straight year, that they had no business sharing this stage with him.
"The natural adrenaline, just the environment and how loud it was, I think definitely helped," Schlittler said. "Just being able to lean on that."
The Red Sox, who face elimination Wednesday night, are unsure what Anthony's status will be moving forward. They're unsure whether he'll need another MRI. What is certain, though, is that this series becomes even murkier without him. Anthony, who led off Tuesday night, represented so much of what the Red Sox believed they had been missing. Against Schlittler and a Yankees staff built on velocity -- something Boston's lineup has struggled with collectively -- he was perhaps their best answer.
"He's obviously coming off that [initial injury]," Tracy said. "With that, you'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something, it's fine, it goes away. But today it was obviously coming out of the game. Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable."
Now, the hand brings back a question that followed Anthony throughout the summer: Can the Red Sox count on him to stay on the field?
It is a difficult question to ask of a 22-year-old, particularly one who has already missed 101 games because of the same injury. But the postseason has a way of making those questions immediate. The Red Sox face another formidable starter in Max Fried. And they are again left wondering whether Anthony will be there for it.

item.title: [New York Post] Chad Tracy’s controversial call to pull Payton Tolle backfired for Red Sox in horrific fashion in Game 1 blowout
item.dc:creator: Matt Ehalt
item.description: Payton Tolle had just retired Paul Goldschmidt for the third time on one pitch, running his pitch count to a manageable 83 with two outs in the fifth inning Tuesday, when Chad Tracy decided he’d seen enough. With Boston trailing by one run and Ben Rice, who doubled in the first inning, due up next, the manager opted to remove his pitcher who had settled into the pitching duel by that point. item.content:encoded:
Payton Tolle had just retired Paul Goldschmidt for the third time on one pitch, running his pitch count to a manageable 83 with two outs in the fifth inning Tuesday, when Chad Tracy decided he’d seen enough.
With Boston trailing by one run and Ben Rice, who doubled in the first inning, due up next, the manager opted to remove his pitcher who had settled into the pitching duel by that point.
And it backfired in horrible fashion for Boston.
Lefty reliever Erik Miller immediately surrendered a long solo homer to center field to Rice — the first of his two against Boston relievers — and it completely changed the tone of the game in Boston’s 9-0 loss to the Yankees in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium.
Boston’s b-tier relievers ultimately surrendered eight runs in 3 1/3 innings.
“Not just the pitch count necessarily, but you’re trailing already, you’re moving through the third time,” Tracy said. “Rice had already hit a double in the gap off of him, and you have a nice lane there for Miller, and obviously he got him. Just felt like it was the time to go.”
This postseason marks Tracy’s first calling the shots and moments like this one Tuesday night are what ultimately can swing series.
Sure, Boston did not score, but being down 1-0 to Cam Schlittler and the Yankees bullpen is a vastly different world than trailing by two entering the seventh.
Tolle allowed four hits over the first nine batters but settled down to retire eight of the next 10 batters and navigated a two-on, no-outs situation in the fifth while trailing 1-0.
He began the sixth by retiring Austin Wells on six pitches and then sitting down Goldschmidt, leaving him certainly with room to possibly navigate six innings if he worked effectively.
Tracy, though, opted for a new look in Miller, ending Tolle’s day after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball.
“I thought he threw the ball well,” Tracy said. “They did an effective job of grinding the count up as well. He had traffic. They put traffic on him. He was able to navigate his way through that. I think he competed extremely well for the time that he was out there and gave us what he could.
“I think the number being up there in the mid-80s, still trying to get through five, probably higher than what you normally see with Payton, and to be expected in an environment like this. But I thought he competed his butt off.”
Miller, a midseason trade acquisition, struggled to end the regular season and those issues carried over to the postseason when he fired a middle-middle 97-mph heater that Rice hit out to dead center.
Tolle said that as a competitor, he felt he could have gone longer but understood the decision due to the strength of Boston’s bullpen during the regular seaosn.
Boston is now one loss away from a second straight early postseason exit at the Yankees’ hands.
“Wasn’t good enough,” Tolle said. “They had a good plan and I threw a lot of balls … just didn’t feel like I could command the zone, kind of let some at-bats get away from me. A lot of pitches.”
He added about the bullpen: “Those guys picked me up a lot this year.”

item.title: [USA Today] What happened to Alex Bregman? Scary injury can't keep Cubs slugger from MLB playoffs
item.dc:creator: Bob Nightengale
item.description: What happened to Alex Bregman? Scary injury can't keep Cubs slugger from MLB playoffs SAN DIEGO — Just nine days after suffering eight broken bones in his face, third baseman Alex Bregman was back in the Chicago Cubs' lineup Tuesday facing the San Diego Padres as the designated hitter for Game 1 of the National League wild card series. item.content:encoded:
What happened to Alex Bregman? Scary injury can't keep Cubs slugger from MLB playoffs
SAN DIEGO — Just nine days after suffering eight broken bones in his face, third baseman Alex Bregman was back in the Chicago Cubs' lineup Tuesday facing the San Diego Padres as the designated hitter for Game 1 of the National League wild card series.
Bregman, who began taking ground balls the past few days after suffering the injury Sept. 20 when a foul ball by teammate Michael Busch hit him in the face while standing near the on-deck circle, tried to convince Cubs manager Craig Counsell that he was good enough to play third base with the swelling in his face dramatically reduced.
Yet, Counsell said that Bregman’s bat is too valuable to take the risk of Bregman being back in the field.
“I played it safe, I'll be honest with you," Counsell said. “I just think this is a man seven days off of facial fractures, and I want his at-bat. I think his at-bats are the most critical thing for our team is that he gets his at-bats this series. That's what's most important.
“I feel like this is a better way to guarantee that he gets these at-bats. There's just more risk playing the field. Could it go fine? Yeah. Does he want to play the field? He does. This is just a safer way to go to make sure he gets all his at-bats."
Still, just the fact that Bregman is back in the lineup so quickly, his teammates say, is a huge boost for their morale, much less their lineup, where he’ll bat second.
“That fires you up,” Cubs MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong said. “Knowing him and how wonderfully crazy he is, just about his work and how much he loves the game, it’s not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is that he’s coming back after facial fractures and whatnot, I’m just not that surprised.
“He lives for this kind of baseball. Most importantly, I’m glad he’s healthy enough to do what he loves. …Simply put, Alex Bregman makes our lineup better. So, it’s huge that he’s getting himself game ready.”
Certainly, he proved in the Cubs’ season-finale that his bat is just fine, going 4-for-4 with two home runs.
“I’ll do whatever it takes,’’ said Bregman, who finished his first year with the Cubs hitting .265 with 28 homers, 93 RBI, and an .819 OPS in 155 games. He had a sensation second half, producing a 1.010 OPS compared to a .696 OPS before the All-Star break.
Now, he becomes the 11th player in MLB history to play in 10 consecutive postseasons with the advent of the wild-card.
“He's the man, to be honest,’’ Cubs reliever Jaco Webb said. “That's tough to do. That's really cool and shows the kind of character that he has going through such a crazy injury.
“I mean, you're putting your career on the line at that point, but he knows what he's doing. The biggest thing is he wants to be here. He wants to win."
Cubs starting lineup today: Game 1 vs Padres
- Pete Crow-Armstrong (L) CF
- Alex Bregman (R) DH
- Michael Busch (L) 1B
- Seiya Suzuki (R) RF
- Ian Happ (S) LF
- Nico Hoerner (R) 2B
- Pedro Ramírez (S) 3B
- Carson Kelly (R) C
- Dansby Swanson (R) SS

item.title: [heavy.com] Red Sox’ Mickey Gasper Gets More Bad News After Missing Playoff Roster
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: Mickey Gasper’s stunning breakout season with the Boston Red Sox ended in an instant Friday, when a two-strike swing tore his right biceps clean off the bone, according to a report by Red Sox WEEI reporter Rob Bradford. Boston will play its wild-card playoff series, and any other playoff series should they advance, without the utility man whose midsummer power binge turned into one of the best stories of the club’s late-season turnaround, leaving manager Chad Tracy’s bench thinned out at the wor
item.content:encoded:
Mickey Gasper’s stunning breakout season with the Boston Red Sox ended in an instant Friday, when a two-strike swing tore his right biceps clean off the bone, according to a report by Red Sox WEEI reporter Rob Bradford.
Boston will play its wild-card playoff series, and any other playoff series should they advance, without the utility man whose midsummer power binge turned into one of the best stories of the club’s late-season turnaround, leaving manager Chad Tracy’s bench thinned out at the worst possible time.
Gasper was catching Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader against the Chicago Cubs at Fenway Park when he swung through a fifth-inning strikeout and immediately grabbed at his arm. He grimaced walking back to the dugout, and Connor Wong took over behind the plate before the top of the sixth.
How Mickey Gasper’s Boston Red Sox Injury Happened
“At this point, it looks like a significant biceps injury, so he’s going to still be seeing more doctors and stuff like that,” Tracy said, as quoted by MLB.com‘s Ian Browne. “We’ll get the final conclusion, but it’s a pretty significant biceps injury. It’s probably going to take him out.”
That turned out to be an understatement. According to Bradford, Gasper will return to Boston where he will have surgery on his right biceps on Friday.
Sports medicine physician Jesse Morse described a full-thickness tear of the tendon, meaning the biceps separated entirely from the bone and surgery is the only fix. Morse said recovery typically runs six to eight weeks with no expected long-term effect, putting Gasper on track to be ready for offseason work and spring training in 2027.
The Red Sox placed Gasper on the 10-day injured list Sunday, retroactive to Sept. 26, with a right biceps strain. As a result, Gasper was left off the Red Sox playoff roster, but worse than that, the 30-year-old from New Hampshire‘s season, and any hope of playing in the postseason, is over.
Gasper’s bat against right-handers had turned into a real option against playoff pitching. Now Boston enters October counting on Jarren Duran and Roman Anthony to cover left field and DH against right-handers, with one fewer safety net.
Mickey Gasper’s Breakout and Long Road to Boston
Gasper made his major league debut in August 2024, and proceeded to go 0-for-18 in his brief call-up.
Gasper hit just .243 in his first big league stint of this year before Boston optioned him back to Triple-A Worcester in late June. Recalled Aug. 16 after Masataka Yoshida’s injury, he turned into a different hitter almost overnight, running a scorching stretch that produced the second-highest monthly OPS by any hitter with at least 40 plate appearances in a single month, trailing only Barry Bonds’ otherworldly April of 2004.
He backed it up with a seven-game run that ranked sixth all time in OPS, behind only Bonds, Shawn Green, Bryce Harper, Babe Ruth and Josh Hamilton. He finished the year having hit 10 homers with 24 RBI in 67 games, splitting time at catcher, first base and designated hitter.
The switch-hitter’s path to Fenway Park ran through eight minor league seasons. The Yankees took him in the 27th round of the 2018 draft out of Bryant University, where he became the first position player from the program to reach the majors, joining pitchers Keith MacWhorter and James Karinchak, his old college roommate. He debuted with Boston in 2024, went to Minnesota that winter in a trade, bounced through Washington on waivers, landing back with the Red Sox to start 2026.
Gasper is expected to be back in the mix for a utility role next season. For now, the Red Sox move forward into the playoffs without the unlikeliest hitter of their season.

item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Boston Red Sox start their AL Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
The Red Sox will be looking to get revenge against the Yankees after losing to them last year in the AL Wild Card series.
Now, with Game 1 just about here, Boston has announced a notable decision with Caleb Durbin.
Caleb Durbin Dropping to Bottom of the Red Sox's Batting Order
The Red Sox have announced that Durbin will be their ninth hitter against the Yankees on Tuesday.
Durbin dropping to the bottom of Boston's batting order comes after he hit seventh in their last game against the Chicago Cubs.
Here is the Red Sox's full batting order, as reported by Underdog MLB: R. Anthony DH A. Rutschman C W. Contreras 1B W. Abreu RF C. Rafaela CF N. Sogard 2B J. Duran LF T. Story SS C. Durbin 3B
Looking at Durbin
Durbin is entering the playoffs with the hope of heating back up. He had a tough finish to the regular season, as he went 1-for-17 in his last five games.
With this, it makes sense that Boston is dropping Durbin to ninth in their batting order. It will be intriguing to see if he can have a big bounce-back game for Boston against New York.
In 153 games this regular season for the Red Sox, Durbin posted 13 home runs, 64 RBI, and a .248 batting average.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Adley Rutschman justifies Red Sox trade with pre-playoff hot streak amid injuries and uncertainty
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: The Boston Red Sox have not entered the postseason on a high note. Not only are Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela not at 100 percent health-wise, Mickey Gasper, Eli White, Tyron Guerrero and other players are down with injuries. The Sox's offense has seriously struggled in the lead up to the postseason, as well. Boston posted a league-worst .651 OPS and 71 runs scored in September — that's 18 fewer runs than the Philadelphia Phillies, the second-worst run scoring team in the season's final
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have not entered the postseason on a high note. Not only are Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela not at 100 percent health-wise, Mickey Gasper, Eli White, Tyron Guerrero and other players are down with injuries.
The Sox's offense has seriously struggled in the lead up to the postseason, as well. Boston posted a league-worst .651 OPS and 71 runs scored in September — that's 18 fewer runs than the Philadelphia Phillies, the second-worst run scoring team in the season's final month.
But as the rest of his team has faltered, Adley Rutschman is heating up just at the right time. The former Baltimore Orioles catcher is slashing .266/.299/.547 in September, which might not seem like a huge breakout, but he batted just .170/.254/.245 in August, his first month in Boston.
Rutschman's last week is the most encouraging sign yet for the Sox. He's slashing .346/.370/.577 with a home run in his last seven games. Baseball is a game of momentum and Rutschman is one of the few Red Sox entering the Wild Card series hot. Boston will need his best work at the plate this series, especially from the right side, given the injuries it's dealing with. Thankfully, Rutschman is finally thriving from the right-handed batter's box.
Adley Rutschman is heating up for the Red Sox right at the perfect time
The Red Sox paid a hefty price for Rutschman at the trade deadline to bring a much-needed upgrade to their catcher spot. The 28-year-old is one of the best defensive catchers in the league and he effectively eliminates any advantage opposing teams have at the plate and on the base paths, a boost Connor Wong certainly doesn't bring on his start days. Now, Rutschman is finally starting to give the Sox the offensive production they hoped for when they sold all their best minor league pitchers and more for him.
Boston has rewarded Rutschman with the No. 2 spot in their Wild Card Game 1 lineup (subscription required). Manager Chad Tracy foreshadowed his placement in the lineup during the last game of the season against the Cubs, in which Rutschman went 1-for-2 with a homer and a walk. Batting him second is quite a risk, given the catcher's offensive trouble this season, but the Sox need all the help they can get at the plate and Rutschman is their hottest bat.
Rutschman doesn't have a ton of playoff experience from his tenure with the Orioles, but the five games he's played in October are more than many Sox players have under their belt. As one of their only players who's felt the pressure of the postseason on more than one occasion, the Red Sox need Rutschman to stay hot.
