The longtime rivals are gearing up for Game 1 of the hi
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will be taking on the New York Yankees in the American League wild-card round this year, which is a rematch from last season.
Boston was able to clinch a spot in the postseason following an impressive run during the middle of the year to get back into the race. But the Red Sox couldn't do enough to overtake the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East, and now they will be entering a three-game series that will determine their fate.
The longtime rivals are gearing up for Game 1 of the highly anticipated series, with each trying to make a statement against the other. New York won the season series 7-6, but the entire matchup was extremely close, leading to the thought that this playoff matchup will be as well.
Last season, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox in three games to move on to the ALDS. Boston will be looking for some revenge here, and the series is again being played in New York.
Jarren Duran Decision Made by Red Sox
Ahead of Game 1, the Red Sox have now released the lineup that they will use against the Yankees. Within the lineup, outfielder Jarren Duran will be hitting seventh for Boston today.
Duran will be playing in left field.
Duran has seen a tough season at the plate take place, and it's hurt the overall ceiling of this Red Sox team. Overall, the former All-Star has hit .207 with 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, and 21 stolen bases, while posting an OPS of .627.
Boston has been waiting for Duran to break out of his slump all season long, but to this point, nothing has worked. But if he can get his bat going in the playoffs, his struggles from the regular season will be forgiven.
Can Red Sox Take Down Yankees?
For the Red Sox to win this series, guys like Duran are going to need to step up heavily. New York will be without star Aaron Judge due to injury, and the Red Sox need to take advantage of this fact.
Boston's pitching staff will be counted on heavily in this series as they try to match the strong starting rotation from the Yankees. But luckily for the Red Sox, the team will be getting back ace left-hander Garrett Crochet from injury.
It has been a long time coming for Crochet, with him last pitching on April 25 for this team. Crochet has been trying to come back all year, but the Red Sox finally saw progress over the last few weeks, and he has been added to the playoff roster.
If Crochet can make an impact as a relief pitcher, it could go a long way for this team against the Yankees. Boston is behind the eight ball when it comes to the pitching in the series, and Crochet gives them at least a fighting chance.
The Red Sox and Yankees will kick off the opening game of the series at 5:00 p.m. PT/8:00 p.m. ET from Yankee Stadium.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Decision Before Yankees Wild-Card Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Red Sox’ Sonny Gray compares time with Yankees to a growing downhill snowball
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell
item.description: The Boston Red Sox starter in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series on Wednesday needs no introduction to the boo birds. He’s got plenty of familiarity with the Bronx cheer, unfortunately for him, coming from his time with the Yankees. Sonny Gray will toe the slab for Chad Tracy’s squad in a pivotal playoff game back in the place that was home to arguably the lowest point of his MLB career. “I came from Oakland, and Oakland to [New York]. I think that maybe during my time there was a lot of outside
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox starter in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card series on Wednesday needs no introduction to the boo birds. He’s got plenty of familiarity with the Bronx cheer, unfortunately for him, coming from his time with the Yankees.
Sonny Gray will toe the slab for Chad Tracy’s squad in a pivotal playoff game back in the place that was home to arguably the lowest point of his MLB career.
“I came from Oakland, and Oakland to [New York]. I think that maybe during my time there was a lot of outside this, outside that, unfamiliarity with me and my situation and my family,” Gray said before Tuesday’s Game 1. “It’s kind of like one of those things that you have a snowball or whatever, right?
“And there’s a snowball that kind of starts rolling down a hill. If you don’t ever stop it, then the snowball just gets bigger and bigger and bigger, and it picks up traction, and it just gets more snow. And it just continues to go down this thing. And then the bigger the snowball gets, the harder it is to stop it or take a step back.
“And for me, it just took me to get away and get myself into a different environment and then reflect on those things, right, like reflect on what was good, what was bad, what didn’t work. And that took some time.”
Gray pitched 41 games during his season-and-a-half with the Bombers — 4.51 ERA — and Yankee faithful will surely remember his time with the team on Wednesday.
The veteran starter is expecting the obvious in terms of the reception he’ll receive as he goes out to try and win a postseason game for the Red Sox.
“I think it will be a playoff energy on the road, playoff atmosphere on the road,” said Gray. “As far as reception, this or that, it will be what it will be. I’m not going to sit here and try to control something that I can’t control because I ultimately have no control over that.
“It will be what it will be, and I’ll just do my part to be ready to go out there and compete and to pitch and to go win a game.”
Gray was acquired from the Athletics at the 2017 trade deadline prior to the Bombers’ unexpected and memorable run to Game 7 of the ALCS. The 36-year-old was acquired to be a frontline starter behind Luis Severino at the very beginning of the ‘Baby Bombers’ era.
The right-hander’s first run with the Yanks was respectable as he pitched to a 3.72 ERA in 11 games during the 2017 season and even added a strong ALCS start, throwing five innings and allowing one earned run against the Houston Astros. However, the wheels fell off in 2018, when he owned a 4.90 ERA in 30 games and heard an awful amount of boos from the home crowd before being shipped off to the Cincinnati Reds in the offseason.
Despite the rough experience, Gray greatly values his time in New York and attributes it not only to the pitcher, but to the man he is today.
“I do know that playing here made me a stronger person, made me a better man, a better husband. Ultimately, it made me a better pitcher, a better baseball player. And that’s kind of what I take from my time here. …
“I learned a lot. I learned what to do, what not to do. I mean, it was a bump in the road for me, but ultimately it made me a better person.”
Gray found success immediately after departing the Bronx. He was an All-Star for the Reds in 2019 and then again with the Minnesota Twins in 2023. The veteran enters the postseason riding a very successful season in which he pitched to a 2.72 ERA in 29 games with the Red Sox.
The Tennessean is not focused on any sort of revenge and doesn’t need any added motivation to stick it to the Yankees. Instead, he’s solely focused on trying to win for the Bo Sox.
“That’s kind of how I look at it. I don’t look at it as any other thing than that.”

item.title: [Motor City Bengals] Jahmai Jones resurgence, postseason with Red Sox is s double-edged sword for Tigers
item.dc:creator: Connor Muldowney
item.description: Get traded away from the Tigers, put up career numbers. It’s a tale as old as time and it’s happening in real time throughout MLB as the playoffs begin. item.content:encoded:
Get traded away from the Tigers, put up career numbers. It’s a tale as old as time and it’s happening in real time throughout MLB as the playoffs begin.
There are several former Tigers whose new teams have made the playoffs but the headliners have to be Casey Mize and Tarik Skubal. Both joined teams destined for the playoffs at the trade deadline (though Mize was left off the Padres' Wild Card roster). Then there were guys like Jahmai Jones and Jake Rogers who joined hopeful playoff teams — and it ended up working out for them.
The biggest surprise of that group of four former Tigers is probably the fact that Jones has been raking with the Red Sox and may have had the best final two months of the season of the four.
Everyone knew Skubal would be just fine and after posting a 3.00 ERA in August with the Dodgers, he notched a 2.25 ERA in September. He may have gotten hit around a little more than he’s used to with his WHIP creeping over 1.00 with Los Angeles. He was still one of the best pitchers in baseball, but he struggled to adjust at times.
Mize, too struggled with the Padres, posting a 7.46 ERA and 1.68 WHIP after enjoying a 2.70 ERA with the Tigers through the first three months of the season. He also only had 25 strikeouts in 44 innings.
But Jones now looks like the steal of the year, and that's a double-edged sword for the Tigers. They absolutely needed to dump him after his horrendous start to the season, but now he’s hitting the cover off the ball like he did with Detroit in 2025.
Oh, and he’ll be fighting for a World Series berth.
It’s good to see the former Tiger play so well with the Red Sox after struggling through 57 appearances this season and needing a change of scenery. Funny how that always seems to work out, right?
Jahmai Jones has been a revelation with the Red Sox
The Red Sox were already likely to make the playoffs when they acquired Jones and they went 21-16 in games that he played. He was an overall plus player for Boston, posting a 0.8 WAR as well.
What really stands out is his .993 OPS. All he did when he got to Boston was get on base. His on-base percentage is .408 with the Red Sox and he also hit .308 (20-for-65). This is bittersweet to see because the Red Sox are experiencing the same Jones that Tigers fans fell in love with during the 2025 playoff run when he hit .287 with a .937 OPS over 72 games.
Plus, his start to the 2026 season was so bad, there’s no way that anyone in the Tigers’ front office saw him breaking out of a slump like he did with the Red Sox. He hit .137 and had a .440 OPS in 57 games with the Tigers — Detroit was 20-36 in games when he recorded an at-bat.
After getting picked up by the Red Sox in mid-July, Jones got red-hot. His OPS in July was 1.278 which is a video game number and then he doubled down in August with a 1.284 OPS and .474 average. He did come back down to earth in September with a .614 OPS and .182 average over 33 at-bats, but he heads to the postseason with a fresh start again. And we know how that works out for him.
It’s great to see the former Tiger having success with a change of scenery, but it had to come at the expense of a playoff berth for Detroit. The baseball gods have a twisted sense of humor.

Contreras was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas R
item.content:encoded:
After the Boston Red Sox went on their summer run to climb safely into an American League wild-card spot, that proved to be huge. Nobody can predict injuries, but it was a rough month of September in terms of injuries.
Not only did manager Chad Tracy lose Gold Glove outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela to an injury early in the month, but he also lost All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras to an injury with 10 days left in the regular season. Contreras was hit on the hand by a pitch against the Texas Rangers. He played in just one game after that.
He’ll be back in the Red Sox lineup for Game 1 of the AL wild-card series on Tuesday night against the New York Yankees. Boston is also getting Rafaela back in the Bronx, but the lineup will look different against Cam Schlittler.
Ceddanne Rafaela Batting Fifth in Game 1 vs. New York Yankees
Boston announced their lineup hours before Game 1 and Rafaela will be hitting fifth. Here is the lineup for the Red Sox,
Wilyer Abreu RF
Caddanne Rafaela CF
Nick Sogard 2B
Jarren Duran LF
Trevor Story SS
Caleb Durbin 3B
Rafaela was placed on the injured list with a right quadriceps strain, which caused him to miss 17 games. He returned against the Cleveland Guardians on Sept. 23 before exiting the game with right hamstring tightness while legging out a single. The next day, testing came back clean, and he was diagnosed with a hamstring cramp. He went 2-for-6 against the Guardians and Chicago Cubs in three games before the playoffs with a pair of singles.
Red Sox Big Wild Card Lead Led To Key Rest for Ceddanne Rafaela
If Rafaela can return and produce for Tracy, the big lead in the playoff race in the American League was huge. It allowed Boston to give not only Rafaela time to rest, but also Contreras as well.
Boston will be without utility infielder Mickey Gasper, who suffered an injury last Friday in Game 1 of a doubleheader against the Cubs at Fenway Park. He was placed on the 10-day injured list, which takes an underrated bat out of Tracy’s lineup and off his bench.
The Red Sox will send young left-hander Payton Tolle to the mound against the New York Yankees, who will send this lineup out for manager Aaron Boone,
Ben Rice DH
Heliot Ramos RF
George Lombard Jr. SS
Amed Rosario 3B
Anthony Vole 2B
New York won’t have Aaron Judge for the series, as he was not part of Boone’s roster. This figures to be a low-scoring series given the projected pitching matchups for the three games, if it goes that far. Boston getting Rafaela and Contreras back while the Yankees not having Judge feels like an advantage for the Red Sox. Winning Game 1 is big in a best-of-three series, especially for the Yankees, with Boston having Sonny Gray scheduled to go in Game 2 on Wednesday night.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Red Sox's Romy Gonzalez: Option for ALDS

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said Tuesday that Gonzalez is still recovering from a hyperextended elbow injury suffered at Triple-A Worcester but is "very much in play" for the ALDS roster if Boston advances, Tim Healey of The Boston Globe reports.
Gonzalez slashed just .185/.264/.308 in 19 games for the Red Sox this season and spent the final two months of the year at Worcester. However, the 30-year-old had a .978 OPS versus lefties in 2025, so he could be a useful reserve for the Red Sox in subsequent rounds if he can get healthy.

item.title: [NBC Sports] Romy Gonzalez recovering from elbow injury
item.dc:creator: George Bissell; Romy Gonzalez
item.description:
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy told reporters Romy Gonzalez is recovering from a hyperextended elbow.
Tracy added that Gonzalez is “very much in play” for the remainder of the postseason after suffering the injury towards the end of the regular season at Triple-A Worcester. The fact that he’s still a little banged up is presumably why he wasn’t added to Boston’s postseason roster as a bench option against left-handed pitching.

item.content:encoded:
The fantasy baseball season is over, and the MLB Playoffs have begun. Yet, before we fully close the book on the 2026 MLB regular season, we got all the Rotoworld MLB writers together to vote for their fantasy MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, and so much more.
TUNE IN FOR EVERY PITCH OF THE MLB WILD CARD ROUND ON PEACOCK AND FOLLOW ALONG WITH OUR LIVE BLOG OVER AT NBCSPORTS.COM
Fantasy Baseball MVP
We all chose Pete Crow-Armstrong. After struggling in the second half last year, people wrote him off as a volatile fantasy asset, and he responded by putting together a 40/40 season with a .280 average, 107 RBI, and 119 runs. He was clearly the top player in fantasy, and you probably didn’t use a first- or second-round pick on him.
Fantasy Baseball Cy Young
“Cam Schlittler was outstanding in his first taste of MLB in 2025, but was even better in his first full season with the Yankees this year. The runaway favorite for the AL Cy Young award, he was the third overall player in the Razzball player rater in standard 12-team leagues.” - Nick Shlain
Everybody else chose Jacob Misiorowski. “This was the easiest call to make during this exercise. Especially considering the ADP (outside the top 100), his season was even more remarkable for fantasy managers. Misiorowski led the majors in ERA (1.80), strikeouts (252) and WHIP (0.80), nearly sweeping all the standard fantasy categories. Only two pitchers topped his 16 wins, so the young fireballer was plenty helpful there as well. The only downside was an abbreviated start during the fantasy playoffs, but that’s a mere nitpick. It was an emphatic and historic season, with every reason to think it will continue if health cooperates.” - D.J. Short
Fantasy Baseball Rookie of the Year
“Kevin McGonigle‘s power and speed didn’t produce gaudy totals, but he played 156 games with solid production across the board. Scoring 97 runs on an otherwise pedestrian Tigers offense is nothing to sneeze at. He also gave fantasy managers something to dream on with 10 home runs in 63 games in the second half.” - Nick Shlain
“Outfield somehow feeling the shallowest spot in fantasy led me to Carson Benge here; he went 20-20 and hit .282 despite starting in a very, very rough funk in April, finishing inside the top 60 in 5x5 value.” - Rivers McCown
“Sal Stewart was going outside the top 150 picks and still earned almost $28 of value. He was the 13th overall hitter on FanGraphs’ Player Rater, and hit .263 with 32 home runs and 111 RBI. He looks like a locked-in stud moving forward.” - Eric Samulski
“I think it’s just so hard to find elite pitching options late in fantasy drafts or on the waiver wire, so for Parker Messick to put together the type of season that he did from an ADP of pick 275 in NFBC Main Event leagues is pretty remarkable. He was absolutely elite with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, and 193 strikeouts over 186 1/3 innings while chipping in a solid 12 victories as well. That made him not just one of the most valuable rookies in the fantasy space this season, but one of the most valuable pitchers overall.” - Dave Shovein
Fantasy Baseball’s Most Disappointing Pick (top 50 overall pick)
“If you remove the guys who failed to produce value because they got hurt (Aaron Judge, Garrett Crochet, Edwin Diaz), then the clear answer is Vladimir Guerrero Jr. He was taken on the 1-2 turn and managed to earn just $4 of value in a full season of 600 plate appearances. The power was nonexistent, the team around him didn’t help, and he probably should have been cut in a lot more fantasy leagues.” - Eric Samulski
“Kyle Tucker was drafted as a first-round pick in NFBC Main Event leagues at pick 14 overall and was a tremendous disappointment from that lofty draft spot. He was supposed to see a major increase in his counting stats moving to the vaunted Dodgers’ lineup and being sandwiched around superstars, but instead he had the worst offensive season of his career in his age-29 season – slashing .233/.330/.385 with just 17 homers, 70 RBI, 12 stolen bases and 90 runs scored while staying healthy and playing in 154 games. Just a brutal effort overall given the draft cost and the situation that he was stepping into.” - Dave Shovein
“This one is obvious, right? Edwin Díaz was never right from the moment he put on a Dodgers uniform. He was justifiably viewed as an elite closing option with a proven track record of sustained success joining a superstar-laden roster pursuing their third straight World Series title. The fact that he was a complete non-factor fantasy-wise was one of the more unexpected developments of the entire season.” - George Bissell
“Paying the price for Cal Raleigh this spring after his enormous 2025 campaign always seemed like a bad idea, but there was no reason to think it’d work out that poorly. Raleigh hit .226 and averaged 32 homers and 88 RBI in the two years leading up to his record-breaking season. This year, though, he came in at .182 with 23 homers and 69 RBI. His .664 OPS was 134 points lower than his previous career mark. He was actually at .556 through Aug. 15 before rebounding nicely to hit .250 with 11 homers and a .946 OPS in his final 36 games. Of course, most who selected him were focusing on their fantasy football drafts by that time.” - Matthew Pouliot
Fantasy Baseball’s Best Value Pick (drafted outside the top 150)
“Alec Burleson shockingly led the league in RBI this season. The past four leaders were Kyle Schwarber, Aaron Judge, Matt Olson, and Pete Alonso. Always a fine hitter, a 1 1/2 jump in bat speed helped him find much more power, and a revamped top of the order for the Cardinals put plenty of guys on base to drive in. It was kismet and led to Burleson returning nearly first-round value after being drafted around pick-200.” - James Schiano
“I was a longtime backer of Miguel Vargas, but unfortunately, that pretty much came to a halt this spring. He was adequate but really nothing more than that while getting to play a full season for the White Sox in 2025, and it was hard to see much mixed-league upside in store for 2026. So much for that. Vargas’s average bat speed improved from 70.6 mph to 73.9 mph this year. He overtook nearly half the league in the process, going from being in the 25th percentile to the 70th percentile in the category. He doubled his homer count from 16 to 33 and also went from six steals to 22, turning into a top-20 overall fantasy performer in the process.” - Matthew Pouliot
“There are many answers to this, and I want to give a special shoutout to Jake Bauers, who was not even drafted. However, the answer has to be Jordan Walker. He had an ADP outside of the top 500 in some formats and hit .269 with 29 home runs and 22 steals. Yes, he slowed down at the end of the season, but he was your best pick or waiver add of the year.” - Eric Samulski
OTHERS RECEIVING VOTES: Sal Stewart and Brandon Lowe
Best Fantasy Baseball Waiver Add
“Since we listed Jordan Walker already, this is going to be Bryan Baker. The Rays closer was undrafted in most formats and wound up leading the league with 41 saves. If you drafted any of Jeff Hoffman, Daniel Palencia, Ryan Walker, etc. and wound up picking up Baker on waivers, it could have saved you your season.” - Eric Samulski
“Louis Varland became baseball’s best undrafted closer by a long shot, finishing with 35 saves and a 1.27 ERA. It wasn’t quite Mason Miller, but it wasn’t far off, either. Along with Jacob Latz and Bryan Baker, Varland headlined an absurd free agent closer crop this year.” - Rivers McCown
OTHERS RECEIVING VOTES: Cade Cavalli, Parker Messick, Jordan Walker, Jake McCarthy
Fantasy Baseball Comeback Player of the Year
“Eduardo Rodriguez was a complete afterthought in fantasy drafts in March, with an ADP in NFBC Main Event leagues well after pick 400 overall. He hadn’t seen any relevance from a fantasy perspective since making 26 strong starts for the Tigers during the 2023 campaign. Over the next two seasons, he compiled a miserable 5.02 ERA and 1.53 WHIP over 204 1/3 innings and looked like his career could be over. Instead, he ramped up early and helped Venezuela to win the World Baseball Classic, then went on to go 16-7 with a 2.89 ERA, 1.24 WHIP and a 143/62 K/BB ratio over 189 2/3 innings in 32 starts for a Diamondbacks’ team that lost out on a playoff spot on the final day of the season. Making that type of comeback in his age-33 season was completely unexpected, and yet he still probably won’t get the type of respect that he should heading into the 2027 campaign.” - Dave Shovein
“Here’s an oversimplification: Jake McCarthy was one of the most impactful power and speed combo outfielders in the fantasy landscape just a few months after the Diamondbacks were willing to trade him within their own division coming off a season where he played just 67 games and spent most of the year in Triple-A purgatory. He showed he could be an impactful fantasy contributor with three consecutive 20-steal seasons from 2022-2024, but McCarthy nearly doubled his previous career-high mark in the home run department, finishing with 15 round-trippers, while also posting a career-best .291 batting average. The fact that he went up a level across the board in his Colorado debut, while also notching a career-high 32 steals, was completely unexpected.” - George Bissell
“Nolan Arenado was left for dead by the fantasy community. The 35-year-old third baseman had hit 28 home runs over his last two seasons combined, but managed to hit 30 home runs for the first time since 2022 this year.” - Nick Shlain
“Although his shoulder led to diminished velocity late and cost him a start at the end of the year, Dylan Cease wound up throwing one more inning and allowing 40 fewer earned runs in 29 starts for the Blue Jays this year than he did in 32 starts for the Padres in 2025. He struck out 239 and allowed a total of 11 homers, and his .180 average against was the sixth-lowest mark of the century for starters with 162 innings pitched. The Blue Jays really couldn’t have asked for anything more in year one of his seven-year, $210 million contract.” - Matthew Pouliot
“Multiple years off a major league mound couldn’t stop Cade Cavalli from being a top-20 starting pitcher in earned value this season. When he returned late in 2025, his knuckle-curve carried too significant of a weight in his arsenal, and when it wasn’t right, he struggled to put hitters away. This summer, he found a new feel for a cutter and became more confident in his sweeper as a whiff pitch against right-handed batters. Finding these adjustments on the fly after his collection of injuries and the layoff they caused was wildly impressive, and he’s set to fly up draft boards next spring.” - James Schiano
“The only reason Oneil Cruz doesn’t feel like more of a bounceback is that he missed major time with injuries. He hit .280, stole 30 bases in just 97 games, and hit 20 homers. After barely hitting .200 last year, Cruz became sort of a draft enigma. This season should have him in the top-50 mix for 2027.” - Rivers McCown
Biggest Fantasy Baseball Lesson Learned in 2026
“To be a judicious roster churner on pitchers. I got better at reading the underlying stats and moving on when they looked bad.” - Rivers McCown
“Stop getting overly excited about spring training velocity gainers.” - Matthew Pouliot
“Hitters with elevated strikeout rates (over 30 percent) are getting more opportunities than ever before. An exorbitantly high strikeout rate isn’t automatically disqualifying anymore.” - George Bissell
“I had too much confidence in pitchers who were coming off injury but returned for some of last season. Instead of just being in on guys like Kyle Bradish and Eury Perez because they flashed upside when they returned in 2025, I bought them in 2026 as if they were LOCKED INTO returning to their peak. That was bad business.” - Eric Samulski
Fantasy Baseball Player to Avoid for 2027
“Ronald Acuña is a generational talent just a few years removed from one of the greatest fantasy seasons ever. That’s part of the problem. He’s a massive name, and there will probably be at least one manager in every redraft league paying up for the possibility that he stays remotely healthy and delivers first-round value. He’s the type of outlier that could defy the odds, but he’s played more than 120 games only once in the last six seasons since 2021. Someone will inevitably pay for the upside, but I’m not willing to pay the early-round freight entering his age-29 season with his omnipresent health concerns hanging overhead.” - George Bissell
“Piggybacking off of my lesson from this season, you’re not going to find me taking lots of shares of Justin Steele, Nick Pivetta, or even Garrett Crochet if we’re still pricing him as a top 5-8 starting pitcher.” - Eric Samulski
“Michael King was effectively the Padres’ ace this season, staying healthy for 32 starts while posting a 3.21 ERA. He gets to pitch in San Diego again in 2027, so it’s a great situation, but his underlying numbers provide reasons for caution. King’s strikeout rate collapsed to 21 percent this year, down from 24.7 percent in 2025 and 27.7 percent in 2024. 59 pitchers with at least 120 innings surpassed him in strikeout rate. King also posted his highest walk rate since moving into the starting rotation. Put it all together, and you can see why his xERA was 4.42 for the year. It’s great that he stayed healthy, but that’s no sure thing going forward, either. King looks like an easy fade if there’s an aggressive ADP in 2027.” - D.J. Short
“Pitchers in the first two rounds; you simply can’t make up the production if you lose them.” - Rivers McCown
Fantasy Baseball Player to Target for 2027
“Bryce Eldridge’s season came to an unfortunate end due to concussion symptoms, but his strong finish puts him on the radar for a full-fledged breakout in 2027. The 21-year-old rebounded from a midseason slump by slashing .330/.423/.541 with five home runs and 28 RBI over his final 29 games. For the season as a whole, he struck out 26.6 percent of the time. Fantasy managers can live with that moving forward. Eldridge also showed plenty of patience, increasing his appeal in OBP leagues. Most encouraging is the quality of contact, as Eldridge was in the 96th percentile in hard-hit percentage and the 95th percentile in average exit velocity. Oracle Park isn’t an ideal place for offense, so that will impact his counting stats, but Eldridge could be a 30-homer candidate if he adds more loft next year.” - D.J. Short
“Healthy Konnor Griffin and second-year Kevin McGonigle will feed families.” - Rivers McCown
“I wouldn’t be surprised if Carter Jensen is next year’s Drake Baldwin, but the real answer for me is Henry Bolte. He changed his approach in the minors, making more contact and lifting the ball more. It took a while for that change to carry over when he got promoted, but it started to. He plays in a great home park. Has elite raw tools and an emerging approach. He’ll be a key target of mine.” - Eric Samulski

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team. Brewers: Lack of Power The Brewers were baseball’s best team
item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.
Follow rumorsandrants

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

item.content:encoded:
We’ve already got goosebumps.
For the seventh time in MLB history, the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox are meeting in the playoffs.
This time around, the Bronx Bombers and BoSox will go toe-to-toe in the Wild Card round in a best-of-three series that determines who gets to take on the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The trio of games will all take place at the Bronx’s Yankee Stadium. They’re slated go down:
Game 1
Tuesday, Sept. 29
8 p.m.
Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA) vs. Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA)
Game 2
Wednesday, Sept. 30
8 p.m.
Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA) vs. Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA)
Game 3
Thursday, Oct. 1
8 p.m.
Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA) vs. Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA)
If you’d like to be there, the lowest price we could find on tickets for any one games was $129 including fees on Vivid Seats.
Prices start at $131 and $135 including fees for the other two contests.
Over the course of the regular season, New York and Boston met 13 times; the Yankees took seven of those showdowns. In their final battle, the Yankees walloped the Sox 16-1 on Aug. 30. Heliot Ramos, Paul Goldschmidt, José Caballero and Austin Wells all homered for the Bombers that afternoon.
Both teams went 5-5 in their last ten games of the regular season.
As for this series, manager Aaron Boone left Aaron Judge off the Wild Card round roster but activated Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham after both have been inactive for months and weeks at a time, respectively.
“[I’m] real confident if we play our game and pitch like we’re capable of, we got a chance to move on,” Boone said. “We got to play our best starting Tuesday.”
See you there, Bleacher Creatures.

item.title: [Over the Monster] Chad Tracy could swing the series between the Red Sox and Yankees
item.dc:creator: Keagan Stiefel
item.description: Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series. The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of
item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees y Red Sox revelan a sus pitchers abridores para la Serie de Comodines
Yankees y Red Sox se enfrentan por segundo año consecutivo al comenzar la postemporada de la MLB.
Velando armas para una nueva batalla en la que ambos se juegan la temporada, Yankees y Red Sox anunciaron a sus pitchers abridores con los que se enfrentarán a partir de este martes en una nueva Serie de Comodines para abrir los Playoffs 2026 en las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB).
Abridores para la serie Yankees vs. Red Sox
- Juego 1: Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03) vs. Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95)
- Juego 2: Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72) vs. Max Fried (5-5, 2.80)
- Juego 3: Ranger Suárez (8-5, 3.22) vs. Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61)
Juego 1: Cam Schlittler vs. Payton Tolle
Los Yankees apostaron todo al alinear a Cam Schlittler, el principal contendiente para competir por el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, para el Juego 1. Schlittler, quien creció a los alrededores de Boston siendo un aficionado de los Red Sox, fue el verdugo del equipo de su infancia el año anterior cuando tiró 8.0 entradas de 12 ponches para ganar el decisivo Juego 3.
Esta temporada, Schlittler tuvo efectividad de 0.74 pues apenas recibió dos carreras limpias a lo largo de 24.1 entradas ante los Red Sox este año, aunque admitió 4 carreras inmerecidas el 25 de junio.
Su antagonista será Payton Tolle, el novato zurdo que tomará por asalto la lomita del Yankee Stadium. Con 23 años y 332 días de edad, Tolle será el tercer pitcher más joven en abrir una serie de postemporada para los Red Sox. En dos actuaciones ante los Yankees, Payton tuvo marca de 1-0 con efectividad de 0.69 y 18 ponches, a cambio de solo tres pasaportes.
Juego 2: Max Fried vs Sonny Gray
Sonny Gray tomará la pelota para el Juego 2 por los Red Sox. El as en la rotación en la ausencia de Garrett Crochet tuvo un año increíble y busca trasladar ese éxito a la postemporada ante unos Yankees a los que dominó en dos aperturas: la primera en 6.1 entradas de 3 carreras, mientras que en la segunda tiró una joya de 7.1 entradas en un solo hit y 9 ponches.
Los Yankees optaron por Max Fried en el Juego 2, otro lanzador que fue dominante ante los Red Sox la postemporada anterior tirando 6.1 entradas en blanco pese a admitir 4 hits y regalar 3 bases por bolas; ponchó a 6 rivales. Desde entonces, Fried acumula 18.0 entradas de una sola carrera y 19 ponches ante los acérrimos rivales de los Bombarderos del Bronx.
Juego 3: Gerrit Cole vs. Ranger Suárez
En caso de un decisivo Juego 3, los Yankees saltarán al terreno con Gerrit Cole, el lanzador que históricamente ha sufrido ante los Red Sox. Cole no le ha ganado un juego a Boston desde el 17 de julio de 2022 y su efectividad de por vida ante los patirrojos es de 5.30, la segunda más alta que tiene ante cualquier rival, solo debajo de los Mets (7.28).
Ranger Suárez cerró fuerte para ganarse la confianza y ser el abridor de los Red Sox para el Juego 3 de esta Serie de Comodines. Durante el último mes de temporada en su año de debut con los Red Sox, el venezolano Suárez cerró con marca de 3-1 y efectividad de 1.09 en septiembre; sin embargo, ante los Yankees fue sumamente contrastante al admitir 10 carreras en 10.0 entradas de dos juegos que perdió y 6.1 entradas de una carrera en un juego sin decisión.

item.title: [The Boston Globe] If the Red Sox can get past the Yankees, the Chad Tracy story goes from a good one to a great one - The Boston Globe
item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Because there are odds on everything these days, Will Venable is the favorite to be the American League Manager of the Year, with Kevin Cash the second choice.
Venable led the White Sox to the postseason after losing 102 games last season. He deserves all the plaudits.
But what about Chad Tracy?
Tracy was called away from managing a game with Triple-A Worcester on April 25 and told that Alex Cora was getting fired and he would manage the Red Sox the next day in Baltimore. It was the baseball equivalent of getting thrown out of a plane without a parachute.
After making the announcement, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said he couldn’t guarantee Tracy would finish the season as manager.
Five months later, the Sox are in the playoffs after a remarkable turnaround, and Tracy is the only rookie manager whose team is still playing.
It’s a good story, complete with Tracy agreeing to a three-year contract last week. But in two or three more days, it could be a great story.
The Sox have not won a postseason series since 2021. If they fall to the Yankees again this season, nothing will have changed. But if they beat their rivals and advance to the Division Series, it’s a major step forward for this largely unaccomplished group of players.
“It’s drastically different,” Tracy said Monday when asked to compare becoming manager to managing in his first postseason game. “It’s the playoffs. There’s more riding on it.”
Tracy said he gave himself some grace that first day in Baltimore. There was so much to learn, so much to do. He knew he wouldn’t be fully prepared. Plus, several of the players were still furious that Cora had been fired after only 27 games.
“It was go out and be with the guys and give them a hug and enjoy being with them and let the game go be what it is,” Tracy said.
Tracy leaned on his father for advice throughout the season. Jim Tracy managed 1736 major league games from 2001-12 for three teams and had plenty of good answers. But he was 2-6 in postseason games, losing first-round series with the 2004 Dodgers and 2009 Rockies.
As a manager’s son, Tracy suffered those losses, too.
“This is the playoffs. We’re at the point in the season for the teams that are remaining where it’s a three-game series. You’ve got to win the series or you go home,” he said. “There’s more riding on it.”
For 162 games, managers are forced to think about the next day, the next series, and the next set of roster moves. Bruised egos get massaged, and you move on. Even great teams lose dozens of games. That’s baseball.
Not in the playoffs. Everything goes into winning that day, and feelings are disregarded. Just win.
“When you get to this part of the year, it’s all hands on deck. I think everybody’s pretty aware in the playoffs it’s high intent and winning moments and being aggressive and all those things,” Tracy said.
“All of our guys that have been around understand that. They’re going to play their butts off, and we’re going to manage and try to do whatever we can to win the game.”
That would be the case if the Sox were playing the Astros. But it’s magnified by the power of 100 when it’s the Yankees.
The Sox made history against the Yankees with their comeback in the 2004 American League Championship Series. They brushed past the Bombers in the division round en route to the 2018 championship. Fenway Park was practically shaking during the 2021 Wild Card game.
“I don’t like to give that way more attention than it needs. But I won’t shy away from it,” Tracy said. “Two historic franchises, big rivalry, well aware of that.”
Tracy has already made one bold move, selecting Payton Tolle as his Game 1 starter instead of the more seasoned Sonny Gray. More big decisions are coming.
There’s no grace now.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.description: Red Sox Video A whopping 503 days. That was the time frame between Tanner Houck’s last start in the major leagues and his start in game 162 of this season. The right-hander missed significant time after an attempted rehab assignment in 2025 ultimately led to Tommy John surgery back in August of 2025. item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Video
A whopping 503 days. That was the time frame between Tanner Houck’s last start in the major leagues and his start in game 162 of this season. The right-hander missed significant time after an attempted rehab assignment in 2025 ultimately led to Tommy John surgery back in August of 2025.
Despite the timeline for Tommy John surgery typically taking close to a full season before a pitcher can begin throwing seriously in a rehab assignment, Houck had a plan in place for being back on a mound and throwing meaningful innings by the end of September of this season. To get there, he worked extremely hard, getting into rehab assignments with Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester before their respective seasons concluded.
And after just over 12 months of rehab and recovery, Houck kept to his word. The right-hander was given the start for the Boston Red Sox's final game before the playoffs and showed flashes of his past dominance. Tossing three innings, Houck took the loss as he allowed three runs (all of them on two Alex Bregman home runs) on four hits while not walking a batter and getting one strikeout. In the outing, he tossed exactly 50 pitches, roughly what he threw during his rehab appearances.
Despite the positive stat line for a pitcher making his first start in over a year and a half, there were some concerns for Houck, namely that his velocity was down from even 2025, a sign that the right-hander is still working on ramping back up. His sinker, which he threw 15 times yesterday, averaged just 92.4 mph compared to its 94.5 mph from the 2025 season. Even his four-seam fastball saw a decline of almost two mph as it averaged 93.3 mph compared to 95 mph in 2025. The right-hander also struggled to miss bats, getting just one whiff out of 24 swings by the Chicago Cubs.
Despite that, he still showcased some positives that could help his chance of being on the playoff roster. Despite giving up a home run early in the game to Bregman, Houck didn’t fall apart. Instead, the right-hander followed that up by retiring seven of the next eight batters he faced, giving the offense a chance to get back into the game. That string of retired batters was then broken up with one out in the third inning as Bregman took a sweeper that caught too much of the plate and deposited it into left field to put the Cubs back ahead 3-2. Houck then finished his outing by getting the next two batters out before giving way to the bullpen for the fourth inning.
Despite taking the loss in what would eventually be a 6-2 Cubs win, Houck was around where he should be in his return from injury. Not completely dominant, but good enough to give the team a chance to win with his outing. Outside of his two mistakes to Bregman, Houck only allowed two hits, both of them singles. In a relief role, that would be a welcomed performance if he can limit the long balls, especially with the Red Sox having lost Tyron Guerrero right before the playoffs.
While it might not seem likely for Houck to make the playoff roster, the sudden loss of Guerrero opens a path for the right-hander. While his velocity is nothing in comparison to the flamethrower, Houck has experience out of the bullpen as he served as closer briefly in 2022, earning eight saves before an injury ended his season. That’s not even talking about how in the 2021 playoffs he came out of the bullpen five times. Despite the struggles he had that season, the experience would be appreciated for a bullpen that, outside of Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock, has very minimal playoff experience.
He may not look like a high-leverage reliever at the moment, but he could help shorten the game and bridge the gap to the back-end of the bullpen. As a bulk reliever, he could be relied upon to take the ball from one of the starting pitchers and hand it to an arm like Whitlock or even Erik Miller who will be asked to step up with the loss of Guerrero. In his lone outing this year, Houck surrendered six hard hit balls, though two of them were the home runs he surrendered. Of the remaining four, only one (the first hit he allowed all game) turned into a hit. With the defense Boston has lined up behind him, Houck could be able to allow a hard hit ball here or there and still mitigate the damage.
The biggest concern, however, is the velocity, which will limit his ability to get swings and misses. Everyone knows the age-old thought that velocity plays in the postseason—just look back at the 2018 Red Sox roster that had a bullpen containing Joe Kelly, Matt Barnes and Heath Hembree. With Houck being in the low to mid-90s at the moment, the team could decide to turn their attention to a harder thrower.
Whatever decision the Red Sox make with Houck, it’s a positive sign that he stepped back onto a major-league mound as quickly as he did. His future is a lot less murky with his return officially in the books.

item.content:encoded:
With the MLB playoffs starting this week, the New York Mets will be watching from afar.
After a disappointing 2026 season, all eyes will be on the Mets this offseason to turn things around.
Among the list of things the Mets could add, a depth starter (or any starters, for that matter) is likely at the top of the list.
Recently, FanSided.com's Jake Elman linked the Mets to free agent starter Shane Bieber, who has spent the last two seasons with the Toronto Blue Jays.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Receive Clarity on Phillies' Pitching Plans Ahead of Wild Card Series
Should the Mets Pursue Former Cy Young Winner Shane Bieber?
He's sort of long removed from winning the AL Cy Young, but Shane Bieber was once one of the best starters in all of MLB.
While the free agency period doesn't open up until the end of the current season (so, November), teams like the Mets are thinking about what big splashes they can make.
Bieber suffered a season-ending injury in 2026, and has pitched just 95.1 innings over the last two seasons.
Here is what Elman had to say about the Mets potentially being in on Shane Bieber:
"That said, the Mets must add another veteran starter this offseason. Peralta and Clay Holmes are obviously gone, and Kodai Senga is likely facing a trade or a permanent move to the bullpen."
It's an interesting name to watch for, but my intuition would lead me to believe David Stearns and company may want to target a more durable, effective starter if they are going to bring out the Brink's truck.
More MLB on Heavy: Chicago Cubs Quietly Demote Player Before Padres Playoff Series
